jobs.title: PhD student in Limnology: Modelling phytoplankton succession in lakes
jobs.department: Uppsala University, Department of Ecology and Genetics
jobs.description_html:
Are you interested in exploring the driving processes behind phytoplankton succession in lakes and assessing how phytoplankton will respond to future environmental changes? Are you looking for an employer, who invests in sustainable career development and offers supportive working conditions? We welcome you to apply for a PhD student position at Uppsala University, which will be placed at the Department of Ecology and Genetics within the Limnology program.

The Limnology program is an internationally renowned working environment with staff and students from all over the world. The program engages in research and education on the biogeochemistry and ecology of inland waters, spanning from microscopic to global scale. The program actively promotes a collegial and inclusive research culture through regular social activities, encouraging well-being, creativity, and professional growth.

Project Description
Phytoplankton form an important foundation of lake food webs and their community composition changes markedly throughout the year in response to physical and chemical changes as well as predation pressures. These changes are in turn moderated by different functional traits between groups, which determine how they respond to environmental conditions. Using models, we can study how environmental changes (such as climate warming, eutrophication, and extreme weather events) influence successional patterns in phytoplankton and identify conditions that create windows of opportunity for specific functional groups. We can then use these models to assess potential future changes. We are seeking a highly-motivated PhD student who is keen to use process-based biogeochemical models to investigate these dynamics. The outcomes of this work will improve our ability to forecast changes in phytoplankton communities, with direct application to lake ecosystem functioning and drinking water provisioning. The position is based at Uppsala University’s Department of Ecology and Genetics, within the Limnology program.

Duties
Your duties will have a strong focus on data handling and process-based, dynamical modelling, but also include teaching, course work, and collaborating in research teams.

Requirements
To meet the entry requirements for doctoral studies, you must

  • hold a Master’s (second-cycle) degree in limnology, aquatic ecology, environmental sciences, geoscience, biology, environmental engineering or other relevant subjects at the time of employment, or
  • have completed at least 240 credits in higher education, with at least 60 credits at Master’s level including an independent project worth at least 15 credits, or
  • have acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way.

Candidates who have not yet completed their degree but are expected to meet the degree requirements before the start date are encouraged to apply.

This work lies in the intersection of physics, biogeochemistry, and ecology, and has a strong numerical emphasis. Eligible candidates need to demonstrate skills with advanced numerical approaches (e.g. modelling, statistics, or large-scale data analysis). Some programming experience (for example in R or Python) is required. Candidates must be able to express themselves to a very high degree in spoken as well as written English. In the evaluation of candidates, particular emphasis will be put on personal qualities such as independence, strong motivation and teamwork skills.

Additional qualifications
A range of additional qualifications is desired, such as:

  • Previous experience with lake or other process-based models
  • Familiarity with lake processes such as stratification and aquatic biogeochemical cycles
  • A good understanding of phytoplankton ecology

Rules governing PhD students are set out in the Higher Education Ordinance chapter 5, §§ 1-7 and in Uppsala University's rules and guidelines.

jobs.title: Doktorand i resilienta elkraftsystem
jobs.description_html:
Elektrifiering och digitalisering tillhör framtidens största områden för omställning till hållbara samhällen. Institutionen för elektroteknik bedriver framgångsrik forskning och utbildning inom dessa områden – däribland förnybara energikällor och elfordon, industriell IoT, 6G kommunikation och trådlösa sensornät men även forskning och utbildning inom Life Science, hälsoteknik, smarta elektroniska sensorer och medicinska system. Institutionen för elektroteknik är en internationell miljö med ca 170 medarbetare som bidrar till viktiga tekniska energi- och hälsolösningar vid Ångströmlaboratoriet.

Vi söker nu en Doktorand i resilienta elkraftsystem.

Kom och jobba med oss!
Tjänsten är placerad vid avdelningen för elektricitetslära inom institutionen för elektroteknik. Här hittar du en trevlig arbetsmiljö med ett aktivt doktorandnätverk och en mängd experimentella projekt. Avdelningen samarbetar med svenska företag – både offentliga och privata – samt andra intressenter inom de olika forskningsområdena. Vi ser fram emot din ansökan. Var med och bygg framtiden med oss!

Läs mer om våra förmåner och hur det är att jobba inom Uppsala.

Projektbeskrivning

Elkraftsystemets betydelse för samhällets funktion ställer ökade krav på robusthet, återhämtningsförmåga och effektiv drift, särskilt i ljuset av ett försämrat säkerhetsläge, ökad elektrifiering och ett högre nyttjande av befintliga transmissions- och distributionsnät av el. Inom dessa doktorandprojekt kommer avancerad modellering, systemsimuleringar och scenarioanalyser att användas för att utveckla metoder som stärker elkraftsystemets resiliens vid kris, krig och andra ansträngda driftförhållanden.

Projekten omfattar såväl optimerad drift av elkraftsystemet efter omfattande störningar som utveckling av nya nyckeltal, prognosmetoder och styrstrategier för att mäta, analysera och förbättra elkraftsystemets förmåga att upprätthålla leveransen av el under ansträngda förhållanden. Arbetet sker i nära samverkan med energibranschen och omfattar tillämpningar i simuleringsverktyg. Projekten genomförs inom kompetenscentret RESILIENT, ett nationellt forskningscentrum som samlar akademi, industri och samhällsaktörer för att utveckla framtidens resilienta och hållbara energisystem genom nära samverkan mellan forskning och tillämning.

Arbetsuppgifter

  • Bedriva forskning inom resilienta elkraftsystem med fokus på elsystemets funktion, drift och återgång under kris-, krigs- och andra ansträngda driftförhållanden.
  • Utveckla metoder, modeller och beslutsstöd för att stärka elkraftsystemets robusthet, resiliens och återhämtningsförmåga.
  • Genomföra teoretiska studier i kombination med modellutveckling, systemsimuleringar och scenarioanalyser för att validera forskningsresultat.
  • Använda och vidareutveckla modeller i simuleringsverktyg såsom PowerFactory, PowerWorld och PSS®E eller motsvarande.
  • Analysera frågor kopplade till systemdrift, systemåterhämtning, resiliensmått, prognoser och styrstrategier för framtidens elkraftsystem.
  • Publicera forskningsresultat i vetenskapliga tidskrifter och presentera resultaten vid nationella och internationella konferenser.
  • Samverka med industri, myndigheter och andra forskningsaktörer inom kompetenscentret RESILIENT.

Undervisning och övrig institutionstjänstgöring kan komma att ingå i arbetsuppgifterna, dock max 20% av arbetstiden.

Kvalifikationskrav

Behörig till utbildning på forskarnivå är den som har

  • avlagt examen på avancerad nivå så som civilingenjörsexamen inom energisystem, elektroteknik, system i teknik och samhälle eller motsvarande, eller
  • fullgjort minst 240 högskolepoäng varav minst 60 högskolepoäng på avancerad nivå inklusive ett självständigt arbete om minst 15 högskolepoäng, eller
  • på något annat sätt förvärvat i huvudsak motsvarande kunskaper.
  • Säkerhetsprövning ska kunna genomföras för att kunna samarbeta med säkerhetsklassade svenska myndigheter.
  • Du behöver vara målmedveten, strukturerad och analytisk samt ha ett öga för problemlösning och tycka om att jobba mot mål.

Vi lägger stor vikt vid personliga egenskaper såsom god samarbets- och kommunikationsförmåga samt förmåga att arbeta självständigt.

Kandidaten ska ha god/ mycket god förmåga att uttrycka sig på engelska och svenska, både i tal och skrift.

Meriterande

  • Kunskap inom statisk och dynamisk analys av elkraftsystem.
  • Helhetsperspektiv och förståelse för system och hur olika system sammanlänkas.

Om anställningen

Tidsbegränsad anställning i 48 månader, enligt HF 5 kap § 7. Omfattningen är heltid. Tillträde 2027-01-01, eller enligt överenskommelse. Placeringsort Uppsala.

Bestämmelser för doktorander återfinns i Högskoleförordningen 5 kap §§ 1-7 samt i universitetets regler och riktlinjer.

Upplysningar om anställningen lämnas av
Professor Robert Eriksson, robert.eriksson@uu.se.

Instruktioner för ansökan
Ansökan ska innehålla 1) ett brev som beskriver dig själv, dina forskningsintressen och varför du vill doktorera, 2) ditt CV, 3) en kort beskrivning av din utbildning, 4) en kopia av din masterexamen och dina kursbetyg samt en kopia av din masteruppsats 5) eventuellt andra handlingar som du önskar åberopa, 6) namn och kontaktuppgifter till referenspersoner (e-postadress och telefonnummer), och 7) eventuella publikationer. Ansökan bör skrivas på svenska.

Välkommen med din ansökan senast den 12 november 2026. UFV-PA 2026/2920.

jobs.title: PhD student position in Bioinformatics/Evolutionary Microbiology
jobs.department: Uppsala University, Department of Medical Biochemistry and Microbiology
jobs.description_html:
The Department of Medical Biochemistry and Microbiology (IMBIM) at Uppsala University provides a broad international environment for research and teaching. Research at IMBIM spans biochemistry, molecular and cell biology, structural biology, tumour biology, comparative genetics, functional genomics, immunology, bacteriology and virology. The research has a basic-science orientation, with strong relevance to mechanisms of health and disease in both animals and humans. More info: Research – Department of Medical Biochemistry and Microbiology – Uppsala University

We are looking for a highly motivated PhD student to join the project “A two-billion-year history of infections: evolution of host-adaptation in early Gammaproteobacteria”, funded by the Swedish Research Council and led by Lionel Guy. The PhD student will be located at the Biomedical Centre, Uppsala, Sweden.

Project description

The ability to feed on other organisms through phagocytosis is a crucial step in the evolution of eukaryotes, a prerequisite for food webs, multicellularity and probably the acquisition of mitochondria. It also paved the way for intracellular parasitism, as some bacteria avoided digestion by their hosts and multiplied in the nutrient-rich cytoplasm.

Here, we focus on the Deep-branching Intracellular Gammaproteobacteria (DIG), a large group of related bacteria (e.g. Legionella and Francisella) with a wide variety of host-adaptation strategies. We hypothesize that the last common ancestor of DIG appeared during eukaryogenesis, 2 billion years ago, and was among the first bacteria to infect eukaryotes.

In this project, the PhD student will gather a solid set of DIG genomes, including isolates belonging to 30 novel species of Legionella, reconstruct their evolutionary history, assess their metabolic potential, and identify their host-adaptation genes. They will screen genomes for horizontal gene transfers from early eukaryotes or Asgard archaea and specifically analyse the evolution of the Legionella genus.

A better understanding of the relationships between the first eukaryotes and their early invaders will shed light on eukaryogenesis, and particularly on the role of phagocytosis.

Required Qualifications

To meet the entry requirements for doctoral studies, you must

  • hold a Master’s (second-cycle) degree in bioinformatics, molecular biology, microbiology, microbial ecology or a similar field or
  • have completed at least 240 credits in higher education, with at least 60 credits at Master’s level including an independent project worth at least 15 credits, or
  • have acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way.

The degree should be completed, or expected to be completed, before March 2027.

  • Documented coding skills in Python or R
  • Experience in using and/or developing methods in metagenomics and molecular evolution
  • Background understanding of, and interest in, microbial evolution
  • Proficiency in spoken and written English
  • Ability to plan, carry out and complete research projects independently
  • Creativity and good teamwork skills

 Desirable qualifications

  • Experience of building pipelines for high-performance computing (HPC) clusters
  • Competence in handling large datasets
  • Experience with DNA extraction and sequencing library preparation 

The selection is based on the following criteria: completion of the above qualifications, grades in relevant courses, the relevance of those courses to the research programme, and previous experience of work and research in the wider area of the project described above. An overall assessment of the applicant will be made in order to employ the best possible candidate, who can succeed in the doctoral studies and contribute to a positive development of the research programme. Emphasis will be placed on personal qualities, including analytical ability, accuracy, flexibility and collaborative skills.

Rules governing PhD students are set out in the Higher Education Ordinance chapter 5, §§ 1-7 and in Uppsala University's rules and guidelines.

The employment is a temporary position according to the Higher Education Ordinance chapter 5 § 7. Scope of employment 100 %. Starting date as soon as possible or as agreed. Placement: Uppsala

The Department of Informatics and Media has a broad research profile grounded in contemporary research fields, including information systems, interaction design, and media and communication. Within the discipline of Media and Communication Studies, research focuses on various forms of communication and media in both global and local contexts. The work within the research environment is connected through a deeply interdisciplinary and critical approach, employing both qualitative and quantitative methods. We study media and communication as fundamental to understanding contemporary social change as well as to defining the conditions and challenges of human coexistence.

jobs.title: PhD student in hydrology - wildfires effect on Arctic water cycle

jobs.description_html:
PhD student in hydrology with a focus on wildfires effect on Arctic water cycle

Are you interested in working on cutting-edge research in hydrology, with the support of competent and friendly colleagues in an international environment? Are you looking for an employer that invests in sustainable employeeship and offers safe, favourable working conditions? We welcome you to apply for a PhD position at Uppsala University.

The Department of Earth Sciences is Sweden´s most comprehensive academic environment for research and education in geoscience. It offers a broad range of expertise that can contribute to solving important societal issues.

Earth is a dynamic and constantly changing planet. To understand how this planet works, our researchers seek answers in the field, through laboratory experiments and advanced models. Our research and education cover a wide range of disciplines, including rocks and minerals, weather and climate, the evolution of life, natural disasters, wind power and energy, environmental and water engineering, and sustainable development.

Our research combines natural sciences and technology with social sciences and is often interdisciplinary. More than 300 people from over 30 countries work at the department, both in Uppsala and at Campus Gotland.

Our six research divisions:

• Geophysics • Air, Water and Landscape Science • Mineralogy, Petrology and Tectonics • Natural Resources and Sustainable Development • Palaeobiology • Wind Energy For more information see: www.uu.se/earthsciences

The successful candidate will be enrolled in the Air, Water and Landscape Science programme (LUVAL). The position includes close collaboration with researchers at Uppsala University, SMHI and SLU, offering opportunities for interdisciplinary research, international networking, and engagement with societally relevant climate and environmental challenges.

Project description

The Arctic is rapidly warming, leading to changes in freshwater systems through melting glaciers, thawing permafrost, and shifting hydrological regimes. Understanding how these changes affect runoff generation, evapotranspiration, river discharge, and freshwater availability is a key challenge for Arctic hydrology. At the same time, wildfires activity is increasing across large parts of the Arctic, creating an additional disturbance that can alter vegetation, soils, permafrost conditions, and water flow paths.

This PhD project will investigate how climate change and increasing wildfire activity are reshaping the Arctic water cycle. By combining Earth Observation (EO) satellite data with large-scale hydrological modelling, the doctoral student will study the impact of various wildfire-related landscape changes on hydrological processes in Arctic drainage basins. The project will generate new knowledge regarding the drivers and controls of hydrological changes in the Arctic and contribute to an improved understanding and better predictive models for future freshwater resources in northern regions.

Duties
The doctoral work consists of investigating how climate change and increasing wildfire activity affect hydrological processes across the Arctic. Duties include analysis of Earth Observation and hydrological data, hydrological modelling, and statistical analyses, as well as writing scientific articles. The PhD student will work with hydrologists from Uppsala University, SMHI and SLU, and is expected to contribute to the overall progress of the project.

The doctoral education comprises four years of full-time studies, including courses and independent research. The applicant will also have the opportunity to participate in teaching, supervision, and other departmental duties, which may extend the employment by up to a maximum of 20%.

Requirements

To meet the entry requirements for doctoral studies, you must

  • hold a Master’s (second-cycle) degree in Hydrology, Physical Geography, Geosciences, Environmental Sciences, Environmental engineering or another relevant subject,
  • have completed at least 240 credits in higher education, with at least 60 credits at Master’s level including an independent project worth at least 15 credits, or
  • have acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way.

Applicants must fulfill the above requirements before the admission can be started. You must also have good oral and written proficiency in English, strong quantitative and analytical skills, and experience in processing and analysing environmental or geospatial data. The position requires basic programming skills for scientific data analysis, the ability to work both independently and as part of a team, and a strong interest in hydrology and environmental change. Great emphasis will be placed on personal qualities such as analytical ability, initiative, creativity, flexibility and problem-solving skills.

Additional qualifications

Experience with hydrological modelling, remote sensing, GIS, and programming (e.g., Python or R) is considered an advantage. Knowledge of Arctic environments, cold-region hydrology, or wildfire impacts on ecosystems and water resources is meritorious.

Rules governing PhD students are set out in the Higher Education Ordinance chapter 5, §§ 1-7 and in Uppsala University´s rules and guidelines.

Are you interested in working with experimental nuclear physics, with the support of competent and friendly colleagues in an international environment? Are you looking for an employer that invests in sustainable employeeship and offers safe, favourable working conditions? We welcome you to apply for a PhD position at Uppsala University.

The research conducted at the Department of Physics and Astronomy encompasses a wide range of physics topics, distributed over nine divisions. The department is located in the Ångström laboratory and employs nearly 400 people, 100 of whom are doctoral students. It offers a broad physics curriculum to undergraduate and graduate students, participation in nationally and internationally leading projects for researchers, and opportunities for partnership with industry and various outreach activities. Read more on www.uu.se/physics.

The Department of Physics and Astronomy, Division of Applied Nuclear Physics, at Uppsala University conducts research and education in applied nuclear physics. Its activities aim to deepen our understanding of the properties of atomic nuclei and apply this knowledge in areas such as energy and materials research.

The successful candidate will join a research group with a strong international profile and active collaborations at leading research facilities, including GANIL (France), JRC-Geel (Belgium), CERN n_TOF (Switzerland), GSI (Germany), and JYFL (Finland). The group’s research focuses on advancing our understanding of nuclear-reaction dynamics, with particular emphasis on neutron-induced reactions.

Through dedicated experiments, the research group produces high-precision nuclear data that extend beyond current experimental limits. These results contribute to the development of state-of-the-art nuclear-reaction models and evaluated nuclear-data libraries, supporting safe, reliable, and competitive technologies for both existing and future nuclear-energy systems, as well as societal applications in cancer treatment, radiation-tolerant microelectronics, and other radiation-based technologies.

Duties
The doctoral project will investigate the competition between different reaction mechanisms governing light-ion emission in neutron-induced reactions over a broad range of neutron energies. Particular attention will be given to the transition from compound-nucleus-dominated behaviour to pre-equilibrium and direct-reaction dynamics. The measurements will produce new high-precision nuclear data, including total production cross-sections and the energy and angular distributions of emitted light ions as functions of neutron energy. These results will advance the understanding and modelling of nuclear reactions and contribute to improving evaluated nuclear-data libraries.

The project also has important applications for structural materials used in nuclear installations and other irradiation environments. In future fusion devices and fast reactors, light-ion emission can lead to gas production and bubble formation, potentially affecting the mechanical properties and service life of structural materials.

As a doctoral student, you will conduct a substantial part of your experimental research at GANIL in Caen, France, one of the group’s principal international partner facilities. The project will focus on experiments at the Neutrons for Science facility, NFS, using its white-neutron beam to investigate light-ion emission in neutron-induced reactions.

A central part of your work will involve the Medley experimental setup, which was originally developed by the research group and is now permanently installed at GANIL. You will contribute to the simulation, preparation, optimisation, and further development of the experimental setup and its associated systems. You will also take an active role in preparing and carrying out measurement campaigns at GANIL, working closely with researchers and technical specialists at NFS.

Following the experiments, you will be responsible for analysing the collected data and interpreting the results using nuclear-reaction codes such as TALYS. By comparing the experimental findings with model calculations, you will assess the ability of current models to describe light-ion emission, particularly during the pre-equilibrium stage of the reaction. The results are expected to support the further development and validation of nuclear-reaction models.

The position requires extended research visits to GANIL and may include visits to other international facilities. You will communicate your research through scientific publications and presentations at national and international conferences.

Requirements
To meet the entry requirements for doctoral studies, you must

  • hold a Master’s (second-cycle) degree in physics, engineering physics, nuclear engineering, applied physics, or another area relevant to the project, or
  • have completed at least 240 credits in higher education, with at least 60 credits at Master’s level including an independent project worth at least 15 credits, or
  • have acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way.


The position also requires:

  • good knowledge of physics, including nuclear physics and radiation detection,
  • some programming experience, for example in Python, C++, and an interest in further developing these skills,
  • the ability to work independently and in a structured manner;
  • good collaboration skills,
  • good oral and written communication skills in English,
  • availability and willingness to undertake research visits abroad, including extended stays and shorter trips, primarily to GANIL, and to attend scientific conferences.

 

Additional qualifications

Experience in one or more of the following areas is considered a merit:

  • data analysis using ROOT,
  • particle-transport simulations using Monte Carlo codes such as Geant4, FLUKA, or OpenMC,
  • nuclear-reaction calculations using codes such as TALYS,
  • practical experience with radiation detectors, detector electronics, or data-acquisition systems,
  • theoretical modelling in nuclear physics,
  • scientific computing involving large datasets from simulations or measurements, including the use of high-performance computing resources.

Rules governing PhD students are set out in the Higher Education Ordinance chapter 5, §§ 1-7 and in Uppsala University's rules and guidelines.

jobs.title: PhD student in electrical engineering with focus on power system adequacy
jobs.department: Uppsala University, Department of Electrical Engineering
jobs.description_html:
Electrification and digitalisation are among the major areas for the future transition to sustainable societies. The Department of Electrical Engineering conducts successful research and education in these areas - including renewable energy sources, electric vehicles, industrial IoT, 6G communication, and wireless sensor networks, as well as research and education in Life Science, health technology, smart electronic sensors, and medical systems. The Department of Electrical Engineering is an international environment with around 160 employees who contribute to important technological energy and health at the Ångström Laboratory.

We are now looking for a PhD student in electrical engineering with focus on power system adequacy.

Come and join us!
The position is placed at the Division of Electricity within the Department of Electrical Engineering. Here you will find a welcoming working environment with an active doctoral student network and a variety of experimental projects. The division collaborates with Swedish companies – both public and private – as well as other stakeholders within the various research areas. We look forward to receiving your application. Join us in building the future!

Read more about our benefits and what it is like to work at Uppsala University

Project description
Large dependencies of reliable power production from offshore renewable energy systems (RES) is expected in the next decades, in particular onshore and offshore wind and solar PV. Large changes are also seen in energy and electricity supply from non-renewable sources, due to, e.g., recent national policy changes around nuclear power or imported gas and oil. The demand side is transforming as well, driven by changes such as the electrification of transportation and other sectors, and increased use of heat pumps or air conditioning.

Finally, climate change is implying changes in weather, with heat waves and other weather extremes affecting society and the energy system. There are large knowledge gaps regarding the power production reliability under severe weather conditions and transforming energy systems. In this project, the student will investigate the security of electricity supply in the European power system in current and future projected scenarios considering transformations in the energy production, energy consumption, and climate.

The project is part of the Centre for Natural Disaster Science (CNDS), a national research centre that aims to prevent and improve society's preparedness for risks by increasing knowledge of the dynamics and consequences of natural disasters. Cooperation and communication within the CNDS network provide an interdisciplinary platform for exchanging expertise in natural disasters and risk reduction.

The research group at Uppsala University has extensive experience of research in electrical engineering and has a large laboratory activity. We offer a varied and exciting work, planned by the doctoral student and the research group together. The doctoral student will be supervised by at least two supervisors.

Duties
The main task for a doctoral student is to devote themselves to their doctoral education, which includes both participation in research projects and doctoral education courses.

Teaching and other departmental duties may be part of the position, to a maximum of 20% of the working hours.

Qualifications required
To meet the entry requirements for doctoral studies, you must

  • hold a Master’s (second-cycle) degree in electrical engineering, energy systems engineering, engineering physics or similar, or
  • have completed at least 240 credits in higher education with at least 60 credits at Master’s level including an independent project worth at least 15 credits, or
  • have acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way.

Specify other skills, competencies, and qualities that are required for the position.

We place great emphasis on personal qualities such as strong motivation, good collaboration and communication skills with other researchers. You should be purposeful, structured and be able to work effectively both individually and in groups.

The candidate must have excellent communication skills in English and/or Swedish, both orally and in writing.

Qualifications desired

Good oral and written proficiencies in Swedish is a merit. Experience in numerical modelling and programming as well as experimental work is a merit Experience from industry is a merit

jobs.title: PhD student focusing on Scalable Quantum Program Verification
jobs.department: Uppsala University, Department of Information Technology
jobs.description_html:
Are you interested in working in formal verification and programming language techniques applied to quantum systems, with the support of competent and friendly colleagues in an international environment? Are you looking for an employer that invests in a sustainable working environment and offers safe, favourable working conditions? We welcome you to apply for a PhD position at the Department of Information Technology, Uppsala University. 

The Department of Information Technology holds a leading position in both research and education at all levels. We are currently Uppsala University's third largest department, with 350 employees, including 120 teachers and 120 PhD students. Approximately 5,000 undergraduate students take one or more courses at the department each year. You can find more information about us on the Department of Information Technology website.

The position is hosted in a research environment which includes verification experts (Parosh Abdulla, Mohammed Faouzi Atig, Bengt Jonsson, Philipp Ruemmer, Kostis Sagonas, Wang Yi), as well as experts in programming languages (Johannes Borgström, Eva Darulova, Lars-Henrik Erikson, Sofia Ouhbi, Tjark Weber, Tobias Wrigstad). The department is known for both strong theoretical work as well as tool development in these areas (UPPAAL, Concuerror, Nidhugg and other tools), publishing in top conferences such as POPL, PLDI, ICALP and CAV. 

Project description
As both private and public investment in quantum computing continues to surge, the steady upscaling of quantum hardware (now reaching thousands of qubits) has resulted in increasingly sophisticated quantum software pipelines. Given the strategic use of quantum software (e.g. in security), there is an urgent need for verifying the trustworthiness of quantum programs at scale. Features of modern quantum programs such as Quantum Error Correction lead to hybrid quantum-classical architectures, resulting in new challenges for verification. Current tools and techniques do not offer the desired combination of scalability, automation and guarantees to verify such programs. The project aims to address this gap by combining techniques from classical verification and programming language theory with those for complex arithmetic, in order to contribute both theoretical insights and software artifacts advancing the state of the art in quantum program verification.

Duties 
The doctoral student will primarily devote their time to doctoral education. Other departmental duties of at most 20%, including teaching and administration, may also be included in the employment.

Requirements 
To meet the general entry requirements for doctoral studies, you must:

  • hold a Master’s (second-cycle) degree in computer science or mathematics or a related field, or

  • have acquired substantially equivalent knowledge in some other way.

The University may permit an exemption from the general entry requirements for an individual applicant, if there are special grounds (Chapter 7, § 39 of the Higher Education Ordinance). For special entry requirements, please see the subject’s general study plan.

We are looking for candidates with:

  • a mathematical background,
  • excellent problem-solving skills,
  • high motivation and capacity to persistently work on difficult problems,
  • interest in programming,
  • good communication skills with sufficient proficiency in oral and written English,
  • ability to work both independently and collaboratively.

Additional qualifications 
Experience or coursework in one or more of the following areas is considered an advantage: formal methods, programming language theory or semantics, logic, automata theory, automated theorem proving, and quantum computing.

Rules governing PhD students are set out in the Higher Education Ordinance chapter 5, §§ 1-7 and in Uppsala University's rules and guidelines.

Application
The application must include:

  1. A statement (max 2 pages) describing the applicant’s motivation, research interests, a concise summary of their Master’s thesis (or comparable project), and the earliest possible starting date; contact information for at least one reference (no reference letter required at this stage).
  2. A CV.
  3. Degrees and transcripts with grades (officially translated to English or Swedish).
  4. The Master’s thesis (or draft), publications, and other relevant self-produced reports.

Promising applicants will be invited for interviews before a hiring decision is made.

About the employment
The employment is a temporary position according to the Higher Education Ordinance chapter 5 § 7. Scope of employment: 100%. Starting date 15 January 2027 or as agreed. Placement: Uppsala

For further information about the position, please contact: Assistant Professor Ramanathan Thinniyam Srinivasan, email: ramanathan.s.thinniyam@it.uu.se

jobs.title: PhD student in Sustainability Science
jobs.description_html:
Stockholm Resilience Centre (SRC) is a leading international centre in sustainability science at Stockholm University. The Centre advances scientific understanding of the dynamic interactions between people and nature in the biosphere, trains the next generation of sustainability researchers and leaders, and engages in collaborations with change agents. It is a joint initiative between Stockholm University and the Beijer Institute of Ecological Economics at the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences. The SRC currently employs around 165 members of staff.

More information about us, please visit: Stockholm Resilience Centre.

The SRC aims to foster new generations of researchers and academic leaders through our Resilience Research School. The school equips students with a theoretical and practical foundation in Sustainability Science with a focus on resilience in social-ecological systems. Students are encouraged to develop new approaches that integrate methods and concepts from the social, natural and applied sciences. Emphasis is placed on developing student ability to define a problem, develop research methods, and communicate research findings within international scientific and science-policy discussions.

Project description

This PhD position is part of Mistra Finance to Revive Biodiversity, an interdisciplinary research programme hosted by the Stockholm Resilience Centre that investigates the relationships between biodiversity, nature, and the financial system. FinBio brings together researchers across sustainability science, ecology, economics, finance, and related disciplines with financial-sector and other societal partners to develop science-based, decision-relevant approaches for integrating nature into financial decision-making. The programme takes a systems perspective, examining both how finance influences nature and how changes in nature generate risks, resilience, and opportunities for economic and financial systems.

We seek an independent and highly motivated PhD candidate to contribute to the development of next-generation approaches for understanding and managing nature-related financial risks. The project is based on the recognition that nature is not only affected by economic activities, but also plays a critical role in shaping financial risks and opportunities for building long-term resilience. Degraded ecosystems can amplify climate-related hazards such as floods, droughts, wildfires, and pest outbreaks, while healthy ecosystems can reduce vulnerability and strengthen the resilience of both societies and economic systems.

The PhD research will focus on how nature-related risks and resilience can be integrated into financial decision-making, with particular emphasis on the real estate and agrifood sectors. The project will include systematically mapping of the mechanisms through which changes in nature influence economic activities and financial risks. Building on this foundation, the PhD candidate will develop research on how resilience perspectives can be incorporated into financial risk assessment to improve both the credibility and practical usefulness of nature-related risk analyses. The PhD will be a key member of FinBio’s research on risk and resilience which is led by Prof Beatrice Crona. The PhD research will develop a stronger scientific basis for understanding how ecological processes can amplify, transmit, or mitigate financial risks, and how these insights can be incorporated into financial risk assessment.

The PhD research will focus on the real estate and agrifood sectors as case studies to contribute to 1) scientific understanding of nature-related financial risk and resilience and 2) the development and testing of methods, models, and decision-support approaches that can be applied in financial practice. In the real estate domain, this will involve investigating how nature-related risks and nature-based solutions influence property valuation, credit assessment, and financial stability. Within the agrifood sector, the PhD candidate will analyze how investors, lenders, and companies can promote more sustainable and resilient supply chains through governance mechanisms, incentives, and the monitoring of relevant sustainability indicators.

The research is being conducted with FinBio partners, including various institutional investors, banks companies, and other societal stakeholders. The PhD candidate is therefore expected to contribute both to academic publications and to the development of practical methods, recommendations, and decision-support tools for the financial sector.

Applicants should have an academic background in a field such as sustainability science, economics, finance, geography, environmental science, systems analysis, or related disciplines. Please note that both general and specific entry requirements must be met for the application to be considered (see qualification requirements below). Experience with interdisciplinary research, literature reviews, policy analysis, or quantitative methods is considered an asset. Because the project operates at the interface between science and practice, candidates should also be interested in collaborating with non-academic stakeholders and translating scientific findings into practical applications.

This PhD project will be supervised by Professor Crona in close collaboration with Professor Garry Peterson, Dr. Megan Meacham, and Professor Fedra Vanhuyse. The student will collaborate with researchers at the Stockholm Resilience Centre, the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, and the international network of researchers participating in the FinBio project. The successful candidate will be employed by the Stockholm Resilience Centre and will be based in Stockholm.

Qualification requirements

In order to be admitted to postgraduate education, the applicant must have the general and specific entry requirements. The qualification requirements must be met by the time the applicant is admitted to the PhD program at the Stockholm Resilience Centre.

You meet general entry requirements if you have completed a second-cycle degree, or completed courses equivalent to at least 240 higher education credits, of which 60 credits must be in the second cycle, or have otherwise acquired equivalent knowledge in Sweden or elsewhere.

Specific entry requirements for admission to postgraduate studies in Sustainability Science are that the applicant has a total of at least 30 credits, or equivalent, at advanced level in Natural Science, as well as a thesis of at least 30 credits at advanced level in a relevant subject, or equivalent knowledge.

Selection

The selection among the eligible candidates will be based on their capacity to benefit from the training. The following criteria will be used to assess this capacity:

  • Subject knowledge relevant to the research area, for example sustainability science, environmental science, economics, finance, resilience food systems, real estate, or related fields.
  • Ability to synthesize and integrate knowledge from multiple disciplines, such as ecology, climate science, economics, finance, and sustainability science.
  • Demonstrated capacity for systems thinking and analysis of complex social-ecological systems, including an understanding of feedbacks, dependencies, vulnerabilities, and resilience.
  • Quantitative analytical skills, for example statistical analysis, risk assessment, scenario analysis, or modelling of environmental and economic processes.
  • Ability to develop conceptual frameworks and models that structure complex relationships among nature, climate, resilience, and financial risk.
  • Excellent command of English, with strong written and oral communication skills.
  • The applicant's personal references.

In addition, the following qualifications are desirable and will be considered meritorious during the selection process:

  • Experience in policy or governance analysis, including how scientific insights can be translated into decision-support tools, regulatory frameworks, or investment processes.
  • Experience working with geographic or spatial data.
  • Experience conducting systematic literature reviews and evidence syntheses, including the ability to critically assess scientific evidence and identify knowledge gaps.
  • Knowledge of the real estate sector, food systems, or other nature-dependent industries.
  • Fluent Swedish is a valued merit.

About the employment

The period of employment may not be longer than what corresponds to full-time doctoral education for four years. As a doctoral student, you should primarily devote yourself to your own doctoral education, but the employment may include work with education, research and administration to a limited extent (maximum 20 %).

A new employment as a doctoral student is for a maximum of one year, the employment is then renewed for a maximum of two years at a time.

Project description

Your studies in Bioinformatics will be in the project: "AI-driven Multiscale Modelling of Membrane Protein Complexes".

Cell membranes are highly organized assemblies of proteins and lipids whose structure and composition change during disease, drug exposure, and cellular stress, but current structural biology and AI methods largely treat membrane proteins one at a time and rarely capture how proteins, lipids, and glycans jointly shape membrane organization.

In this project, the PhD student(s) will develop deep-learning-based methods to build multiscale structural models of cell membranes, starting from erythrocyte and mitochondrial membranes. Building on our group’s work on AlphaFold-based prediction of protein complexes [1], the project will extend these approaches to (1) predict the structure and interactions of membrane protein complexes embedded in a lipid environment, (2) integrate experimental constraints from proteomics, glycoproteomics, structural mass spectrometry, and lipidomics generated by collaborating experimental groups into the modelling pipeline, (3) scale the predictions from individual protein complexes to the organisation of entire membranes, building on our work on assembling large complexes with AlphaFold and Monte Carlo tree search [2], and (4) compare membrane organization across cell types and conditions - drawing on our proteome-scale map of the human protein interaction network [3] - to identify conserved and disease- or drug-specific remodeling patterns. The project may also connect to work on AI-based prediction of drug transport across membranes, building on our studies of the structural evolution of membrane transporters [4].

The PhD student(s) will work at the interface of structural bioinformatics, machine learning, and membrane biology, in close collaboration with experimental groups in membrane biology and structural biology.

The Elofsson group is located at SciLifeLab, Stockholm University. Elofsson has worked on protein structure prediction, protein evolution and in particular membrane proteins for more than two decades, using machine learning and other computational techniques. Among the group’s most important contributions are methods for assessing the quality of protein models, as well as recent work on predicting protein-protein interactions and building large protein complexes. The group currently comprises seven PhD students, three postdocs, and five senior researchers, and collaborates closely with computational and experimental groups at SciLifeLab and internationally. Arne Elofsson is currently the co-director of CEMERAI. For more information see https://bioinfo.se/.

Representative recent publications relevant to this project are listed below.
[1] Bryant, P, Pozzati, G. & Elofsson, A. “Improved prediction of protein-protein interactions using AlphaFold2”. Nat Commun, 2022 Mar 10;13(1):1265
[2] Bryant P, Pozzati G, Zhu W, Shenoy A, Kundrotas P, Elofsson A. “Predicting the structure of large protein complexes using AlphaFold and Monte Carlo tree search”. Nat Commun. 2022 Oct 12;13(1):6028
[3] Burke, D.F., Bryant, P., Barrio-Hernandez, I., … Elofsson, A. “Towards a structurally resolved human protein interaction network”. Nat Struct Mol Biol 2023, 30(2):216-225
[4] Sudha, G., Bassot, C., Lamb, J., Shu, N., Huang, Y. & Elofsson, A. “The evolutionary history of topological variations in the CPA/AT transporters”. PLoS Comput Biol 2021, 17(9):e1009278

Project description

Project title: "Multiplex chromatin technologies to understand human brain development".

We are seeking a highly motivated PhD student to develop new multiplex technologies for chromatin mapping and apply them to understand the gene regulatory principles underlying human brain development. The project aims to uncover how different chromatin modalities are coordinated as neural stem and progenitor cells give rise to the diverse cell types of the human brain with particular focus on human-specific molecular mechanisms. The student will develop and optimise molecular methods to measure multiple chromatin features in the same cells, building on our laboratory’s work in single-cell epigenomics. By applying these technologies to the developing human fetal brain and stem cell-based models, we will investigate how combinations of chromatin features relate to gene expression, lineage commitment and the establishment of cell identity.

The project combines technology development with an in-depth investigation of human brain biology. Experimental work will be closely integrated with bioinformatic analysis to examine how chromatin states change during development and identify regulatory principles shared across, or specific to, different neural lineages. The student will be involved in method development, experimental design, data generation and biological interpretation. The project is intended to be part wet-lab and part computational and can be partially tailored to the student’s background and interests. Training in both advanced molecular methods and bioinformatic data analysis will be provided.

The successful candidate will join the Laboratory for Single-Cell Epigenomics and Neurobiology, led by Dr. Marek Bartosovic at Stockholm University. Our lab develops single-cell and multimodal chromatin profiling methods and combines molecular biology, neurobiology and computational analysis to understand gene regulation in the developing brain. We offer an interdisciplinary and supportive research environment that encourages scientific curiosity, creativity and professional growth.

If you are enthusiastic about developing new technologies and using them to understand how the human brain develops, we encourage you to apply.

jobs.description_html:
The Department of Meteorology at Stockholm University (MISU) conducts research and education spanning the atmosphere, ocean and physical climate sciences. MISU offers educational programmes at the Bachelor's, Master's and PhD levels. Our research addresses fundamental questions concerning the dynamics, physics, chemistry and biogeochemistry of the atmosphere and ocean relevant to weather and climate. MISU strives toward a broad representation of research within our scientific domain.

We study questions originating from the deep ocean to the upper atmosphere and from the tropics to the poles. In this effort, we use and develop theory, statistical methods, and numerical models in close interplay with observations. We also develop and lead observational research using remote-sensing and in-situ measurements, including satellite missions and icebreaker expeditions to the Arctic.

The department has around 60 employees and is embedded in a larger research environment, including the Bolin Centre for Climate Research, the Baltic Sea Centre and the Swedish e-Science Research Centre. The department is highly international, with over half of our employees coming from outside Sweden and both Swedish and English are used as working languages. We welcome and value diversity in our working environment.

Read more about us here: Department of Meteorology.

Project description

Interactions between aerosol particles and clouds make a potentially important but highly uncertain contribution to the anthropogenic radiative forcing of climate. This project seeks to better understand the ways in which aerosol pollution changes liquid clouds. The PhD student may investigate this topic by testing a new theoretical framework that predicts that aerosol pollution strengthens the updrafts in shallow convective clouds, causing the clouds to become deeper and more reflective. The student may also investigate trends in Earth’s radiation budget caused by aerosol-cloud interactions over the satellite era. Research tasks may involve performing numerical simulations or analyzing satellite data.

Qualification requirements

You meet general entry requirements if you have completed a second-cycle degree, or completed courses equivalent to at least 240 higher education credits, of which 60 credits must be in the second cycle, or have otherwise acquired equivalent knowledge in Sweden or elsewhere.

The specific entry requirements require a minimum of 90 higher education credits in one of the subjects meteorology, oceanography, physics or chemistry, at least 15 higher education credits in mathematics, as well as an independent degree project of at least 15 higher education credits. Furthermore, English language proficiency equivalent to English 6/English Level 2 at upper secondary school is required.

The specific entry requirements may also be met by those who have acquired equivalent knowledge through other means, either in Sweden or abroad.

jobs.description_html:
The Department of Meteorology at Stockholm University (MISU) conducts research and education spanning the atmosphere, ocean and physical climate sciences. MISU offers educational programmes at the Bachelor's, Master's and PhD levels. Our research addresses fundamental questions concerning the dynamics, physics, chemistry and biogeochemistry of the atmosphere and ocean relevant to weather and climate. MISU strives toward a broad representation of research within our scientific domain.

We study questions originating from the deep ocean to the upper atmosphere and from the tropics to the poles. In this effort, we use and develop theory, statistical methods, and numerical models in close interplay with observations. We also develop and lead observational research using remote-sensing and in-situ measurements, including satellite missions and icebreaker expeditions to the Arctic.

The department has around 60 employees and is embedded in a larger research environment, including the Bolin Centre for Climate Research, the Baltic Sea Centre and the Swedish e-Science Research Centre. The department is highly international, with over half of our employees coming from outside Sweden and both Swedish and English are used as working languages. We welcome and value diversity in our working environment.

You can read more about us here: the Department of Meteorology.

Project description

Clouds and their responses to varying environmental conditions are particularly important determinants of current climate and future climate change. However, the resolution of a typical climate model is far too coarse to explicitly represent processes of relevance to cloud formation. Those processes therefore need to be parameterized, or represented as functions of large-scale state variables. Such sub-grid scale parameterizations are associated with large uncertainties, and are also  computationally expensive. 

This project focuses on novel ways to bridge between micro- and global scales, to improve climate model accuracy, efficiency and generalizability, and leverage modern computer architecture. We will explore the use of machine learning (ML) models trained on combinations of observational data and high-resolution simulations, as alternatives to empirical parameterizations of essential, unresolved sub-grid scale processes related to turbulence, cloud formation and aerosol-cloud interaction. The tasks will include deriving and training data-driven models, coupling them to a large-scale climate model, evaluating the results against observations and traditionally parameterized models, and using the ML-enhanced model to estimate climate-relevant quantities like cloud radiative effects and forcing from aerosol-cloud interactions. 

The work will be carried out in close collaboration with data scientists within the Swedish e-Science Research Centre, and contribute to development of methods with applicability also beyond climate science. The successful candidate will thereby develop their skills in atmospheric science and climate modelling, but also in data science and machine learning, and in communicating and collaborating within and across disciplines.

In order to be admitted to postgraduate education, the applicant must have the general and specific entry requirements. The qualification requirements must be fulfilled before admission to the programme.

You meet general entry requirements if you have completed a second-cycle degree, or completed courses equivalent to at least 240 higher education credits, of which 60 credits must be in the second cycle, or have otherwise acquired equivalent knowledge in Sweden or elsewhere.

The specific entry requirements additionally require a minimum of 90 higher education credits in any of the fields of meteorology, oceanography, physics or chemistry; and at least 15 higher education credits in mathematics as well as a degree project of at least 15 higher education credits. At least 60 higher education credits of these courses must be on the second-cycle level. In addition, proficiency in English language, equivalent to English B in Swedish high school, is required.

The specific entry requirements may also be fulfilled by a person who has otherwise acquired equivalent knowledge in Sweden or elsewhere.

The Department of Physics is located in the AlbaNova University Center and has approximately 230 employees, 250 students at undergraduate level and 80 graduate students. These subjects span over several research groups with different research activities. For information about the Department of Physics, see: www.fysik.su.se/english.

Project description

Subject: Theoretical Physics

We invite applications for a PhD position in the theory of quantum sensing at the Department of Physics (Fysikum), Stockholm University. The project will be carried out within the research group led by Sofia Qvarfort and will be based at Nordita as part of the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology (WACQT). The successful candidate will join a collaborative and international research environment in quantum physics, as well as the WACQT graduate school, with opportunities to interact with both theoretical and experimental researchers.

Quantum sensing is a rapidly developing quantum technology that aims to exploit quantum effects to achieve enhanced precision in measurements of weak forces, accelerations, gravitational effects, and other physical parameters. Candidate platforms span a broad range, from individual atoms and superconducting devices to mechanical resonators operating in the quantum regime.

A central question in quantum sensing is what physical resources can provide a genuine sensing advantage, and under which realistic conditions that advantage survives. Improvements in sensitivity can arise through the preparation of non-classical quantum states, changes in the dynamics by which a parameter is encoded, suitable measurement strategies, or by connecting multiple sensors into distributed quantum sensing networks. Understanding the interplay between these mechanisms, particularly in the presence of noise and decoherence, remains an important theoretical challenge.

This PhD project will investigate fundamental limits and new protocols for quantum sensing using tools from mathematical physics, quantum information theory, open quantum systems, and quantum metrology. Possible research directions include nonlinear and anharmonic quantum dynamics, generation and use of non-Gaussian states, distributed quantum sensing, and the role of realistic measurements and environmental noise. The project will be motivated by experimentally relevant quantum technologies, with an emphasis on mechanical resonators in the quantum regime. An important goal is to identify which physical resources and protocols can lead to meaningful improvements in sensitivity under realistic experimental constraints.

We are looking for a curious and motivated candidate with a strong interest in theoretical quantum physics and an enthusiasm for learning new ideas and methods. We value creativity, careful scientific thinking, collaboration, and a willingness to discuss and develop ideas with others. Stockholm University and Nordita strives to provide an inclusive research environment with equal opportunities for all. Project description

Subject: Chemical Physics

The theoretical description of X-ray induced electronic transitions in liquid solutions and solid materials is complicated by the strong influence of the environment and the dynamical response for core-excitations. Recently the development in high-resolution spectroscopy, in particular resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS), allows for detailed investigations of molecular interactions and electron-correlation. However, X-ray spectroscopy in condensed phase requires improvements in theoretical modelling for reliable interpretation of the experimental data. Depending on background and interests, you will primarily develop accurate methods either for treatment of X-ray induced transitions in extended systems using advanced embedding techniques or for the treatment of low energy excitation phonons and vibration.

You will work in a European collaboration involving theoretical and experimental groups, and be involved also in experiments. The project ”Theory Development for High-Resolution RIXS Experiments on Liquid Solutions and Solid Materials” is a collaboration with Prof. Marcella Iannuzzi (University of Zurich) and is financed by the Swiss National Science Foundation. Partner organisations include Dr. Teodoro Laino (IBM Research), Prof. Thorsten Schmitt (Paul Scherrer Institut), and Prof. Lothar Weinhardt (Karlsruhe Institute of Technology, KIT Light Source).

The department is highly international, with over half of our employees coming from outside Sweden and both Swedish and English are used as working languages. We welcome and value diversity in our working environment.

Read more about us here: the Department of Meteorology.

Project description

Clouds regulate how much sunlight reaches the Earth’s surface and how much thermal radiation escapes to space, which ultimately influences how hot or cold the planet is. How much each cloud cools or warms the Earth depends in part on its composition. Is it made up of liquid particles, ice particles, or both? How densely spaced and how large are these particles? The answers to these questions lie partially in the dynamics occurring within the cloud. Even clouds that look calm from the ground may generate motions strong enough to shake an airplane. These motions can form new cloud particles and combine or shatter existing ones. However, these motions are difficult to represent completely in computer models of the atmosphere and in laboratory experiments, and we have yet to understand their full impact. 

The PhD student will build this understanding using over 800 hours of wind and cloud particle measurements that have been recorded by specialized research aircraft during field campaigns run by government agencies in the US and Europe. Data have been collected over the midwestern US and the Caribbean, off the northwestern coast of Africa, between Australia and Antarctica, and in the vicinity of Svalbard. Quality-controlled versions of all data are already available, so analysis can begin at the project start.The PhD student will develop a detailed understanding of aircraft instrumentation through literature review and apply that expertise to the analysis of measurements from dozens of different aircraft-mounted instruments. All analysis will be done in Python. 

The scientific scope initially spans micrometer-scale cloud particles to the dynamical processes that affect clouds, including turbulent eddies and kilometer-scale atmospheric waves. Initial science questions are well defined and focus on identifying statistical relationships between cloud particle properties and cloud-scale dynamics, and investigating how these vary across cloud types and geographic regions.

After the initial stage, the project is more open-ended. The PhD student may choose to focus on the same micrometer–kilometer scales, or to make connections between these scales and the regional or global climate. They may also choose to branch into atmospheric modelling and/or to use machine learning to model observed relationships between cloud dynamics and cloud particles.

jobs.description_html:
Research at the Department of Molecular Biosciences, The Wenner-Gren Institute (MBW) experimentally addresses fundamental problems in molecular cell biology, integrative biology, and infection and immunobiology. State-of-the art and advanced methodologies are applied in a professional research environment characterized by its well-established international profile. The institute has 30 research groups with a research staff of 180, of which 65 are PhD students. More information about us, please visit www.su.se/mbw.

Project description

This PhD student position is available in the Martin Jastroch laboratory. The project addresses molecular mechanisms of mitochondrial bioenergetics, combining molecular simulations and systems levels-models with biochemical, physiological, and metabolic data. jobs.title: PhD student in Psychology
jobs.description_html:
The Department of Psychology is a creative and international workplace for research and education. The Department of Psychology conducts successful research in occupational and organisational psychology, clinical psychology, cognitive psychology, perception and psychophysics, personality, social and developmental psychology, psychobiology and epidemiology.

Our researchers publish regularly in international journals and actively participate as experts in the media. We collaborate extensively with external organisations and we have a constant exchange of visiting students and researchers from all over the world. As a researcher with us, you will have access to modern research infrastructure. We have a recording studio, advanced laboratories for sleep and sensory research, and large databases that enable complex studies over time. We also collaborate with the Stockholm University Brain Imaging Centre, offering state-of-the-art imaging technologies, including MRI, EEG and TMS.

For more information about us, please visit the Department of Psychology.

Project description

The doctoral position is part of an ambitious project aiming to establish a scientific foundation for chronomedicine in psychiatry, a field that seeks to use the body's internal biological clock to improve treatment effectiveness and functioning. Many psychiatric symptoms (e.g., anxiety), cognitive processes (e.g., attention), and stress-related physiology (e.g., cortisol secretion) vary substantially across the day, but it remains unclear to what extent these fluctuations are driven by the circadian system or behavioural and environmental factors such as light, sleep, food intake, and stress exposures.

To address this question, the doctoral student will contribute to several interconnected studies, including ecological momentary assessment (EMA) to track cognition, mood, stress, and physiology in everyday life, a highly controlled laboratory protocol known as constant routine to isolate endogenous circadian rhythms from external factors, and experimental studies examining circadian-timed cognitive probes.

The project offers an opportunity to work at the intersection of psychiatry, neuroscience, sleep and circadian biology, and stress research. The doctoral student will gain training in intensive longitudinal data collection, cognitive and physiological measurements, and advanced statistical methods. 

Qualification requirements

In order to be admitted to postgraduate education, the applicant must have the general and specific entry requirements. The qualification requirements must be met by the deadline for applications.

You meet general entry requirements if you have completed a second-cycle degree, or completed courses equivalent to at least 240 higher education credits, of which 60 credits must be in the second cycle, or have otherwise acquired equivalent knowledge in Sweden or elsewhere.

You meet specific entry requirements for doctoral studies in psychology if you have completed courses equivalent to at least 90 credits at undergraduate or graduate level in psychology or another scientific discipline relevant to the dissertation topic, of which at least 15 credits must consist of independent work (thesis/publication), or equivalent knowledge acquired in another way. The applicant must be able to engage with scientific literature written in English.

See the General Syllabus for Third-Cycle (Doctoral) Studies in Psychology.

Selection

In the selection process, consideration will be given to previous academic merits, and an assessment will be made of the applicant’s ability to benefit from the doctoral training programme. The main basis for this assessment is (1) the thesis/publication to be submitted with the application, and (2) other educational and professional qualifications, including previous publications (CV).

The project involves data collection, partly conducted during the evening and night in the sleep laboratory. Particular merit will be given to applicants with:

  • Experience working in a human sleep laboratory.
  • Experience working with intensive longitudinal study designs measuring stress physiology (e.g., HRV and wearable sensor technologies).
  • Experience with physiological measurements related to stress and autonomic function, such as heart rate variability (HRV) and wearable sensor technology.
  • Excellent English language skills, both written and spoken, as the candidate will be part of an international research environment.
  • Proficiency in Swedish, as the study involves interaction Swedish-speaking participants.

Please see the Department of Psychology’s website for further information and application instructions.

jobs.title: PhD student in Ecology and Evolution
jobs.department: Department of Ecology, Environment and Plant Sciences
jobs.description_html:
The Department of Ecology, Environment and Plant Sciences (DEEP) conducts research and offers education at the Arrhenius Laboratories on the Frescati campus. We are approximately 100 staff members, including doctoral students and postdocs, distributed across 25 research groups.

More information about us, please visit: the Department of Ecology, Environment and Plant Sciences.

Project description

The Department of Ecology, Environment and Plant Sciences invites applications for a four-year PhD position in the framework of the project “Harnessing evolutionary transitions, machine learning, and genomics to decode pollen evolution and unravel sexual selection mechanisms shared across kingdoms” led by Prof. Tanja Slotte in close collaboration with co-investigators Prof. John Fitzpatrick, Prof. Catarina Rydin, and Dr. Allison Hsiang at Stockholm University. 

This project will investigate the evolutionary drivers and genomic consequences of pollen evolution in response to shifts in pollination mode in flowering plants. The thesis work will focus on identifying genomic signatures of selection on pollen in relation to evolutionary transitions in pollination mode. The work will involve comparative genomic analyses in a phylogenetic framework, as well as population genomic and transcriptomic analyses in suitable plant systems. The project is funded by the Knut and Alice Wallenberg Foundation.

Qualification requirements

In order to be admitted to postgraduate education, the applicant must have the general and specific entry requirements. The qualification requirements must be met by the deadline for applications.

You meet general entry requirements if you have completed a second-cycle degree, or completed courses equivalent to at least 240 higher education credits, of which 60 credits must be in the second cycle, or have otherwise acquired equivalent knowledge in Sweden or elsewhere.

Specific entry requirements are described in the general syllabus for doctoral studies in the field of Ecology and Evolution. Specifically, applicants must have completed at least 60 higher education credits in the second cycle, of which 15 credits must be from a course in one of the areas Ecology or Evolution, and 30 credits from a project in one of the areas Ecology or Evolution.

Selection

The selection among the eligible candidates will be based on their capacity to benefit from the training. The following criteria will be used to assess this capacity:

  • documented knowledge of theory and applications in a relevant field of research, such as evolutionary genetics/genomics, population genetics, phylogenomics, and related subjects
  • capacity for analytical and creative thinking
  • documented experience in bioinformatics or other computational analyses
  • initiative
  • independence
  • ability to collaborate
  • excellent written and oral proficiency in English.

Documented experience in molecular genetic lab work, or plant sciences is a merit but not required. Special emphasis will be placed on personal suitability.

The Department of Ecology, Environment and Plant Sciences (DEEP) conducts research and offers education at the Arrhenius Laboratories on the Frescati campus. We are approximately 100 staff members, including doctoral students and postdocs, distributed across 25 research groups.

For more information about us, please visit: the Department of Ecology, Environment and Plant sciences.

Subject area

Ecology and Evolution

The doctoral project will be conducted within the scope of the interdisciplinary project ‘BALANCE wetlands - Bridging Actions for Lowering Atmospheric carbon emissions and Nurturing Conservation Efforts in Wetlands', funded by the Swedish Research Council Formas. The project group includes researchers within ecology, hydrology, and biogeochemistry. The research project aims to study how different objectives can be balanced during wetland restoration, where a key component involves monitoring large-scale restoration measures. The main focus of the PhD project is to investigate how restoration measures affect the abundance and diversity of insects and spiders, as well as studying underlying mechanisms such as oxygen deficiencies in wet soil. In addition, the PhD student will collaborate with other researcher to integrate biodiversity responses and changes in ecosystem processes such as hydrology and biogeochemistry.
