jobs.title: PhD position (1.0 fte, 4 years) in deep-sea benthic ecology in the Arctic Ocean
jobs.description_html:
Do you have a passion for the deep-sea and like join expeditions to the Arctic Ocean to explore how deep-sea life is connected to our climate? Do you enjoy working in an interdisciplinary research setting? The Department of Freshwater and Marine Ecology at the University of Amsterdam is looking for an ambitious candidate for a 4-year PhD position.

About the position
You will be working within an international team of Dutch research institutes (UvA, the Naturalis Biodiversity Center, NIOZ Royal Netherlands Institute for Sea Research) and the German Alfred Wegener Institute (AWI) for Polar and Sea Research on an ambitious project entitled: Plumbing the biological pump: Linking missing carbon flows between pelagic and benthic ecosystems in a changing Arctic Ocean (C-CONNECT).

The team consists of very experienced marine researchers and will recruit in total two PhD candidates and a postdoctoral fellow on this project. The project will contain multi-week expedition(s) to the Arctic Ocean around Svalbard (Spitsbergen) on large scientific research vessels, like the brand new Dutch Anna-Weber van Bosse, including the use of advanced deep-sea technologies, including remotely operated vehicles (ROVs) and stand-alone incubation and deep-sea sensors that can measure ecological processes up to 6,000 m water depth.

This PhD position is a co-supervised position between the University of Amsterdam (main supervisor: Dr. Ir. Jasper M. de Goeij) and the Royal NIOZ (main supervisor: Dr. Furu Mienis). AWI-researchers Prof. Dr. Claudio Richter and Dr. Autun Purser will complement the supervisory team. Research stays at each of the institutes are part of the position and will be planned at the start of the PhD.

What are you going to do?
The global biological carbon pump mediates the cycling and storage of carbon in our ocean and helps to regulate Earth’s climate. Arctic waters are undergoing record changes in temperature, sea-ice cover, and acidification. However, our understanding of climate-change impacts on the size of the Arctic carbon pump and speed of flows remains incomplete, due to the limited capacity to analyse existing data and absence of carbon flux measurements at the seafloor.

Therefore, the main aim in C-CONNECT is to perform plumbing to the Arctic biological carbon pump by connecting important missing parts, e.g., shelled zooplankton and benthic faunal communities to the carbon cycle! C-CONNECT will improve the ability to project how future Arctic carbon cycling evolves under continued climate change and will provide essential information on Arctic ecosystem services to aid (policy and management) decision making.

In this PhD project, you will combine fieldwork, laboratory work and data analysis: On the basis of a unique 26 years time-series of environmental, sediment and megafaunal benthic community data from AWI's "Hausgarten" Observatory in Fram Strait connecting to the Arctic, you will combine empirical findings with new and unique benthic field experiments on carbon uptake and metabolism, involving state-of-the-art sample analyses in the laboratory. You will present the results of your work in scientific publications forming the basis of your PhD-thesis, at international conferences and in the media.

Tasks and responsibilities:
  • Prepare, organize, and participate in multi-week fieldwork expeditions;
  • Collect, preserve and analyze field samples;
  • Analyze large data sets;
  • Publish and present the results in scientific publications and at conferences, synthesize your findings in a PhD thesis;
  • Participate in the supervision of Bachelor and Master students and in our educational programs.

Your profile
You have a strong passion for the ocean, especially the deep-sea. You are open-minded and (hopefully) not going to be sea-sick… You are a team-player and when it gets busy, you keep it cool!

Your experience and profile:
  • You have a Master degree in ecology, biology, or biogeochemistry and preferably water-science related;
  • You have experience in both fieldwork and lab;
  • You have good scientific skills, such as data analysis, statistics and writing;

jobs.title: PhD: Reconstructing Zeeland’s historic landscape developments
jobs.description_html:
The PhD position is part of the larger research project Re-Flex Zeeland that aims to reconstruct and visualize Zeeland's natural landscape formation processes during historical periods of rapid sea-level rise, with a focus on the last 12,000 years. The project is funded by the Delta Climate Centre (DCC) in Vlissingen and consists of two PhDs and one postdoc position in a collaboration between Utrecht University, Wageningen University & Research (WUR), NIOZ, Scalda and UNESCO GeoPark Schelde Delta.

Your job
The present-day landscape of Zeeland is highly regulated to support key societal, economic, and flood-safety functions. Allowing more space for natural processes to shape the landscape can contribute to flood protection and restoration of biodiversity, however, knowledge of how natural landscapes have evolved in the past and of the ecosystem services they once provided remains limited. This phenomenon is often described as shifting baselines, whereby each generation perceives the contemporary environment as the long-term norm. In reality, the Dutch landscape—and that of Zeeland in particular—has been extraordinarily dynamic and adjusting flexibly to changes in sea level. Over the Holocene, Zeeland has transitioned from an subarctic environment with boreal forest to alternating phases of peatland and intertidal environments, before becoming largely regulated through human embankment only in the past few centuries.

For the work package “Holocene peat deposits as natural archives of landscape developments” we look for a motivated PhD student who investigates these landscape and ecosystem dynamics in Zeeland based on fossil plant remains preserved in peat and lake sediment records.

What will you be doing?

You will design and carry out field work to map the locations and ages of peat deposits along an east-west transect around the major marine estuaries of Zeeland. You will integrate existing and new field data and investigate the botanical composition of the peat and, using pollen analysis, improve the current knowledge on past landscape reconstructions with a focus on peat to intertidal transitions. You will also co-supervise BSc and MSc courses and thesis projects that contribute to this.

The gathered data will provide new insight in the exact timing and variability in past landscape changes. Your results will furthermore contribute to computer simulations of coastal dynamics in a parallel PhD project conducted at WUR and provide context for visualisations of historic landscapes developed by a postdoc at NIOZ in a collaboration with Scalda and UNESCO GeoPark Schelde Delta.

jobs.title: PhD Position in "Modifying Synapses to Mitigate Alzheimer's Disease"
jobs.description_html:
Are you interested in the neurobiological processes of learning and memory, and how we can use this knowledge to make the brain more resilient to the cognitive decline seen in Alzheimer’s disease (AD)? Then this position might be perfect for you. Join us!

Join us!
Glutamatergic synapses are critical for synaptic plasticity and memory formation. The composition of their receptors can modulate resilience and sensitivity to memory deficits, in particular those induced by amyloid beta (Aβ), a major hallmark of Alzheimer’s Disease. In this project you will investigate whether and how modifying the composition of glutamatergic receptors at synapses, using both molecular tools and behavioral interventions, can reduce age-related cognitive decline in and thereby enhance resilience to AD pathology. In addition, you will study the role of engram cell ensembles in this process.

The position is embedded within the Memory and Plasticity team of dr. Harm Krugers at the Swammerdam Institute for Life Sciences, University of Amsterdam (UvA). This is a collaborative project with Prof. dr. Helmut Kessels (Cellular and Circuit Neuroscience group, UvAmsterdam) and Prof. dr. Paul J Lucassen (Brain Plasticity group, UvAmsterdam). The PhD candidate works in the respective groups where complementary and excellent expertise is available (e.g. electrophysiology will be combined with chemogenetics and behavioral interventions).

This is what you will do
You will use behavioral paradigms to assess learning and memory in a rodent model of AD. You will apply viral technologies to identify and measure the properties of synapses and engram cells and establish their role in memory. These techniques can include electrophysiology, proteomics, dendrite and spine reconstructions, chemogenetics, and memory engram-specific interventions.

Tasks and responsibilities:
  • complete and defend a PhD thesis within the official appointment duration of four years;
  • gain knowledge of the field through literature, discussions with team members and internal lab meetings;
  • contribute to the design of experiments, perform experiments in the lab and analyse and interpret results of these experiments;
  • take a leading role in writing manuscripts;
  • be an active member of the research teams at both the Swammerdam Institute for Life Sciences (UvA) and present results at (inter)national scientific meetings;
  • participate in the Faculty of Science PhD training programme;
  • assist in teaching and supervise Bachelor and Master’s students

What we ask of you
You are excited about science and have a particular interest in, and preferably have experience with neurobiological approaches towards learning and memory. You like a challenge and can combine work on preclinical rodent models with techniques like behaviour, electrophysiology, molecular biology and structural analysis. You have good statistical skills and experience with molecular tools and data-analysis. You are a team player and a pleasant colleague who enjoys being part of an interdisciplinary team of scientists. Finally, you have good time management skills enabling you to meet the projects’ deadlines for finishing analyses, reports and other deliverables.

Your experience and profile:

  • a MSc degree in Neuroscience or related fields;
  • affinity and experience with performing animal experiments;
  • affinity and experience with common behavioural and/or neurobiological techniques;
  • good analytical, writing and presenting skills;

Based on a full-time appointment (38 hours per week) the gross monthly salary will range from €3.204in the first year to €4.051 (scale P) in the last year. jobs.title: PhD Candidate in the research project 'Entangled with Seaweed', case studies in Scotland
jobs.description_html:
Do you want to contribute to ethnographic research into the politics of valuing seaweed in Scotland?
The Leiden University's Institute of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology, based within the Faculty of Social Sciences, is looking for an ambitious PhD-candidate to study the impacts of economization of seaweed as part of ‘blue economy’ strategies in Scotland. Research focuses on the impacts on coastal communities considering that in Scotland colonial legacies still influence patterns of unequal access to and use of coastal areas. You will work within the project ‘Entangled in seaweed: The politics of economising nature in Scotland and South Africa’ funded by an NWO Open Competition grant.

Project Description
The project investigates the impacts of economisation of seaweed as part of a global drive to develop ‘blue economy’ strategies. Seaweed harvesting and cultivation (as food, or fertilizer- and bioplastic ingredient) are increasing considerably and promoted as contributing to sustainable development. The project focuses on coastal communities in Scotland, which has developed a comprehensive blue economy strategy. Building on insights from political ecology and valuation studies and inspired by the multispecies turn in anthropology, this project aims to study local impacts of new forms of economisation of seaweed, and the possible contestations these may entail. It seeks to incorporate the ideas, interests, and knowledge from local groups who live from, in and with seaweed ecologies, examining how new versions of economisation affect local social relations, including the entanglements with non-humans these ecologies and economisations depend on. It does so by focusing on valuations of seaweed ecologies, based on an understanding of values as enacted through practices by all (human and non-human) stakeholders. The project employs a collaborative approach vis-à-vis research participants and a wider audience through a visual storytelling approach.

What you will do
You will work in a project team consisting of two PhD-candidates and researchers at Leiden University, collaborating with project partners in Scotland. You will:
  • Develop a research proposal in the context of the overall project theme, and conduct twelve months of ethnographic research in Scotland. An ethics review and contribution to the data management plan are included in the proposal development. Research includes historical document/policy analysis, participant observation, interviews, and the application of participatory visual storytelling methods.
  • Analyse research findings and write a dissertation that contributes to the objectives of the ‘Entangled with Seaweed’ project.
  • Actively contribute to the output and dissemination of the research project, which includes collaborating with the other team members on academic and non-academic publications, science communication, and the organisation of workshops, seminars and an exhibition.
  • Participate in relevant PhD-courses and masterclasses, organised in accordance with the guidelines of the Faculty of Social Science and the Institute of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology. PhD-courses at the University of Edinburgh, our partner in the project, can be included in the individual training and supervision plan as well.
  • Participate in the PhD programme and other academic activities of the Institute of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology at Leiden University. During your stay in Scotland you will also be able to participate in the PhD-programme at the University of Edinburgh as well as academic activities organised by the Scottish Association for Marine Science (SAMS).

Where you will work
The Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences consists of five institutes: the Centre for Science and Technology Studies, Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology, Education and Child Studies, Political Science, and Psychology. The faculty is home to approximately 7,000 students and 1,000 staff members. Our institutes are dedicated not only to education but also to groundbreaking research that expands our understanding of human behavior and societal structures. What makes our faculty unique is the diversity of research topics, the variety of teaching approaches, and the structure of professional support. This provides you with the opportunity to explore and develop your interests and expertise. For an introduction to our faculty, visit our website: Welcome to the Leiden Faculty of Social and Behavioural Sciences – Leiden University.

Leiden University's Institute of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology (CADS)
Leiden University's Institute of Cultural Anthropology and Development Sociology concentrates on 'global vulnerability and social resilience'. The institute has three main themes: diversity, sustainability, and digitalisation. CADS is dedicated to making a real-world impact, not just studying change, but also working with communities to promote positive change through education and research. We use a unique approach that blends qualitative, quantitative, audiovisual, and digital methods based on ethnographic fieldwork.

With our unique blend of interdisciplinary interests, comparative regional studies, and social science research methods, we emphasize our role in the extensive collaborative network within Leiden University. In both our research and education, we engage in extensive interdisciplinary and international networks.

The project team
The project team at Leiden University works closely together with colleagues at the University of Edinburgh, the Scottish Association for Marine Science, and Stellenbosch University. The PhD-students will be jointly supervised by Leiden University and Stellenbosch University, and Leiden University and the University of Edinburgh respectively. A project assistant will assist with training and dissemination activities.

What you bring
  • A Master’s degree in Anthropology, Sociology, Environmental Humanities, Science and Technology Studies, or another relevant discipline within the social sciences or humanities.
  • Demonstrable excellent qualitative research skills and experience with ethnographic fieldwork.
  • Affinity with the topics of sustainability and environmental justice.
  • Excellent oral and written communication skills.
  • Strong command of English;
  • Knowledge of one of the other official languages of Scotland (Scots, Scottish Gaelic) is a bonus.
  • Excellent social and organisational skills and the ability to work independently as well as in a team.

What we offer
Our goal is to work together to create a transparent and inclusive work environment in which everyone feels welcome and appreciated. Our organisation is always evolving and we need your ideas for improvement and innovation to take us further. We want to devote attention to your personal development.

You can count on an enjoyable job within the socially relevant world of education and research. The University's challenging and international work environment is located just steps away from Leiden’s lively city centre or the bustling city centre of The Hague. We also want to work with you to devote attention to your health and vitality, for example with the fun activities we organise through Healthy University.

We also offer:
  • PHD: An employment contract for 38 hours per week as a PhD candidate, initially for a period of 1 year, with the possibility of extension for 3 years after a positive evaluation. This contract falls under the CLA of Dutch Universities;
  • A salary between €3204 - €4051 gross per month, based on a full-time appointment (38 hours) (PhD student);
  • A holiday allowance (8%), an end-of-year bonus (8,3%), and an attractive pension scheme at ABP;
  • Full reimbursement of public transport commuting costs for home-to-work travel;

  • Lots of options when it comes to secondary employment conditions; we can, for example, discuss options for a sabbatical or paid parental leave. Within our terms of employment individual choices model, you can exchange leave days and/or salary for benefits such as an advantageous sports subscription and bicycle scheme;

For more information about employment conditions, see https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/working-at/job-application-procedure-and-employment-conditions

What we value
Promoting an inclusive community is central to Leiden University’s values and vision. Leiden University aims to be an inclusive community in which all students and staff members feel valued and respected, and are able to develop to their full potential. Diversity in experiences and perspectives enriches our teaching and strengthens our research. High-quality education and research means inclusive education and research.

If you would like more information about what the job entails, please contact prof. dr. Marja Spierenburg, project leader, at at +31715276699 or by email: m.j.spierenburg@fsw.leiden or dr. Mandy de Wilde, project member, by email: m.de.wilde@fsw.leidenuniv.nl. You can apply until 7 November 2026; applications will be processed immediately. Interviews will take place during the last week of November and the first week of December 2026.

To help us get to know each other better, we follow a number of steps in the application procedure. For more information, see https://www.universiteitleiden.nl/en/working-at/job-application-procedure-and-employment-conditions

jobs.title: PhD: 3D radiation in clouds and wildfire plumes using GPUs and machine learning
jobs.description_html:
This PhD project is part of ORCRIST: Optimized Ray-tracing for Cloud-Radiation Interaction Simulations in 3D using GPUs and Machine Learning, funded by the NWO Open Technology Programme.

Sunlight and heat radiation move through the atmosphere in three dimensions, yet almost every weather and climate model still treats radiation as a purely vertical process. We want to change that. As a PhD candidate in Wageningen, you will help build the first Monte Carlo ray tracer for the atmosphere that is fast enough for forecasting, and use it to find out how 3D radiation shapes clouds, solar energy availability, climate sensitivity and wildfire plumes. You will work in a tandem with a fellow PhD student in computer science at Leiden University, who focuses on GPU optimization, while you lead the physics. Together you will develop a machine-learning denoiser that brings the ray tracer to operational speed. Your research has a clear route to society: throughout the project you will work with a user committee of KNMI, weather forecasting company Whiffle, TNO, software company VORtech and Columbia University.

Your duties and responsibilities include:
  • Setting up three benchmark simulations in the GPU-accelerated model MicroHH: solar energy forecasting, tropical climate, and a real wildfire plume.
  • Developing a 3D thermal radiation solver within the RTE-RRTMGP-CPP ray tracer, including smart strategies for sampling radiation sources.
  • Quantifying how 3D radiation changes clouds, surface irradiance and plume dynamics compared to conventional 1D radiation.
  • Co-developing a physics-informed machine-learning denoiser with your Leiden colleague, and evaluating it together with the user committee in operational settings.
  • Publishing your results in leading journals and presenting them at international conferences and to users from the field.

You will work here
The research is embedded within the chair of Meteorology (Meteorology and Air Quality Group), led by Prof. Vilà-Guerau de Arellano. You will be supervised by Dr.ir. Chiel van Heerwaarden and Dr.ir. Menno Veerman, both at WUR, and by Dr. Ben van Werkhoven at Leiden University. The team is small, open and collaborative, and has a track record of building widely used open-source simulation codes. You will have access to national and European supercomputers (Snellius, LUMI) and dedicated GPU hardware.

jobs.title: PhD – Resilience against disaster and war in the Netherlands
jobs.description_html:
There is an increasing risk of disasters and war in the Netherlands. The government is therefore trying to increase societal resilience. In this PhD research, you look at the implementation and impact of such resilience initiatives to discover how well they prepare residents for crises.

Your duties and responsibilities include:
  • You carry out a literature review to identify which characteristics make communities resilient against disasters and war and/or how resilience initiatives contribute to resilience.
  • You study the implementation and impact of resilience measures from the government as well as spontaneous resilience projects from communities.
  • You analyze who begin resilience initiatives, who participates in them, who takes decisions, and who benefits from them.
  • You collect data in different municipalities and/or Safety Regions in the Netherlands to formulate new theory and contribute with scientific insights to disaster sociology, for example through developing new knowledge on community resilience, disaster vulnerability, and emergent organizing.
  • You support in formulating recommendations to administrators and policymakers who deal with resilience and present your research results.

You will work here
The research is embedded within the chair Sociology of Development and Change , which is led by Prof. Bram Büscher. You will be co-supervised by dr. Jori Kalkman and dr. Esther van ‘t Veen.

jobs.title: PhD – Militarization of Societal Resilience
jobs.description_html:
The Dutch government aims to strengthen societal resilience against war and disaster. The military plays a prominent role in these efforts, raising concerns about militarization and its adverse impact. In this PhD, you study how militarization in the Netherlands unfolds and examine its effects.

Your duties and responsibilities include:
  • You conduct a literature review on ‘militarization’ in the context of crises, domestic security, and resilience.
  • You analyze Dutch policy documents to determine whether/how these documents contribute to a militarization of society and whether/how it contributes to militarism.
  • You collect qualitative, empirical data on the implementation of resilience measures (e.g. expansion of military terrains, emergency booklets, citizen mobilization, increased civil-military, and new crisis plans) to critically examine their effects.
  • You write and publish several scientific articles to contribute to critical scholarship on resilience and critical military studies.
  • You contribute to policy and practice by sharing constructive reflections on current and proposed policies, and by presenting your findings.

You will work here
The research is embedded within the chair Sociology of Development and Change , which is led by Prof. Bram Büscher. You will be co-supervised by dr. Jori Kalkman and dr. Sumit Vij.

jobs.title: PhD Researcher in Atmospheric Sciences - Emerging extreme fire weather risks
jobs.description_html:
Are you a meteorologist or climate scientist with a passion to investigate the interactions between climate extremes and wildfire risks? Do you want to work on a research project that aims to understand the most extreme fire weather events possible, and how they will evolve in a warming world? Then this position may be the perfect opportunity for you!

The Meteorology and Air Quality (MAQ) Group at Wageningen University and Research is looking for a PhD candidate with a background in meteorology, atmospheric or climate sciences to work on unprecedented and emerging fire weather risks.

Extreme fire weather, referring to the meteorological component of fire risk that reflects the combined effects of heat, drought, wind, and atmospheric aridity, is one of the key factors influencing wildfire spread and intensity. Climate change is increasing the frequency and severity of fire weather extremes across many regions, including the Northern Hemisphere mid-latitudes. Therefore, understanding and anticipating the most intense, persistent or otherwise most impactful fire weather conditions plausible today, as well as how these conditions may worsen under future warming, is crucial for fire risk assessment and preparedness. What are worst-case fire weather conditions possible under current climate versus in a warmer world, what atmospheric or climatic mechanisms drive them, and how this relates to actual fire occurrence and behaviour, are all questions that will be addressed within this PhD project. To answer them, you will investigate the most extreme events in the historical record and how they compare to the most extreme events in state-of-the-art climate modelling experiments.

This project will be supervised by Dr. Laura Suarez-Gutierrez in collaboration with Prof. Guido van der Werf and carried out in the highly multidisciplinary setting of the MAQ group. You will join a thriving, highly collaborative research environment with leading expertise in weather and climate extremes, fire dynamics, and their interactions.

jobs.title: PhD position on explainable DeepFake detection using Foundation models
jobs.description_html:
The challenge:
In the past decades, photographs and videos of events were regarded as reliable evidence for both news media and forensic investigations. However, recent developments in AI technology now make it possible, with minimal technological knowledge or skills, to create extremely convincing manipulated or synthesised images, audio and video data, often called DeepFakes.

This fact is a serious threat to the trustworthiness of news in the media and forensic processes in criminal investigations. Therefore, development of reliable methods to detect manipulations and distinguish bonafide from synthesised data is of utmost importance. In addition, especially for forensic investigations, simple detection is not sufficient. An explanation of the traces of manipulation and tools used for the synthesis or
manipulation should be produced as well.

In the EU project DEFORM, 14 research institutes, universities and companies from 6 different countries aim to develop methods and tools for explainable detection of DeepFakes using Foundation models and other techniques.

At the University of Twente, we are looking for a PhD
researcher who will work in close collaboration with the
other partners on detection of fake videos using
inconsistencies in video as well as audio.

jobs.title: PhD Position(s) Diffractive Electron Imaging of Surfaces
jobs.description_html:
Challenge: How do we watch material surfaces evolve?
Change: Building a surface-sensitive diffractive microscope.
Impact: Enabling high-resolution imaging of surfaces during operation.

Job description
We are looking for two PhD candidates to join the Curious Beams Lab at Delft University of Technology and develop a new approach to imaging materials surfaces with electrons. The positions are part of BEAMSurf: Diffractive Atomic-Scale Surface Imaging with Backscattered Electrons, an ERC Starting Grant project led by Dr. Georgios Varnavides.

Surfaces control many of the properties and processes that determine material functionality, from chemical reactions in catalysis to interfaces in nanoelectronic devices. Yet, observing surfaces at high spatial resolution while they operate remains challenging. BEAMSurf will develop a new scanning electron microscope that uses coherent backscattered electrons for diffractive imaging of surfaces, with the potential to overcome conventional resolution limits for low-energy SEM.

As a PhD candidate, you will help build the experimental and computational foundations of this imaging technique. The two PhD candidates will have complementary roles and work alongisde a postdoctoral researcher leading the instrumentation development.

PhD 1: Electron Optics and Experimental Imaging

You will help develop and experimentally realize the new electron-optical imaging platform. Working closely with the postdoc, you will design, characterize, and integrate miniature electron-optical components into a high-vacuum SEM. A central challenge is to separate the desired backscattered electron signal from the primary beam and direct it towards a dedicated detector.

Your work will span electron optics, ray tracing simulations, nanofabrication, vacuum technology, and experimental microscopy. As the project develops, you will also help establish the experimental imaging methodology and optimize the microscope for diffractive imaging.

This position is suited to candidates interested in building new instrumentation and working across physics and engineering. Experience with electron optics, electromagnetic simulation, MEMS, nanofabrication, vacuum systems or instrumentation is valuable but not required.

PhD 2: Computational Imaging and Surface Science

You will develop the computational methods needed to extract high-resolution surface information from coherent backscattered electron measurements. You will develop forward models and inverse-scattering approaches for reflection-mode electron imaging, using simulations and experimental reconstructions to understand the capabilities and limitations of the technique.

As the experimental platform matures, you will work closely with the instrumentation team to apply these methods to experimental measurements and establish high-resolution surface imaging. An important goal is to move beyond static images towards studying surfaces as they evolve, including processes such as oxidation, interfacial reactions, and electrically driven changes.

This position is suited to candidates interested in computational imaging, inverse problems, electron scattering, open-source numerical techniques, and/or surface science. Experience with electron microscopy datasets is useful but not essential.

Research Environment:

You will join the Curious Beams Lab, led by Dr. Georgios Varnavides, within the Microscopy and Instrumentation Techniques (MInT) cluster of the Department of Imaging Physics at TU Delft, Applied Sciences.

The MInT cluster brings together multiple research groups working across electron microscopy, from semiconductor inspection and metrology, to cryogenic electron microscopy for biological samples. The cluster has access to state-of-the-art field-emission SEMs and FIB-SEMS, with a new microscope being acquired primarily for this project.

More broadly, the ImPhys department provides an interdisciplinary environment spanning multiple imaging modalities, wavelengths, and length scaels, including extreme ultraviolet imaging, optical super-resolution, ultrasound and MRI, as-well as AI-based medical imaging.

jobs.title: PhD Position Optimizing Multi-actor Transport and Logistics Systems
jobs.description_html:
Would you like to develop new theory and algorithms for problems with multiple interacting actors? Are you interested in working at the intersection of game theory and mixed-integer optimisation?

Job description
Transport and logistics systems consist of many players with potentially conflicting objectives that continuously strive to maximize their performance. The competition and collaboration between these players can influence their decision-making, which is something that traditional Mixed Integer Linear Programming (MILP) formulations with a single decision-maker cannot capture. The goal of this PhD is to develop novel methodologies at the intersection of operations research and game theory to address these problems. Applications can go beyond the transport and logistics domain.

Your research will focus on mathematical modelling and algorithm development for planning and operating multi-actor systems, taking into account that the actions of one actor influence the opportunities and performance of others. A central methodological component of the position is the development of scalable optimisation algorithms for large and computationally challenging problem instances. You will formulate mathematical programming models and design solution approaches based on techniques such as column generation, branch-and-price, and Benders decomposition.

You will be expected to:
  • develop new game-theoretic/optimization models for multi-actor decision problems;
  • design scalable solution methods for large-scale optimisation problems;
  • contribute to scientific publications in leading journals in operations research, transportation, and logistics;
  • communicate research findings to an interdisciplinary audience.

You will join the Transport and Logistics section of the Department of Engineering Systems and Services

Job requirements
  • We are looking for a candidate who meets the following requirements:
  • An MSc degree in operations research, econometrics, applied mathematics, computer science, industrial engineering, systems and control, or a closely related discipline.
  • A strong background and demonstrated experience in mathematical optimisation, in particular mixed-integer programming.
  • Excellent programming skills (e.g., Python, Julia, Java, or C++) and experience with optimization solvers.
  • Very good academic writing and communication skills in English.
  • An open and collaborative attitude and the ability to work effectively in an interdisciplinary and international research environment.

jobs.title: PhD Position Quantum Physics - Rare-earth Ion single Photon Emitter
jobs.description_html:
Creating quantum networks with rare-earth ions

Job description
Silicon-based microchips are the essential building block of modern electronic hardware, such as computers and cell phones. Can silicon also play a critical role in building the next generation of the internet - the quantum internet? In order to realize a fully functional and scalable quantum network, we are developing highly coherent single photon emitters using erbium ions operating in the telecom C-band and directly embedded in a solid state crystal, such as silicon. Crucially, we are able to realize high-quality light-matter interfaces and directly enhance the photon emission into an optical channel using photonic crystal cavities. By leveraging different isotopes for long-lived and programmable quantum registers, we are planning on realizing all the critical parts for a quantum network using fully integrated and highly scalable structures.

In order to help us achieve our ambitious goals, we are looking for a talented and motivated person, with strong curiousity of rare-earth ion physics, single-emitters in solid-state systems or experimental AMO physics. The successful candidate will work in a dynamic team environment.

At the Groeblacher Lab we have a vision: we thrive to be an inclusive place where a diverse mix of talented people want to come, to learn, to live their passion and do their best work. We are dedicated to promoting equality, creating a safe environment for everyone, and believe deeply in diversity of race, gender, sexual orientation, religion, ethnicity, national origin, age, socioeconomic background and all the other fascinating characteristics that make us different. We truly think diversity is a strength and working in a diverse environment, and being exposed to a variety of perspectives makes us stronger scientists and better human beings.

jobs.title: PhD Candidate in AI and Hardware Security
jobs.description_html:
Are you passionate about uncovering and addressing vulnerabilities in AI systems, from algorithms to hardware?

Join Us!
We are looking for a highly motivated candidate with a computer security and/or machine learning background to join the Parallel Computing Systems (PCS) group at the University of Amsterdam. We look for vulnerabilities of AI systems across the whole AI system: from adversarial examples, backdoors and model extraction attacks to physical side-channel and fault injection attacks on AI chips. We build defenses that are both robust and efficient. A strong background in machine learning, hardware or security, together with the drive to develop expertise in the other areas, is highly valued. You'll get hands-on access to the hardware lab and close supervision.

This is what you will do
In this project, you will work to secure AI hardware by investigating vulnerabilities at the algorithm, software, and hardware levels and developing countermeasures to address them. You will study how weaknesses in one layer can be exploited through another. For example, side-channel leakage from an accelerator can be used to extract neural network parameters.

Tasks and responsibilities:
  • designing and carrying out realistic security evaluations on AI algorithms and hardware, such as model extraction, fault injection, and side-channel analysis, on platforms including NPUs, GPUs and other AI chips;
  • investigating how vulnerabilities arise and how weaknesses at the algorithm, software, and hardware levels interact, and developing models and tools to explain these mechanisms;
  • developing models and tools to explain why these vulnerabilities arise. Designing hardware-aware countermeasures that are robust, low-overhead and practical to deploy;
  • validating your methods experimentally on real device in hardware lab, not only in simulation;
  • publishing your results in leading international conference and journals, and completing a PhD thesis within four years;
  • presenting your work at international venues and helping to build collaborations with academic and industrial partners;
  • contributing to teaching (about 10% of your time), for example as a teaching assistant or by supervising Bachelor and Master students.

What we ask of you
Your experience and profile
  • an MSc in computer science or a related field;
  • a strong background and interest in AI and hardware security;
  • a demonstrated ability to perform research (for instance in the form of publications or a Master thesis);
  • the willingness to work collaboratively with other researchers;
  • professional command of English and presentation skills

This is what we offer you
A temporary contract for 38 hours per week for the duration of 4 years (the initial contract will be for a period of 18 months and after satisfactory evaluation it will be extended for a total duration of 4 years). The preferred starting date is as soon as possible. This should lead to a dissertation (PhD thesis). We will draft an educational plan that includes attendance of courses and (international) meetings. We also expect you to assist in teaching undergraduates and master students.

The gross monthly salary, based on 38 hours per week and dependent on relevant experience, ranges between € 3,204 to € 4,051 (scale P). This does not include 8% holiday allowance and 8,3% year-end allowance. The UFO profile PhD Candidate is applicable. A favourable tax agreement, the ‘30% ruling’, may apply to non-Dutch applicants. The Collective Labour Agreement of Universities of the Netherlands is applicable.

Curious about our extensive secondary benefits package? You can read more about it here.

You will work in this team
The Faculty of Science has a student body of around 8,000, as well as 1,800 members of staff working in education, research or support services. Researchers and students at the Faculty of Science are fascinated by every aspect of how the world works, be it elementary particles, the birth of the universe or the functioning of the brain.

The mission of the Informatics Institute (IvI) is to perform curiosity-driven and use-inspired fundamental research in Computer Science. The main research themes are Artificial Intelligence, Computational Science and Systems and Network Engineering. Our research involves complex information systems at large, with a focus on collaborative, data driven, computational and intelligent systems, all with a strong interactive component.

The Parallel Computing Systems (PCS) group at the University of Amsterdam performs research on the design, programming and run-time management of parallel and distributed computer systems. The modeling, analysis and optimization of the extra-functional aspects of these systems, such as performance, power/energy consumption, thermals, reliability, and security but also the degree of productivity to design and program these systems, play a pivotal role in this work.

Want to know more about our organisation? Read more about working at the University of Amsterdam.

If you feel the profile fits you, and you are interested in the job, we look forward to receiving your application. You can apply online via the button below. We accept applications until and including 25 October 2026.

Applications should include the following information (all files besides your cv should be submitted in one single pdf file):
  • a detailed CV including the months (not just years) when referring to your education and work experience;
  • a letter of motivation;
  • the names and email addresses of two references who can provide letters of recommendation.

jobs.description:
Three Doctoral Positions in History and Theory of Urban Design and Architecture Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Three Doctoral Positions in History and Theory of Urban Design and Architecture 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair of the History and Theory of Urban Design (Prof. Dr. Tom Avermaete) at the Institute for the History and Theory of Architecture (gta), ETH Zürich, is looking for three doctoral candidates within the ERC Advanced Grant Project “Co-opolis: Another Architectural History of the European City (1890–1990).” The positions are expected to start in March 2027 and are fully funded for four years. Project background The ERC Project explores how third-sector actors, such as cooperatives, mutual aid societies, associations, and other collective institutions, co-produced the city following precise values and collectivist agendas centred on the shared provision, usage, and maintenance of built resources, resulting in housing and civic structures (e.g., people’s palaces, cultural centres) that complemented and shaped the urban spaces produced by the state and the market. To this end, the project compares selected examples from Sweden, France, and Switzerland from 1890 to 1990 to examine how the ideologies and practices of third-sector actors influenced the built environment within the evolving frameworks of European welfare states. The project seeks to demonstrate the contribution of collective initiatives to the making of contemporary European cities and to assess the lessons they can offer for current challenges such as affordable housing, social inclusion, and sustainable urban development. Job description The three PhD candidates within the “Co-opolis” project will investigate the conditions of emergence, spatial characteristics, and endurance of architectural and urban projects at the intersection of welfare regimes and third-sector collective actors in France, Sweden, and Switzerland over the project’s timeframe. Each candidate will focus on one of these countries, examining how housing projects and civic infrastructures developed through the initiatives of third-sector actors within different welfare regimes. Specifically, the candidates will: Focus on the line of enquiry previously described, producing research on the case studies as well as bringing their own original ideas to the topic. For this reason, we ask potential candidates to include a short description of a possible research direction with the application documents. Complete the PhD dissertation within the given timeframe (March 2027–March 2031). Contribute to the activities and outputs of the overall ERC project, such as workshops, seminars, authoring articles, presenting their research at international conferences, and contributing to the project’s website. Actively engage with the courses and seminars of the PhD programme at the gta Institute, as well as in the academic activities of the Chair of the History and Theory of Urban Design, including participation in research discussions and occasional contributions to teaching activities, such as critiques, reviews, and examinations. jobs.description:
Doctoral Student in Environmental Bioengineering Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in Environmental Bioengineering 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Environmental Microfluidics Group of Prof. Roman Stocker in the Institute of Environmental Engineering is seeking a dynamic and motivated doctoral student with an engineering background for a project on how bacterial chemotaxis accelerates plasmid transfer, including the spread of antibiotic resistance. The position is funded by a recently awarded SNSF grant, and the project is a joint effort with Prof. Jonasz Slomka at the University of Warsaw. This position will be based in the laboratory of Prof. Roman Stocker. Project background Bacterial conjugation, the contact-dependent transfer of plasmids between cells, speeds up bacterial evolution and is a major route for the spread of antibiotic resistance in the environment, which in turn poses a global health threat. Aquatic environments are full of microscale chemical hotspots, such as the nutrient-rich 'phycosphere' around phytoplankton and sinking marine particles, and chemotactic bacteria are known to find and accumulate rapidly at these locations. This project will test the hypothesis that this accumulation enhances plasmid spreading in the environment, contributing to a cutting-edge view of the role of antibiotic resistance in nature. The project seeks to study when, where and how strongly this enhancement operates across different chemical hotspots, fluid flows and bacterial strains, and what it means for the spread of antibiotic resistance among aquatic bacteria. Job description This is a primarily experimental PhD at the interface of engineering and microbiology. The student will: Design, build and characterize new instrumentation to couple existing chemotaxis assays to controlled shear systems. This includes mechanical design, 3D printing, control systems and integration with a fluorescence microscope. Run chemotaxis and conjugation experiments with bacterial donors and recipients of plasmids and a range of chemoattractants, with the opportunity to learn and use advanced techniques such as flow cytometry and plate-reader-based plasmid transfer quantification. Image and track fluorescently labeled bacteria and chemical plumes in shear flow, and analyze the data with quantitative image- and data-analysis pipelines. Test clinically relevant bacteria and freshwater (e.g. lake) bacteria, to assess the potential for chemotaxis-driven spread of resistance in the environment. Contribute data to mathematical models of plasmid spread. Profile We are looking for a hands-on, skilled and curious engineer who loves to build new tools and is interested in using them to answer fundamental scientific questions. Ideal candidates hold an MSc degree in bioengineering, mechanical engineering, mechatronics, electrical engineering, environmental engineering, physics or a related discipline, and have some (not necessarily all) of the following skills: Practical experience in prototyping and manufacturing, for example CAD, 3D printing, machining (strongly preferred). Experience with control systems and instrumentation, for example motor control, sensors, microcontrollers, and automation or data-acquisition code (Python, MATLAB, LabVIEW or similar) (preferred). Openness to gain experience in the microbiology laboratory: bacterial cultures, sterile technique, plate readers and flow cytometry. Familiarity with microscopy, image analysis, fluid mechanics or microfluidics (beneficial but not necessary). Fluency in English (oral and written), enthusiasm for working in an interdisciplinary and international team, and the drive to pursue scientific excellence (required). You will be guided by Prof. Roman Stocker and by members of his lab with extensive experience in microbiology, experimental techniques and environmental processes. You will have the opportunity to work in a cutting-edge, fast-paced research environment, interact with researchers from many different disciplines (engineers, physicists, microbiologists, oceanographers, chemists, mathematicians), gain technical experience across diverse research approaches and interact with world-class collaborators. Two Doctoral Positions in Tropical Forest Ecology, Animal-Plant Interactions and Forest Restoration Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Two Doctoral Positions in Tropical Forest Ecology, Animal-Plant Interactions and Forest Restoration 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Species Interactions and Ecosystem Health group at ETH Zürich is seeking two motivated Doctoral candidates to join the SNSF Starting Grant project AniCaRes – Animating Carbon Restoration: The Role of Animals in Carbon Sequestration During Forest Restoration. Tropical forest restoration is a key strategy for addressing climate change and biodiversity loss. However, forest recovery depends not only on trees but also on animals, which influence seed dispersal, soil processes, plant establishment and seedling survival. AniCaRes investigates how animal communities shape tropical forest regeneration and carbon recovery across spatial scales. The project combines tropical field experiments, molecular ecology, DNA metabarcoding/eDNA, animal monitoring, remote sensing and ecological modelling, with fieldwork primarily in Panama and Brazil. Job description We are recruiting candidates for two complementary Doctoral projects: Doctoral position 1 – Animals, seed dispersal and seedling establishment The project will investigate how animals influence forest regeneration through seed dispersal, nutrient cycling and the dispersal of soil microorganisms, particularly mycorrhizal fungi The candidate will combine field experiments, molecular approaches and ecological analyses Fieldwork will primarily take place in Panama, in collaboration with the Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) Doctoral position 2 – Herbivory, animal communities and seedling survival The project will investigate how herbivores and predators influence seedling survival, plant community composition and carbon recovery in regenerating tropical forests The candidate will work with exclusion experiments, animal monitoring, vegetation surveys and ecological modelling Fieldwork will primarily take place in Brazil Both candidates will work closely with the PI, other group members and an international network of collaborators They will contribute to data collection, analysis, scientific publications and dissemination of project results Profile We are looking for highly motivated candidates with a strong interest in tropical ecology, animal-plant interactions, biodiversity, forest restoration and ecosystem functioning. Applicants should have: A Master's degree in ecology, biology, environmental sciences or a related discipline Strong interest in quantitative ecological research and tropical ecosystems Experience with data analysis, preferably in R and/or Python Ability and willingness to conduct extended fieldwork in tropical environments Excellent written and spoken English Ability to work independently as well as collaboratively in an international research team Previous experience with molecular laboratory work, DNA-based ecological methods and/or fieldwork in tropical ecosystems will be considered a strong asset. Experience with GIS, remote sensing, animal monitoring, experimental ecology or ecological modelling is also advantageous, but candidates are not expected to have expertise in all these areas. jobs.description:
Doctoral Students in Quantum Networking with Superconducting Circuits Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Students in Quantum Networking with Superconducting Circuits 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Quantum Device Lab is looking for highly motivated Doctoral Students for the development of a superconducting qubit quantum network and research in quantum networking applications. A team of researchers led by Andreas Wallraff from the Quantum Device Lab , at the Department of Physics of ETH Zurich has developed a unique superconducting qubit system consisting of two dilution refrigerators equipped with superconducting qubit chips, separated by 30 meters, and connected through a cryogenic link. By exchanging microwave photons across the link, this system can generate remote entanglement between the separated chips as a resource for quantum information experiments and applications. The platform has already enabled demonstrations including loophole-free Bell tests and randomness amplification . We are now expanding the platform through advances in chip fabrication, packaging, networking protocols, and distributed control systems. These developments will enable research into further potential application areas of quantum networks, including loss-tolerant photonic state transfer, distributed quantum computing and quantum error correction, blind quantum computing, and non-local sensing. To ensure this project's success and fast progress, we are looking for highly motivated Doctoral Students in quantum networking with superconducting circuits. Job description You will become part of our team developing and running a two-node quantum network You will be working closely with the rest of the Quantum Device Lab, a well-established research group with a strong background in quantum computing with superconducting qubits, and be able to both benefit from the expertise developed there and contribute to its progress You will perform collaborative research towards the realization of quantum networking technologies You will get to contribute to diverse aspects of the experimental effort, both technical (design of electronics and mechanical components, building of microwave setups, fabrication of superconducting circuit chips) and conceptual (design of experiments, exploring quantum networking applications, planning of future research strategies) In the lab, you will pursue the development of the platform by enabling and implementing quantum networking protocols on a network of multi-qubit superconducting circuit chips Profile You have a strong interest in experimental realizations of quantum information processing systems, with a focus on remote and non-local applications You are dedicated to pursuing a successful career in research, development, or education, either in academia or industry You have experience and a proven record in one or more of the following: Quantum information processing and its implementations (e.g. with superconducting circuits, quantum dots, ion traps, NMR) Experimental quantum optics and atomic physics (cavity quantum electrodynamics) Micro and nano-electronic devices and their fabrication (lithography and deposition techniques) Quantum networking and remote entanglement generation Mesoscopic solid state physics Low temperature physics Microwave electronics Digital electronics FPGAs Instrumentation, drivers, and software development Workplace Workplace We offer Your project is embedded into the Swiss Quantum Science and Technology network, the Quantum Center at ETH Zurich, and into the broader context of a diverse set of international research projects. You will have the unique opportunity to contribute to a strong research program conducted at a leading European research institution. ETH Zurich provides a stimulating interdisciplinary research environment in quantum information science. jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in High Intensity Electron Sources for Future Accelerators Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in High Intensity Electron Sources for Future Accelerators 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken Our research group, based at the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI), explores new technologies for future accelerator facilities. Through the development of new technologies and techniques, we develop high intensity particle sources, high gradient particle accelerators and beam diagnostics systems that measure beam qualities down to the sub-femtosecond regime. Our research combines beam/plasma physics, unique RF technologies and high-power lasers to realise the accelerators that exist within the Paul Scherrer Institute and reaching beyond with contributions to CERN’s future circular collider (FCC). This Doctoral Position will be based at PSI Villigen but with teaching assistant duties at ETH Zurich. Project background The project involves developing electron sources for future accelerator facilities at PSI and the institute’s contributions to the FCC. A central shared challenge is shaping the electron beam as it is generated or shortly afterward. For the FCC, precise control of the laser profile in the RF photogun enables the flexible filling schemes needed for top-up operation. For X-ray free-electron lasers, like SwissFEL, transverse laser shaping and early RF compression are key to producing brighter electron beams. This PhD project will advance beam-shaping techniques for both applications. Job description Commission a new electron source test stand and demonstrate pulse-to-pulse modulation of bunch charge, beam size, and laser pulse energy relevant to the FCC-ee electron source concept Compare laser-shaping techniques through beam measurements, build a prototype for photocathode operation, and investigate machine-learning/AI-based optimization to improve performance Study photocathode and laser performance, including the lifetime of semiconductor photocathodes at bunch charges of up to 5 nC Measure gains in beam brightness from both photocathode laser shaping and RF compression with applications to a SwissFEL upgrade (SwissFEL+) Profile Master’s degree (or equivalent) in physics, accelerator science, electrical engineering, photonics, or a closely related field Strong interest in accelerator physics, electron sources and experimental work; experience with beam dynamics, lasers/optics, numerical modelling or scientific programming is an advantage A practical, independent and analytical working style, combined with enthusiasm for interdisciplinary collaboration Professional proficiency in English; knowledge of German is an asset Workplace Workplace We offer We are a dynamic, interdisciplinary research group committed to innovation and collaboration. Doctoral Student in Glaciology and Glacial Hazards Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Student in Glaciology and Glacial Hazards 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We are looking for a Doctoral Student to join the team of the Professorship of Glaciology for four years. Our group is affiliated with ETH’s Laboratory of Hydraulics, Hydrology and Glaciology (VAW) as well as the Swiss Federal Institute for Forest, Snow and Landscape Research (WSL). Project background The Doctoral Student is offered within the project Stability of cold hanging glaciers under climate warming in the French and Swiss Alps (ICEFAL). ICEFAL is composed of a Swiss-French consortium studying the effects of rising ice temperatures on the stability of cold hanging glaciers and their likelihood to be the source of large ice avalanches. The overarching goal of the project is to provide a data-driven method to create an index of hazard potential for all hanging glaciers in the French and Swiss Alps, with applicability beyond the study region. The index combines geometric and thermal considerations. To achieve this goal, the project combines fieldwork, state-of-the-art thermo-mechanical modeling, and regional-scale geospatial analyses. Job description To achieve the project goals, the successful candidate will: Create an inventory of hanging glaciers using manual mapping and possibly machine-learning aided approaches Perform field measurements at high-elevation sites in Switzerland The goal is to  collect measurements of ice temperatures, which will be complemented with mass balance measurements, firn cores, and analyses of long-term ice-avalanche monitoring data Leverage the collected field data as well as available meteorological data to drive a state-of-the-art thermo-mechanical model (Elmer/Ice) to investigate the past and future evolution of the temperature field of the investigated glaciers and possible repercussions on stability Predict basal temperatures of hanging glaciers from approaches developed at VAW-Glaciology and by project partners, and intersect these with stability criteria to derive a hazard index for hanging glaciers in the study region The work will be supported by postdoctoral and senior researchers of VAW-Glaciology and is based in Zurich. Profile The successful candidate brings a combination of the following skills and experiences to the project: Required : A Master’s degree in geophysics, physics, environmental or earth science, environmental engineering, or related fields Excellent knowledge of English, both in oral and written form (C1 to C2) Desired background and interest in the following topics: A keen interest in high-mountain hazards A solid foundation in math and physics Glaciologic training or expertise A willingness to conduct fieldwork in a high-mountain environment Geospatial analysis and processing skills (e.g., QGIS) Experience with hazard and risk management concepts Prior experience with physics-based numerical modeling Familiarity with a scripting language (e.g.,  Python or Matlab) Outdoor or mountaineering experiences Interest and experience working in teams Knowledge of German and/or French We stress that successful applicants do not need to come with all desired skills/experiences. Furthermore, candidates with non-traditional academic backgrounds are strongly encouraged to apply. jobs.title: Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels
jobs.description:
Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral Position in Risk-Based Inspection and Maintenance Planning of Tunnels 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Chair of Infrastructure Management, led by Professor Dr. Bryan T. Adey within the Institute of Construction and Infrastructure Management of the Department of Civil, Environmental and Geomatic Engineering, has an opening for a doctoral student. This position focuses risk-based inspection and maintenance planning for tunnels, including probabilistic risk updating, Value of Information analysis, and intervention program optimisation. This position is part of an interdisciplinary SNSF project in collaboration with the Free University of Bozen-Bolzano, the Hagerbach Test Gallery, and the EuroTube Foundation. The preferred starting date is 1 February 2027, although other dates are negotiable. Project background Tunnels are critical links in transport networks, and many Swiss road and rail tunnels are ageing while being subject to increasing traffic loads, climate-related stressors, and evolving safety requirements. Their maintenance involves two interdependent asset domains, namely structural elements, such as lining, portals, and drainage, and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing systems, such as ventilation, lighting, and fire detection. In current practice, these domains are managed largely in isolation, inspections remain heavily manual, and evidence from different campaigns, sensors, and specialists is fragmented across separate reports and databases. Interventions are therefore often planned using disjointed evidence and conservative heuristics, even where substantial data exist. The project Predictive, Resilient, Integrated Systems for Management of Tunnel (PRISM-T), funded by the SNSF, addresses this challenge through an integrated digital twin workflow for tunnel maintenance decision support. Heterogeneous inspection and monitoring evidence is transformed into uncertainty-aware condition indicators, which are used to update risk, to assess whether additional information is worth collecting, and to derive executable intervention programs. Extended reality (XR) is used to validate decisions and to guide inspection and maintenance work on site. The workflow is developed and validated in the Tunnel Digitalisation Centre of the Hagerbach Test Gallery in Flums, and its transferability is tested at the DemoTube facility of the EuroTube Foundation in Dübendorf. Regular field work at both sites and close collaboration with the partner team in Bolzano form an integral part of the doctoral research. Within this project, the doctoral position addresses the decision layer of the workflow, in which maintenance decision processes are formalised and uncertainty-aware condition indicators, developed in a companion doctoral position, are used to update risk and to optimise intervention programs under realistic tunnel constraints. Job description The successful candidate will map and formalise current tunnel maintenance decision processes for the structural and mechanical, electrical, and plumbing domains through workshops and interviews with practitioners. On this basis, risk and consequence models based on Bayesian networks will be formulated, and incremental risk updating methods will be developed. A computationally tractable Value of Information analysis will be developed using approximation strategies, such as surrogate models and scenario reduction. Intervention program optimisation models accounting for sequencing, bundling, access windows, and resource constraints will be formulated and solved, with outputs traceable to the underlying evidence. The candidate will contribute to validation campaigns at the Hagerbach Test Gallery and the EuroTube Foundation. Profile A Master’s degree in civil engineering, operations research, industrial engineering, applied mathematics, or a related field A strong background in probabilistic modelling, reliability and risk analysis, and mathematical optimisation Very good programming skills, preferably in Python, and experience with optimisation solvers Familiarity with infrastructure asset management, Bayesian networks, decision analysis, Value of Information analysis, or business process modelling would be considered an advantage Willingness to carry out field work in underground environments and to collaborate within an interdisciplinary and international team Proficiency in written and spoken English is required, and knowledge of German is regarded as an asset Workplace Workplace We offer ETH Zurich is one of the world’s leading universities specialising in science and technology. You choose up to three professors you would like to work with, and they review your application. Application deadline: 27 November 2026. Robotic Locomotion and Manipulation: legged robots, robot arms, and hands that move and act reliably in complex terrain and contact-rich tasks. Biohybrid Robots: robots built from living cells, engineered tissue, and synthetic materials, actuated by muscle and powered by chemical energy. jobs.title: PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics
jobs.description:
PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht PhD Position in Experimental Nonlinear Dynamics and Nanomechanics 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We are looking for a highly motivated PhD student to join our nonlinear dynamics team. Do you have a broad interest in physics and technology? Do you like the prospect of working in an experimental project in close collaboration with theory? Are you creative, persevering, independent, and a good team player? You can expect a cutting-edge research project that is very challenging due to the many aspects of science that are involved. For the same reason, it is a highly rewarding experience if you enjoy expanding your knowledge beyond textbook physics. We look forward to meeting you! Project background Is it possible to build artificial neural networks from driven nonlinear resonators? This question builds on the ideas of Hopfield and Hinton, but takes them out of equilibrium: in our resonators, a balance of continuous drive and dissipation sustains stable oscillation states. This gives us access to phenomena that are absent in equilibrium physics. For example, this may allow us to investigate how a physical network turns stored memories into dynamical patterns. In our lab, each node is an electrical circuit or a micro-electromechanical (MEMS) resonator implementing a Kerr parametric oscillator (KPO): a driven, dissipative resonator with two stable oscillation states that act like a bit of memory. We couple several such KPOs, reading out every oscillator simultaneously and in real time. This gives us complete access to the dynamical many-body phase space. With it, we reconstruct the attractor landscape of the network, track how noise drives switching between collective states, and measure probability currents that appear when detailed balance is broken. The central question is whether these currents organize into stable, reproducible temporal patterns and coexisting limit cycles. Networks like these bridge nonequilibrium statistical physics and neuromorphic computing, and could provide a physical route to Ising and Boltzmann machines that operate on dynamical rather than static states. Job description Build and operate a programmable network of coupled KPOs with up to eight nodes, including control and readout electronics and measurement software. Map attractor landscapes, switching statistics and probability currents from measured trajectories. Compare experiment with simulations and analytical models in close contact with our theory partners (Prof. O. Zilberberg at the University of Konstanz) and publish and present your results internationally. Profile You hold (or are about to complete) an MSc in physics, electrical engineering or a related field, with a solid background in nanomechanics, nonlinear dynamics, or statistical physics. You enjoy hands-on experimental work (electronics, signal processing, Python) and are not afraid of a bit of analytical theory. Experience with MEMS, lock-in detection, or FPGAs is a plus. You communicate well in English. jobs.description:
Doctoral position in cognitive and moral heuristics in lay people’s reactions to climate change adaptation Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht Doctoral position in cognitive and moral heuristics in lay people’s reactions to climate change adaptation 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken We are looking for a motivated doctoral student who is interested in applying psychological concepts and methodologies to environmental topics. The position is available starting January 2027. Project background While climate change mitigation (e.g., reduction of greenhouse gas emissions) remains important, it is also clear that societies need to adapt to the unavoidable hazards associated with climate change. The recent heat waves in Europe and the health and economical damages they caused, exemplify that adaptation measures are not yet sufficiently in place. Heuristics (mental shortcuts) can bias people’s risk perceptions and affect moral considerations. As such they can influence people’s private adaptation behaviors and their perceptions of technologies that could help societies to deal better with the consequences of climate change. By influencing regulations, they can also impact the exposure of vulnerable groups to hazards, such as heat. The aim of this doctoral thesis is to gain insights in how cognitive and moral heuristics influence the effective implementation of climate change adaptation measures. Job description Conceptualization and conduction of empirical studies (quantitative or qualitative designs are possible) Writing manuscripts and publishing studies in scientific journals Dissemination of research results (e.g., at conferences) Supervising bachelor and master students Supporting lectures Profile Master’s degree in psychology, environmental science, or social sciences Knowledge and first experiences with descriptive and inferential statistics Advanced German and English skills Ability to think conceptually and work independently Strong interest in research and methodologies from psychology and social sciences Workplace Workplace We offer Your job with impact: Become part of ETH Zurich, which not only supports your professional development, but also actively contributes to positive change in society You can expect numerous benefits , such as public transport season tickets and car sharing, a wide range of sports offered by the ASVZ , childcare and attractive pension benefits chevron_right Working, teaching and research at ETH Zurich We value diversity and sustainability In line with our values , ETH Zurich encourages an inclusive culture. PhD Position in Atmospheric Chemistry Sprachauswahl FAQ de Deutsch English Stellenportal chevron_left Übersicht chevron_left Übersicht PhD Position in Atmospheric Chemistry 100%, Zurich, fixed-term print Drucken The Atmospheric Chemistry group at the Institute for Atmospheric and Climate Science (IAC) – ETH Zurich invites applications for a 4-year PhD position on “Investigating oxidized nitrogen in the troposphere”. The Atmospheric Chemistry group at ETH conducts research exploring the processes controlling tropospheric composition (gases and particles) and their intersection with global change. Research makes extensive use of global modeling tools (GEOS-Chem and CESM) and analysis of large observational datasets. Nitrogen oxides (NOx) emitted into the troposphere contribute to the formation of fine particulate matter (PM2.5) and ozone (O3). NOx thus plays a central role in global air quality and climate. Despite this key role, the complex cycling of NOx with other forms of oxidized nitrogen in the troposphere is not well constrained. Our growing understanding of sources and chemical transformations are not yet well represented or tested in large-scale models. The goals of this PhD project will be to better represent these processes in a global 3D model, to test resulting simulations against airborne, surface, and satellite observations, and finally, to investigate how changing NOx emissions have altered the cycling and impacts of tropospheric NOx over time. Job description Develop skills in atmospheric chemistry, global modeling, and data analysis of field observations. Have opportunities to develop scientific communication skills through presentations at conferences. Develop skills in writing scientific papers and in management by co-supervising bachelor’s and master’s theses. The project will be supervised by Prof. Colette Heald. Profile Applicants should hold an MSc degree in atmospheric science, earth science, environmental science, chemistry, physics, or a related discipline (obtained prior to the PhD start date) The candidate will have experience in atmospheric chemistry. Experience with regional or global modeling is desirable. Strong programming skills are necessary. Good knowledge of English (spoken and written) is essential.
