jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Engineering Gene Drives for Pest Insect Suppression
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Professor Tracey Chapman

Mediterranean fruitfly (medfly) is a global agricultural pest that causes annual billion-dollar losses and threatens food security. It is predicted to spread to the UK within the next 2 decades due to climate warming. CRISPR-based technologies enable significant advances for population suppression, and gene drives in particular offer promise for self-propagating, sustainable alternatives to pesticides for medfly and other key pests. However, a central obstacle remains: existing drives in medfly work in principle but are not field-ready. Through the receipt of interdisciplinary training, you will build, test and optimise critical components needed to close the gap to field readiness for this innovative control technology.

Based at the UEA, you will gain in-demand skills in CRISPR design, gene drive construction, single-nucleus transcriptomics, quantitative phenotyping and population modelling, supported by placements at Keele (applied agricultural entomology) and Imperial College (gene drives, synthetic biology).

You will develop and apply a split-drive optimisation pipeline, using the separation of Cas9 and gRNA components to directly identify the parameters that govern gene drive performance. A key focus is discrimination and optimisation: isolating which promoters, guides and targets improve homing while suppressing the factors that degrade drive efficiency such as resistance alleles and shadow drive. You will focus initially on optimising components and establishing phenotyping protocols, before moving on to selecting targets to test for field-deployability. Throughout, you will build translational insights.

You will be immersed within a tailored training environment designed to foster innovation and independence. This will equip you with state-of-the-art skills in CRISPR editing, cloning, insect handling, bioinformatics, and modelling, giving you a strong set of varied skills for future career development and ensuring that you are well-prepared to contribute to genetic biocontrol innovations from concept to application.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: From Brain to Germline: How Perception Affects Genetic Inheritance
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:  

Natural environments are changing rapidly as average temperatures rise and heatwaves become more frequent. How species respond will help determine whether populations adapt or decline. Reproduction is especially vulnerable: fertility can be disrupted at temperatures below those that threaten survival, and males are often more sensitive than females. 

Heat can also alter the genetic and epigenetic information carried by sperm and eggs. These changes may be passed to offspring and affect how later generations respond to temperature. They are usually assumed to result from direct heat damage to reproductive tissues in exposed organisms. 

And alternative idea is that temperature-sensing neurons, without increasing the temperature, can change small RNAs and the activity of transposable elements in the germline. This raises an important question: can sensing heat prepare or protect the germline before damage occurs? This project will test whether the germline responds to perceived as well as actual temperature change, and whether these responses influence future generations. 

Methodology:  

You will test how zebrafish react to perceived and actual temperature changes, and perform experimental work by training fish and measuring the effects on phenotypic data such as behavioural changes as well as effects of their offspring. You will collect samples for transcriptome sequencing and molecular assays and perform bioinformatic analyses on the resulting data. Multigenerational crosses and fitness assays in juvenile and adult fish will determine whether these changes are inherited, improve survival or reproduction under later heat stress, or carry costs in later generations. Together, these approaches will reveal whether sensing temperature prepares the germline and helps populations adapt to climate change. 

Training:  

You will gain practical experience in a wide range of skills including animal husbandry and behavioural conditioning, experimental and multigenerational design, and fitness assays in juvenile and adult fish. You will develop molecular and computational skills through quantitative PCR, small-RNA and transcriptome sequencing, statistical analysis and bioinformatics, while building expertise in evolution, genomics, physiology and reproductive biology. Training in scientific writing, presentation and career development will be supported through ARIES courses, conferences, local seminars, research discussion groups and journal clubs.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The Net Effect of Sex on Adaptation
jobs.description_html:
Background  

Why is sexual reproduction nearly ubiquitous among eukaryotes? Investing into offspring that are only half yours is known as the 2-fold cost of sex. What stops an asexual mutant lineage from invading and taking over? One hypothesis is that sex allows more efficient purging of deleterious mutations from the genome. But not all genetic variation is selected in such a sexually concordant (SC) way. Sexually antagonistic (SA) genetic variation, where opposite alleles are fitter in males versus females, can drive populations toward extinction and/or maintain genetic variation for future adaptation. The relative impact of SA versus SC selection in the long-run remains untested. This integrative project will advance our understanding of the impact of sex on evolutionary adaptation with relevance to wildlife management, preparing you for careers in academia and industry alike. 

Project 

The research integrates comparative genomics in Drosophila with population genetic simulations: 

  • What is the net effect of males?  

- Computer simulations in SLiM to establish the theoretical net effect of SA and SC selection on population viability and adaptation. 

  • Is sex-specific selection adaptive in the long-run?  

- Comparing lab-estimated genomic targets of selection among ten Drosophila species. 

  • How do facultatively asexual species differ?  

- Contrasting genomic targets of sex-specific selection between ten obligate sexual versus six facultatively asexual species of Drosophila.  

  • How has sex-specific selection shaped Drosophila’s temperate-climate adaptation?  

- Population genomic analyses of SA and SC genomic targets in relation to Drosophila’s recent adaptation out of Africa.  

 Training  

UEA is an enriching research environment, part of the broader Norwich Research Park including numerous biotech institutes offering bioinformatic training and support. The department features a highly collaborative community of leading experts in evolutionary biology and forms part of the Centre for Ecology, Evolution and Conservation. You will receive direct training from the primary supervisor (KG) and his lab in evolutionary theory, population genetics, Drosophila husbandry, experimental design, biological statistics, bioinformatics, and scientific writing.

Degree in biology / ecology / evolution / genetics / similar 

Helpful skills: Drosophila experience, evolutionary knowledge, enthusiasm to learn statistics / coding / bioinformatics.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Quantification and Characterisation of Genetic Diversity and Population Structure of Wild Fisheries Species
jobs.description_html:
The characterisation of genetic diversity and demographic structure of fish populations are essential in assessing and maintaining stocks sustainability.  

Population structure and genetic diversity of stocks have mainly been assessed using limited genetic markers. While useful for broad population estimates, these methods lack power to quantify gene flow and cannot detect structural variants. Furthermore, fish population demographics are commonly estimated from otolith growth rings, a destructive method requiring specialist expertise and sacrifice of individuals. In contrast, long-read DNA sequencing generates genome fragments tens to hundred of kilobases with high accuracy capturing both single nucleotide  and structural variants. These technologies also detect chromatin methylation, enabling non-lethal and accurate age prediction from small tissue samples. 

With CEFAS researchers, this project aims at 1) generating pangenomes to capture genomic variation, 2) quantifying genetic diversity, 3) characterising population demographics for commercially harvested populations of two species: the Atlantic Blue Fin tuna (Thunnus thynnus) and the Atlantic herring (Clupea harengus). These species exhibit contrasting population trends in UK waters. The Atlantic Bluefin tuna has recovered from severe decline and is now classified by the IUCN as Least Concern, whereas herring stocks continue to fluctuate and face reduced catch limits.  By comparing diversity, population structure, and demographic patterns in these species, the project will provide insights into their evolutionary histories and support more effective, sustainable fisheries management. 

The student will gain highly transferable skills in bioinformatics, genomics, and population genetics, fisheries management and evidence-based policy making. Engagement with academic and industrial collaborators will provide exposure to advanced long-read sequencing methodologies and analytical approaches. The project is expected to generate at least two publications. Participation in journal clubs, lab-meetings, conferences, and collaborative research networks will support professional development and scientific independence. The student will be encouraged to  explore new questions inspired by their aspirations, such as population modelling, and demographic forecasting. Leveraging our collaborative networks, the student could extend the geographical remits of their investigations. 

We are looking for an enthusiastic student with interests in genomics, population genomics applied to the sustainable management of fish stock. Experience in population genetics and genomics would be desirable.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Engineering Biology to Decode Gene Regulatory Networks in Lateral Root Initiation
jobs.description_html:
Are you a motivated undergraduate with a passion for engineering biology and plant science?

We’re offering an exciting PhD opportunity with the Guiziou Group at the Earlham Institute using engineering biology and single-cell genomic technology to drive forward our understanding of lateral root initiation.

This PhD project aims to use DNA-based recorders (based on serine integrase) to reconstruct the gene expression programme during lateral root founder cell specification. You will combine this cutting-edge methodology with single-cell RNA sequencing to dissect spatiotemporal gene regulation of lateral root initiation.

You will build and optimise integrase-based genetic circuits in Arabidopsis to record the order in which genes of interest are expressed. Using fluorescence microscopy, you will analyse the resulting Arabidopsis lines to better understand the gene regulatory network underlying lateral root founder cell specification, with high spatiotemporal resolution.

You will also use single-cell RNA sequencing (combined with FACS) to determine the cell state of precise lateral root founder cell subpopulations marked with the engineered genetic circuit. During this project, you will develop your critical thinking and scientific independence, with the final part of the project being up to you to shape.

This project offers:

  • Comprehensive training in engineering biology, automation, molecular biology, microscopy, plant transformation, protoplasting, FACS, single-cell RNA sequencing and analysis.
  • Opportunities to present your work at international conferences and industry symposia.
  • A vibrant, supportive research environment with excellent career progression: past students at the Earlham Institute became biotech CEOs, group leaders, and research scientists.
  • A highly collaborative and supportive research community with access to training and career development opportunities across the Norwich Research Park.

You will become an expert in plant engineering biology through this project and take part in the mission of the Guiziou group, which is to have a tangible impact on sustainable agriculture.

jobs.title: PhD Studentdship: Design, Modelling and Experimental Investigation of Inflatable and Multistable Mechanical Metamaterials
jobs.description_html:
Research Studentship in Engineering

3.5-year DPhil studentship 

Project: Design, Modelling and Experimental Investigation of Inflatable and Multistable Mechanical Metamaterials

Supervisor: Prof Antonio Elia Forte

Mechanical metamaterials derive their properties from their internal architecture, offering opportunities to create structures with programmable shape, stiffness and load-bearing capacity. This project will investigate metamaterials formed from inflatable and multistable units, exploring how geometry, internal pressure and interactions between units control their collective mechanical response. Particular emphasis will be placed on designing structures that switch between distinct stable configurations, with the aim of achieving controlled deployment and shape retention.

The project draws on recent advances in vacuum–laser fabrication of programmable soft actuators and reconfigurable inflatables through controlled surface crumpling. These studies demonstrate how fabrication methods and mechanical instabilities can be used to programme the deformation and reconfiguration of inflatable structures.

Based in the RADlab within the University of Oxford’s Department of Engineering Science, the student will combine hands-on fabrication and mechanical testing with nonlinear finite-element analysis, reduced-order modelling and design optimisation. Experimental work will include fabricating inflatable units and assemblies, measuring their deformation and force response, and characterising switching behaviour, load-bearing capacity and repeatability. Computational models will explain the underlying mechanics and guide subsequent designs. Together, these approaches will establish how buckling, snap-through and interactions between units can be harnessed to create reconfigurable materials and deployable structures.

Eligibility

This studentship is funded through the Department of Engineering Science and is open to Home students (full award – home fees plus stipend).

The following skills are highly desirable but not essential:

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Historical genomics of the declining red squirrel in Britain
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:  

The red squirrel in Britain is one of the most iconic examples of a declining population. It has suffered greatly since the introduction of the invasive grey squirrel in the late 1800s, but even before then it was struggling due to hunting and deforestation. However, already since the late 1700s, people have tried to counter the decline by bringing in new red squirrels from continental Europe. How all these past processes have affected the genetic make-up, fitness and ancestry of British squirrels is very poorly understood. 

This project will study the rollercoaster history of the red squirrel in Britain using historical DNA, which promises to add a whole new layer of understanding to the histories of species. By tracing the genetics of the red squirrel over the past few hundred years, the project has two goals: 1) To provide general insights into the genetics of population decline and rescue, broadly applicable across organisms. 2) To reconstruct the specific history of the widely cherished red squirrel, to potentially help future efforts to conserve it. 

Research methodology:  

The project will sequence whole genomes from the few surviving British red squirrel populations, and continental reference populations. It will also use historical DNA techniques to sequence genomes from British squirrels in museum collections, to directly analyse how genetic diversity, inbreeding and genetic load has changed over time, and evaluate the effects that the many past translocations actually had on squirrel populations. The project will also address how much native British squirrel ancestry persists today, to test the hypothesis that the many introductions has led to a complete loss of native ancestry and local genetic adaptations (‘genetic swamping’). 

Training:  

The student will receive broad training in molecular biology, historical DNA, genomics, bioinformatics and population genetics. The student will take part in journal clubs and departmental seminars, present their work at conferences, and develop skills in critical thinking and science communication. 

The ideal candidate will have a background in a biological science (e.g. genetics, molecular biology, zoology, evolution, ancient DNA), and have strong interests in genomics, wet-lab work, data analysis, and evolution.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Good Vibrations: Evidencing the Links Between Soil Acoustics and Soil Health
jobs.description_html:
Soil invertebrates play a major role in carbon cycling, soil aggregation, plant health and food web dynamics. Maintaining and enhancing soil biodiversity is therefore fundamental to optimising soil health and function. However, current methods to monitor soil biodiversity and measure its response to soil and land management practices are costly and intrusive. Acoustic monitoring has long been used in terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems to detect individual species and monitor biodiversity. Recent work suggests a valuable role for acoustics in monitoring soils too, with early studies linking soil acoustic characteristics to invertebrate abundance and diversity and detecting changes in soil acoustic characteristics in response to restoration management. 

Despite its potential, the field of soil acoustics is in its infancy, with key knowledge gaps relating to the impacts of soil characteristics on sound propagation, and the relationship between specific soil acoustic characteristics and critical soil functions. The overarching aim of this project is therefore to better evidence the link between soil acoustics and soil health. Specifically, the student will sample and quantify soil acoustic properties at a portfolio of sites across a mosaic of land-use management, crop type and soil characteristics to: 

Obj1: Parameterise and calibrate the relationship between soil biodiversity and soil acoustic characteristics. 

Obj2: Determine the influence of soil texture/structure and properties such as carbon stocks, moisture content and compaction on this relationship. 

Obj3: Establish the links between soil acoustic characteristics and other factors such as land management practices and above-ground biomass. 

Training: The successful candidate will receive extensive training in field and lab data collection skills and the application of ecological principles and concepts to applied issues. You can expect to achieve a high level of competency in statistical modelling, gain a wide range of skills in critical thinking, scientific writing and science communication, and be encouraged to develop independent lines of research alongside the core objectives.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Cloaks and Daggers: Fitness Effects of Ceratotoxin Antimicrobials in a Global Fruit fly Pest
jobs.description_html:
Strong interdisciplinary training, within the ARIES Ecology and Biodiversity theme, to equip you with high-in-demand analytical skills in phenotypic and molecular genetic engineering. Suiting an individual interested in tackling fundamentally important questions with applied potential for control of insects that threaten food security.

In all species that lay eggs externally - in nests, ponds, mudpiles, food or other substrates - eggs and young may face unpredictable exposure to harmful or beneficial microbes. Mothers may manipulate the immediate microbial environment by provisioning eggs with protective antimicrobial compounds. One enigmatic example - the focus here - occurs in a global agricultural pest, the medfly (Ceratitis capitata). Medfly mothers 'cloak' their eggs with potent, broad-spectrum antimicrobial peptides comprising four 'Ceratotoxins' encoded by 7 genes. These kill microbes by punching holes in them. Offspring from eggs lacking protective antimicrobials are slower to develop, giving the first insight into potential benefits and providing a springboard for you to use phenotype engineering, sequencing and gene-editing tools to determine:

(i)Overall fitness benefits of Ceratotoxin egg cloaks under natural conditions

(ii) Functional significance of Ceratotoxin redundancy

(iii) Potential of Ceratotoxins for insect control

Methodology

(i) Fitness benefits

Test major hypotheses for protective egg cloaks:

  • Protecting eggs and larvae from harmful microbes
  • Protecting the female reproductive tract from sexually transmitted infections
  • Creating a beneficial microbial community for larvae and eggs
  • Facilitating vertical transmission of beneficial microbes

Assays of key fitness measures (survival, fertility, semi-natural conditions) using phenotypic manipulations (egg cloak removal, microbial add-backs), sequencing (16S rDNA of microbial communities) and molecular genetics (CRISPR-Cas9 knock-outs of Ceratotoxin gene combinations).

(ii)Functional redundancy

To determine if Ceratotoxin redundancy is adaptive: (i) test antimicrobial spectrum and potency of synthetic Ceratotoxin peptide mixtures, (ii) assay key fitness measures of gene-edited medflies lacking Ceratotoxins.

(iii) Insect control

Depending upon interests, explore (via experimentation, modelling, or quantitative literature synthesis) different possibilities for Ceratotoxin use in control, including via female-specific lethality, fertility loss, X-chromosome shredding, probiotics.

Training

High-in-demand technical (bioinformatics, molecular genetics, microbiology, phenotype engineering) and transferrable (critical thinking, ethics, Open Research) skills. Embedded in thriving, respectful and inclusive research environment.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Comparative Fisheries Management in the Arctic and Antarctic in a Changing Climate
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Climate change is rapidly altering marine ecosystems, particularly in the polar regions where warming is occurring faster than the global average. Changing ocean conditions are leading to substantial changes in the distribution, abundance and productivity of fish stocks, creating challenges for sustainable fisheries management. 

This exciting interdisciplinary project will investigate how climate change may affect key commercial fish species and fisheries management in both Arctic and Antarctic waters. By comparing these globally important systems, through a combination of ecological modelling, evaluation of management implications and policy analyses, the research will provide important insights into how fisheries management can adapt to future change. 

Research methodology:

Based primarily at BAS with time also spent at Cefas and UEA, the PGR will use ecological, fisheries and environmental datasets to undertake quantitative analyses investigating climate change impacts on polar fish species. This will include ecological modelling, climate projections and risk assessments to examine how future climate scenarios may affect distribution, productivity and vulnerability of key species. Potential study species include commercially important species from both regions, such as Atlantic mackerel, cod and toothfish. They will assess and compare how these changes may affect fisheries management in the Antarctic and Arctic, involving analyses of management measures, governance frameworks and policy processes to examine common challenges and contrasting responses. The research will generate novel outputs, including species vulnerability assessments, climate risk assessments, and comparative analyses of management responses to climate change, and will identify opportunities for climate-resilient fisheries management.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Where Does RNA go in the Cold? Visualising Coolair RNA Inside Plant Cells
jobs.description_html:
Plants cannot escape changes in their environment and must continually adjust their growth and development in response to temperature. Successful propagation of winter annual plants relies on vernalization, where prolonged winter cold triggers epigenetic modifications to ensure plants flower in spring. At the heart of this response is FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC), a gene whose activity is progressively switched off during winter. This process involves COOLAIR, a family of anti-sense, long non-coding RNAs produced from the FLC locus. Although we know that COOLAIR responds dynamically to cold, we understand much less about where these RNA molecules go within individual plant cells and how their location contributes to their function


This PhD will use cutting-edge plant RNA imaging and advanced fluorescence microscopy to visualise COOLAIR within Arabidopsis cells. The student will investigate how different COOLAIR RNA isoforms are spatially organised and how this arrangement changes under constant and fluctuating winter temperatures, including freezing events. Natural genetic variation and mutants affecting COOLAIR transcription and processing will be used to uncover the mechanisms controlling RNA localisation and determine how these influence FLC regulation and flowering. The FLC/COOLAIR system is highly conserved in Brassica crops, giving the work broader relevance to understanding plant adaptation to increasingly variable climates.
The project is highly interdisciplinary and will provide training in RNA biology, molecular biology, plant genetics, advanced microscopy, quantitative image analysis and bioinformatics. The successful applicant will join the Ding laboratory at the John Innes Centre and will be supervised by Prof Yiliang Ding, with day-to-day co-supervision from Dr Susan Duncan and collaboration with Prof Caroline Dean. The student will benefit from complementary expertise in RNA biology, quantitative RNA imaging, vernalization and natural variation within a world-leading plant science research environment.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Future-Proofing Celery with Pangenomics, Trials, and AI-assisted Gene Discovery
jobs.description_html:
Can we stay ahead of an emerging crop disease before it becomes established in Europe? This PhD will use genomics to future-proof celery against Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. apii race 4, a highly virulent pathogen that threatens celery production globally.

Working alongside industry collaborators at Tozer Seeds, you will use cutting-edge genomics to help future-proof celery breeding by identifying independent sources of resistance and translating them into practical breeding solutions.

We have evidence of independent sources of resistance to this pathogen in celery, which need to be characterised before they can be incorporated into more durable cultivars against a rapidly evolving pathogen.

You will analyse a large celery diversity panel, including advanced lines, landraces, naturalised and wild material. You will learn population genomics, evolutionary analysis, structural variation and pangenomic studies at the interface of crop genomics, plant pathology and breeding.

The project will be based at the Earlham Institute, a world-class BBSRC research centre of excellence in genomics, engineering, computational biology and AI. Working in collaboration with Tozer Seeds, you will join a highly collaborative and supportive research community and have access to training and career development opportunities across the Norwich Research Park through the Norwich Research Park Biosciences Doctoral Training Partnership.

You will study how celery performs under high disease pressure in large field trials, exploring resistance-associated loci through genome-wide analyses, including SNP-, k-mer-, haplotype- and pangenome-based approaches. You will also use time-course RNA-seq to investigate how celery responds during infection, asking whether independent resistance sources trigger distinct or shared defence pathways. In the final phase, you will shape your own direction using comparative genomics, NLRome analysis, AI-assisted candidate-gene prioritisation with genomic and protein language models, and breeding genetics.

This project’s core value is translation: turning genomic diversity into practical disease-resistance strategies for sustainable vegetable production. It will build transferable skills in bioinformatics, statistics, reproducible analysis, stakeholder communication and industry-facing research. It will prepare you for careers in crop genomics, plant breeding, agri-tech, bioinformatics, R&D, or academic plant science.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Climate change impacts on the Antarctic coastal ocean carbon sink
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Remote Southern Ocean waters take up ten percent of the carbon dioxide (CO2) emitted by human activity, effectively slowing down global climate change. Wintertime sea ice cover controls CO2 uptake by Antarctic coastal waters. Recent and ongoing rapid sea ice decline, strong glacial melt and warming raise concerns on how these changes will impact future CO2 uptake by these polar waters.

Project objectives:

In this PhD project you will address these aims:

  • Extend the unique, year-round marine carbonate chemistry timeseries (2010-2020, https://www.bas.ac.uk/project/rats/) in Ryder Bay, Antarctica, forward through a period of rapid sea ice decline,
  • Develop an innovative, idealised ocean-ice model of processes affecting ocean CO2 uptake in Ryder Bay,
  • Investigate the impacts of climate-driven changes in biological productivity and sea ice extent on inorganic carbon cycling and ocean CO2 uptake along the Antarctic Peninsula.

Research methodology:

In this varied project you will carry out carbonate chemistry analyses. You will explore the effects of a shift to a low sea ice regime on ocean CO2 uptake in Ryder Bay, using your data and model experiments. You will identify long-term changes in ocean CO2 uptake and their drivers along the Antarctic Peninsula using your data, a surface ocean CO2 synthesis (www.socat.info), associated ocean CO2 products, satellite and reanalysis products.

Training:

You will develop skills in chemical analysis, data processing, visualisation and interpretation using coding (Python or Matlab) and learn to develop an idealised ocean biogeochemical model, while part of UEA’s inspiring Centre for Ocean and Atmospheric Sciences. You will collaborate with the dynamic POLOMINTS (http://polomints.ac.uk/) science team via your supervisors at the British Antarctic Survey and the National Oceanography Centre. You will present your findings at an international scientific conference and in peer-reviewed publications. While Antarctic fieldwork is not part of this project, there may be opportunities for it.

Person specification:

We seek an enthusiastic, pro-active team player with strong scientific interests and self-motivation, combining an aptitude for practical research with numerical skills. You will have a degree in natural sciences, environmental sciences, physics, or similar subject.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Exploring the magmatic plumbing system of the Eastern Caribbean volcanic arc
jobs.description_html:
Scientific Background 

One of the key challenges in volcanology is understanding changes in volcanic activities during periods of unrest, particularly transitions from effusive to eruptive activity. Such transitions present significant challenges for hazard management (Joseph et al., 2022). Physical parameters of volcanic systems, including their location, geometry, size, and their temporal evolution, are critical for modelling volcanic processes and understanding these transitions. Geophysical monitoring provides essential constraints on these parameters. A recent example is the successful forecasting and evacuation efforts during the 2021 La Soufrière eruption in Saint Vincent (Joseph et al., 2022). Despite this success, the structure and evolution of the magmatic plumbing system within the shallow crust remain poorly understood. 

Research Methodology 

This project will investigate the crustal structure of the East Caribbean island arc, initially focusing on Saint Vincent. Using seismic data from the Seismic Research Centre (SRC) at the University of the West Indies, together with recordings from a large seismic experiment in 2026, the candidate will apply ambient noise tomography to image the shallow upper crust (Cabrera-Pérez et al., 2023) and reveal temporal changes (Mezcua et al., 2024). The candidate will also explore the use of local earthquake tomography (Bie et al., 2022) to obtain seismic velocity models extending into the lower crust. The combined tomographic model will provide new insights into the magmatic plumbing system. Seismic velocity models will be integrated with other available geophysical datasets, including density and electrical resistivity models, as well as petrological constraints on magma sources. There may also be opportunities to use new satellite geodetic data to constrain the depth and evolution of magmatic pressurization sources (Taylor et al., 2021). 

Training 

The candidate will gain expertise in seismic data processing, tomographic imaging, and numerical modelling, alongside broader training in environmental sciences provided through ARIES. Opportunities for travel include collaborative visits to SRC. The candidate will work within a large multi-disciplinary research team recently funded by NERC.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Watching a fungus fight back: mapping antimicrobial resistance in 3-D as it happens
jobs.department: School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Trey Koev

The chemicals that protect our crops and the drugs that treat fungal infections come from the same family. Fungi in the field meet them first — and are arriving in hospitals already resistant. Yet we still do not know what a fungus actually does in the hours after it meets a chemical that does not quite kill it.

We know it fights back. Our recent work shows that within a day of exposure, Aspergillus fumigatus rebuilds its cell wall and rewires its metabolism, then recovers. What we cannot yet see is where this happens. Does the response begin at the outside of the colony, where the chemical arrives first, leaving a sheltered core that survives and regrows? Or does the whole organism respond together?

This project will find out, using a technique developed in our lab that maps chemistry in three dimensions inside living fungal material without cutting it open. You will combine microbiology with cutting-edge magnetic resonance, working across two Norwich Research Park institutes, and help decide where the project goes next.

We welcome applicants from biology, chemistry, physics, or computational backgrounds. No prior NMR experience is required — you will be trained. What matters is curiosity and an interest in working across disciplines.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Role of non-canonical autophagy in liver lipid metabolism in response to unhealthy diets
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Professor Naiara Beraza

Obesity has epidemic proportions in the UK as more than 60% of adults are overweight and 33% have fatty liver. Poor dietary habits (western diets) are the main contributors to obesity and liver steatosis, where lipid accumulation becomes toxic for hepatocytes leading to cell death and consequent inflammation. Autophagy, which removes intracellular components, is key to regulate lipid metabolism in hepatocytes and its impairment contributes to fatty liver. Importantly, the role of alternative cellular mechanisms of intracellular cargo degradation like LC3-associated phagocytosis (LAP), remains poorly studied in this context.

This project aims to define the mechanisms mediating the lipid update and metabolism in the liver in response to high fat diets. This will enable the PhD student to identify targets to preserve liver metabolic health and prevent disease progression associated to poor dietary habits, which will be investigated in this project.

This collaborative project provides the unique opportunity for the successful candidate to receive broad training on preclinical in vivo models and in vitro work as well as cellular and molecular biology and immunology methodologies including confocal microscopy and spectral flow cytometry.

The project will be supervised by two molecular biologists (Beraza and Rushworth) whose work have a strong translational aim. This collaborative project will enable the student to work in different labs at different institutions (Quadram institute and University of East Anglia) and to present their results to wide-ranging audiences in conferences and meetings. The multidisciplinary nature of this project will contribute to build a broad network and will provide the student valuable transferable skills essential for the progression of her/his scientific career.

This project will be carried out at the Quadram institute, which combines research laboratories with clinical facilities, located at the core of the Norwich Research Park.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Chemical Biology to target bacteria: Inhibiting bacterial growth by controlling cell division protein interactions
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Andrew Beekman

Antibiotic-resistant pathogens are a huge threat in healthcare and farming. The last resorts of conventional antibiotic drugs are unable to treat multi-resistant strains in patients. New approaches towards antibiotics are desperately needed. To spread and survive, bacteria need to divide. Thus, bacterial cell division has emerged as a promising antibiotic target pathway to combat multi-resistant pathogens.

This project aims to target protein interactions that pathogenic bacteria, like the causative agent of TB, Mycobacterium tuberculosis require to spread. Using Mycobacteria smegmatis as a harmless model organisms for M. tuberculosis, the project will design, synthesise and test compounds which specifically prevent the formation of essential protein interaction for cell division.

The appointed student will design, synthesise, and test compounds which specifically prevent essential protein-protein interactions used by pathogens to spread. An innovative platform, developed in the supervisor’s lab, will be used to design peptides that can disrupt the formation of protein complexes that facilitate disease. This interdisciplinary chemical biology and microbiology project will involve training in cutting-edge science including computational design and peptide synthesis, as well as evaluation of the compounds for binding to proteins and their inhibitory activity in bacteria.

Led by Dr Andrew Beekman and Dr Susan Schlimpert, there is an opportunity to learn medicinal chemistry/chemical biology, protein biochemistry, and microbiology, using facilities across the School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology and The John Innes Centre. The student will be based in a highly collaborative research environment with a strong commitment to excellence in science and professional development.

This project will develop a multidisciplinary scientist with expertise from chemical to cell biology. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: How to build an immune receptor: AI-led protein design for engineering disease resistance
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Professor Mark Banfield 

Like animals, plants get sick, but they have an immune system to fight back against infection. Plant diseases are a threat to food production and a constraint on achieving food security against the background of a changing climate and the need to reduce reliance on fossil fuels. Understanding how components of the plant immune system (e.g. evolved plant immune receptors) work to detect and respond to pathogens, and how they can be engineered, offers new opportunities to protecting crops and secure higher yielding harvests in a sustainable way. However, emerging computational protein design tools enable “bottom-up” approaches to develop de novo new-to-nature immune receptors with tailored functions, offering exciting potential in agriculture against a range of important diseases.

This project will investigate how to computationally build and combine recognition-switch-execute modules to recognise pathogen molecules, turn the receptor “on” and elicit a cellular response, which in a host-pathogen infection situation would prevent disease. The project will investigate the molecular mechanisms of how these receptors work using both in vitro and in vivo approaches and explore how they can be deployed to manage plant diseases. The studentship spans interdisciplinary techniques including computational protein design, molecular biology, biochemistry, structural biology, in planta assays, and plant pathology. There will opportunities to work with leading national and international collaborators.

The student will receive expert training in diverse disciplines on a strategically relevant topic, within a stimulating research environment. They will join a team of researchers with shared interests and have access to world-class facilities. Further, it is expected they will attend national/international conferences to present their research.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Geotechnical Engineering
jobs.description_html:
3.5-year D.Phil. studentship 

Project: Nature-based and biomimetic foundation systems

Supervisors: Professor Jonathan Knappett and Professor Chris Martin

The root systems of trees provide ‘foundations’ that develop in response to the loads applied to the tree. For example, trees subjected to high winds (inducing large moments) develop roots prioritising lateral spread rather than depth to maximise overturning resistance. In addition to direct applications, e.g. windthrow hazard assessment, greater understanding of how root system architecture and geometry provide resistance to different combinations of applied loading can suggest new biomimetic foundation concepts that harness similar mechanisms and potentially use significantly less material than conventional solutions.

This studentship will begin by exploring how different tree root system architectures behave under different combinations of vertical (V), horizontal (H) and moment (M) loading and identifying the controlling mechanisms. This will be achieved using a recently developed numerical modelling approach for efficiently simulating complex root-soil interaction, coupled with physical model testing to determine root-soil interaction parameters. The results will have direct application to hazard assessment of trees subject to extreme weather (e.g. windthrow and tsunami protection by mangroves).

The results of the first phase will then inform the development and evaluation of biomimetic foundation concepts that can be scaled-up in size and optimised in configuration for a variety of applications with load cases analogous to those where trees perform well. Such systems can potentially minimise embodied carbon through efficient geotechnical performance and minimise installation plant requirements by being assembled from multiple smaller/lighter elements. This could make them suitable for a range of applications that could include: (i) line-side cantilever gantries for railway electrification; (ii) transmission tower and solar farm foundations; (iii) anchorage systems for floating offshore renewable energy systems; or (iv) low-rise building foundations in remote areas.

Eligibility

The following skills are desirable but not essential:

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Whole genome sequencing from mosquito blood meals
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Anders Bergstrom

Mosquitos can be seen as tiny, autonomous samplers of blood from wild animals. It is well-established that mosquito blood meals contain animal DNA, as well as DNA from animal pathogens. Current environmental DNA (eDNA) techniques are routinely applied to blood meals to survey species presence and absence, but these techniques only make use of a tiny fraction of an organism's genome. This project will go far beyond species detection, and pioneer the sequencing of whole animal genomes from blood meals.

The project will make use of hundreds of collected blood meals with species presences already determined, to address fundamental biological questions about blood meal DNA, and push forward technologies for recovering genomic information from these samples:

- Objective 1. Improve methods to efficiently sequence genomes from blood meals: evaluating and developing protocols for efficient extraction and Illumina sequencing of blood meal DNA, including protocols from the field of ancient DNA.

- Objective 2. Uncover the molecular properties of blood meal DNA: characterising the degradation, damage patterns, and epigenetic information in blood meal DNA, including the use of Nanopore sequencing

- Objective 3. Use blood meal genomes to survey genetic diversity of animals and pathogens: recovering whole genomes from animals to learn about population structure, genetic relatedness, pathogen transmission dynamics, and more.

The student will receive broad training in molecular biology experiments, genomics technologies, bioinformatics, metagenomics, and population genetics. They will develop both wet-lab and computational genomics skills with wide applicability across the life sciences. The student will take part in journal clubs and departmental seminars, present their work at conferences, and strengthen their abilities in critical thinking and science communication.

The ideal candidate will have a background in biology (e.g. genetics, molecular biology, biochemistry, evolutionary biology, biotechnology) and have strong interests in molecular biology lab work, genomics, evolution and data analysis.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Click-to-Connect Cytochromes: Modular Components for Sustainable Electrical Circuits
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Professor Julea Butt

This exciting project will engineer cytochromes for site-selective covalent linkage to multiple redox partners and electrodes thereby delivering proof-of-principle for novel electronic circuitry.  

Harnessing redox-active proteins as an abundant and tuneable source of conductive molecules presents an attractive route to meet the need for sustainable electronic components. Multiheme cytochromes produced by electric bacteria are particularly attractive for this purpose because they are spanned by close-packed chains of redox-active heme cofactors. We have previously demonstrated that such proteins can be engineered to sit between two electrodes and conduct electrons between them.   

Building on our success, this project will use site-specific mutagenesis to create novel cytochromes that extend the opportunities to form protein based electrical circuitry. That mutagenesis will introduce natural and non-canonical amino acids to allow site-selective conjugation of multiple cytochromes in novel conductive configurations.

The project will use site-specific mutagenesis, protein purification, protein engineering, spectroscopy, and dynamic electrochemistry. Working in an enthusiastic and supportive team the successful applicant will become expert in state-of-the-art protein engineering, biochemistry and biophysics. They will also expand their knowledge of synthetic biology and green chemistry, and benefit from opportunities to participate in national and international conferences. 
Informal enquiries are encouraged, please contact Professor Julea Butt (j.butt@uea.ac.uk) for further information.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: How do fungi and bacteria communicate? Decoding the rules of cross-kingdom microbial interactions
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Professor Alessia Buscaino

Microorganisms rarely live alone. Instead, fungi and bacteria form complex communities where they constantly communicate, compete and cooperate. These cross kingdom interactions are increasingly recognised as key regulators of microbiome function, health and disease, yet the fundamental biological rules that govern them remain poorly understood.

This PhD project will investigate how the human fungal commensal Candida albicans interacts with the oral bacterium Fusobacterium nucleatum. Although these microorganisms normally coexist harmlessly, recent studies suggest that their partnership changes dramatically in different host environments and may contribute to diseases such as colorectal cancer. Understanding why the same fungal–bacterial interaction produces such different outcomes is an outstanding biological question with important implications for human health.

Based in the Buscaino and Juge laboratories at the Quadram Institute, you will explore how environmental conditions, microbial diversity and cell surface adhesins shape this interaction. The project integrates fungal genetics, bacterial biology, genomics, bioinformatics, molecular biology and protein biochemistry/biophysics, using cutting edge approaches including CRISPR genome editing, comparative genomics, transcriptomics, confocal microscopy, gut on chip models and protein interaction assays.

You will receive comprehensive training in experimental design, data analysis and scientific communication, and develop highly transferable skills in project management, teamwork, organisation and communication to both scientific and lay audiences. Working within a collaborative, interdisciplinary research environment, you will have access to state of the art facilities, international collaborations and opportunities to present your work at national and international conferences.

This project is ideally suited to motivated students with interests in microbiology, genetics, genomics, host–microbe interactions or microbial evolution, who wish to address fundamental questions in biology while building a broad, flexible skill set for careers in academia, industry or beyond.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Decoding the molecular switches that control fungal growth and infection
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Stefan Bidula 

Fungal infections are responsible for over 1.5 million deaths each year, cause substantial agricultural losses, and are becoming increasingly difficult to treat due to rising antifungal resistance. To develop the next generation of antifungal therapies, we need a better understanding of the fundamental biological processes that enable fungi to grow and cause disease.

This PhD project will investigate the role of unusual DNA and RNA structures known as G-quadruplexes (G4s) in regulating the metabolic changes that occur when fungal spores germinate. Germination is a critical stage in the fungal life cycle, allowing dormant spores to develop into invasive hyphae capable of causing infection and forming drug-resistant biofilms. Using the human fungal pathogen Aspergillus fumigatus as a model, the project will test the hypothesis that G4s act as molecular switches controlling the metabolic pathways required for successful germination.

The successful candidate will receive multidisciplinary training in molecular microbiology, fungal genetics, genomics, bioinformatics, CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing, metabolomics, microscopy and structural biology. They will generate genome-wide maps of G4 formation, engineer targeted mutants, investigate metabolic changes using NMR spectroscopy, and study how these processes influence fungal cell-wall remodelling and antifungal susceptibility.

This project offers the opportunity to work within a collaborative, interdisciplinary research environment alongside experts in fungal biology, nucleic acid biology and NMR spectroscopy. The student will be encouraged to present their work at national and international conferences, publish in leading journals, engage in public outreach activities and develop a broad range of transferable research skills.

Applicants should have, or expect to obtain, at least a 2:1 honours degree (or equivalent) in microbiology, molecular biology, biochemistry, biomedical sciences or a related discipline. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Cracking the carbohydrate code: how carbohydrate-binding modules control starch digestion
jobs.description_html:
Why this matters:

Starch is the principal source of dietary glucose, and the rate at which it is digested has major consequences for metabolic health. Food science still lacks the mechanistic understanding to rationally design starch-based foods with tailored digestion profiles. Starch digestion is initiated by amylases. How amylases and carbohydrate-binding modules (CBM) shape starch-binding affinity and hydrolysis kinetics is poorly resolved, particularly at the solid–liquid interfaces where digestion occurs.

The project:

You will have an opportunity to link CBM identity directly to their function. Working across carbohydrate hydrogel structure/mobility, digestion enzymology and advanced Nuclear Magnetic Resonance (NMR) you will uncover molecular level details of how starch structures interact with amylases at different stages of digestion and their impact on starch hydrolysis in different regions of the human gut. This will benefit rational design of foods with tailored digestive profiles.

What you will do/learn:

  • Materials science: starch interfaces structure and dynamics;
  • Biomedical methods: enzyme assay design, enzymology and biophysical techniques;
  • Spectroscopy: cutting-edge solid- and solution-state NMR for carbohydrates;
  • Data analysis; multivariate and correlative statistical analysis;
  • Translation: integrate findings with rational food design.

You will be jointly supervised in the Khimyak/ Koev / Warren labs—collaborative, cross-disciplinary, and hands-on.

Who should apply:

We welcome applicants with backgrounds in structural biology, pharmacology, biophysics, materials science, or related fields. Some experience with NMR or other advanced structural tools is a plus, and you should enjoy working across disciplines.

The environment:

You will join the Norwich Research Park—one of the UK’s largest concentrations of life scientists—with outstanding facilities and training. The skill set you will build spans molecular biology, enzymology, biophysics, and advanced NMR —preparing you for career in academia or industry.

Interested?

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Breaking Code: Deciphering the Biology of the Selfless Virus-like Gene Transfer Agents
jobs.description_html:
Bacteria commonly exchange genetic information (DNA) in a process called horizontal gene transfer as they evolve and adapt to changes in their local environment. Understanding horizontal gene transfer and how new genetic information is incorporated and domesticated into the existing signalling network and physiology of the host is a fundamental problem in biology. Horizontal gene transfer also contributes to the spread of antimicrobial resistance, which is a leading cause of mortality worldwide. The widespread but so far neglected Gene Transfer Agents (GTAs) are peculiar virus-like particles that were domesticated from ancestral bacterial viruses to now serve as nanomachines for the host bacteria. GTAs facilitate the exchange of genetic information by packaging and disseminating the DNA of the host bacteria. GTAs have a unique but poorly characterized lifecycle yet present an excellent opportunity to study the fascinating biology and fundamentals of domestication of genetic information, and to engineer GTA for biotechnological or therapeutic purposes.      

Several key advances from the community and my group now make it timely to investigate and exploit GTA biology. Building on these key advances, the student will aim to develop a better understanding of fundamental GTA biology and to characterize the process of domestication of genetic information to inform the development and engineering of synthetic GTA particles.

The project comes with a multidisciplinary training, including molecular microbiology, fluorescence microscopy, omics, protein-protein interaction studies and structural biology. This will provide you highly transferrable skills and a wide choice of career options. 

You will be based in the laboratory of Prof. Tung Le (www.tunglelab.org) in the Department of Molecular Microbiology at the John Innes Centre, a world-class institute for plant and microbial research.

Applications are welcomed from students across the biological sciences who have a desire to work on a multidisciplinary project. Informal enquiries to tung.le@jic.ac.uk are welcome.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Engineering protein nanocages for biotechnology applications
jobs.department: School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology
jobs.description_html:
Proteins that self-assemble to yield cage-like structures are of great interest due to their potential applications in biotechnology. The cellular protein ferritin, which functions to detoxify and store iron, is composed of 24 subunits, arranged in a highly symmetric fashion to form an approximately spherical protein shell surrounding a hollow centre. While evolved to store large amounts of iron as a ferric-oxy-hydroxide mineral, the ferritin protein shell can potentially accommodate a range of other molecules. The aim of this project is to use engineering biology approaches to develop bacterial and human ferritins as nanocage platforms for the encapsulation of small molecules, peptides and proteins with applications in biocatalysis and therapeutics/diagnostics. Methodologies for encapsulation will be optimised, and the ability of the nanocages to transfer substrates, electrons and protons across the protein coat investigated. Eventual targets include technologically relevant enzymes such as hydrogenase, which catalyses the reduction of protons to hydrogen gas, and the targeted delivery of molecules for therapeutic and diagnostic applications. This multi-disciplinary protein biochemistry project, which is based in the Le Brun lab in the School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology at UEA, will involve protein purification, bioanalytical methods, spectroscopy, mass spectrometry and microscopy. It offers excellent training potential for the appointed student within a supportive and stimulating environment. Informal enquiries to Prof Nick Le Brun (n.le-brun@uea.ac.uk) are welcome.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Where does Salmonella hide? Using Organ-on-Chip technology to uncover the secrets of persistent infection
jobs.description_html:
Persistent asymptomatic infections remain an important but poorly understood public health challenge. Salmonella infections can become persistent, contributing to ongoing transmission, recurrent disease and potential prolonged antimicrobial exposure. Yet the mechanisms enabling non-typhoidal Salmonella to establish long-term host colonisation remain largely unexplored.

To address this challenge, you will develop comparative infection models representing key tissue environments associated with persistence, including intestinal, hepatic, immune and gallbladder niches. Using progressively more complex experimental systems, from static cell cultures to dynamic Organ-on-Chip technologies, you will investigate the host environments that promote survival, adaptation and the emergence of persistent Salmonella populations.

This unique interdisciplinary project combines bacterial genomics, host–pathogen biology, Organ-on-Chip technology and high-resolution imaging, providing training in computational and experimental infection biology. You will develop expertise across multiple experimental and analytical approaches while addressing a fundamental unanswered question in Salmonella research: how do populations adapt to persist within the human host? The supervisory team combines internationally recognised expertise in Salmonella genomics and persistence (Dr Gemma Langridge) with complementary strengths in host–microbe interactions, advanced imaging and physiologically relevant infection models (Dr Aimée Parker), providing an outstanding interdisciplinary training environment for the next generation of infection researchers.

As an NRP-DTP student, you will benefit from a broad programme of cohort-based training, professional development and transferable skills alongside your research project. You will also undertake a funded three-month Professional Internship, gaining experience in a non-academic setting such as industry, policy, education or science communication. This provides an opportunity to explore potential career pathways and develop skills beyond academic research.

Based at the Quadram Institute on the Norwich Research Park, you will join a vibrant research community spanning microbiologists, bioinformaticians and food scientists, with access to state-of-the-art facilities and opportunities for scientific training, interdisciplinary collaboration and professional development. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Decoding and Designing DNA Replication Origins Using Genome Language Models
jobs.description_html:
Project Supervisor - Dr Conrad Nieduszynski

How does a cell know where and when to copy its DNA? And can we use artificial intelligence to design entirely new genetic elements that control this process?

This exciting interdisciplinary PhD project will tackle a fundamental question in biology: how DNA replication origins are encoded and regulated within genomes.

Working at the interface of computational biology, synthetic biology, and genomics, you will combine cutting-edge genome language models (AI systems trained on whole genomes) with high-throughput experimental approaches to uncover the rules that govern DNA replication. You will develop predictive models of replication origin function, design hundreds of synthetic DNA sequences, and test their performance in yeast using advanced molecular biology and nanopore sequencing technologies.

The project brings together complementary expertise from the Li, Hall, Grandellis and Nieduszynski groups, providing training in machine learning, genome engineering, automation, CRISPR-based genome editing, next-generation sequencing, and data analysis. You will also have access to world-class facilities, including the Earlham Biofoundry and advanced genomics platforms.

The project will be conducted at the Earlham Institute, a world-class BBSRC research centre of excellence in genomics, engineering and computational biology, and AI. You will join a highly collaborative and supportive research community and have access to training and career development opportunities across the Norwich Research Park through the Norwich Research Park Biosciences Doctoral Training Partnership.

Beyond answering fundamental questions about chromosome biology, this research aims to enable the rational design of stable synthetic chromosomes, a key challenge in the future of engineering biology. The project offers outstanding opportunities for collaboration, international conference presentations, and publication, while developing highly sought-after computational and experimental skills relevant to both academia and biotechnology industries.

Join us to help decode the language of genomes and design the chromosomes of the future.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The Cardiac Positioning System – How Do Heart Progenitors Find Their Way?
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Professor Andrea Munsterberg

The first organ to develop in vertebrate embryos is the heart, when two streams of cardiac progenitor cells undertake an epic migration before reuniting at the heart field – the site of future heart formation. How do cardiac progenitors achieve this feat? What clues guide them along the way and how do they “read” them?

In this exciting PhD project, you will use live cell imaging to track migration of cardiac progenitor cells as they navigate towards the embryonic heart field. You will learn molecular functional approaches to identify the cellular apparatus used by these remarkable cells to interpret a complex cell signalling landscape.

Experimentally, you will gain skills in molecular biology to clone candidate genes for mis-expression, or knock them down using CRISPR/Cas9 approaches in migrating cardiac progenitors and map their perturbed migration trajectories. This will reveal how specific gene products influence cell migration and fate decisions during heart formation.

You will join a collaborative supervisory team at UEA (Andrea Münsterberg, Tim Grocott, James Mccoll), gaining skills in developmental biology, molecular genetics, live imaging/microscopy, and computational biology. This multi-disciplinary project offers the opportunity to make fundamental discoveries about the molecular control of heart development.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Listening to La Soufrière: Fibre Optics and AI for the Next Generation of Volcano Monitoring
jobs.description_html:
Scientific Background

A major challenge in volcanology is understanding and anticipating transitions in volcanic activity. Subtle changes within volcanic systems can precede hazardous eruptions, yet remain difficult to detect and interpret. This challenge is the focus of the NERC Large Grant Expecting the Unexpected (Ex-X): Understanding Dangerous Volcanic Transitions (dangerousvolcanoes.org). The 2020-21 eruption of La Soufrière, St Vincent, highlighted the importance of improved monitoring and hazard assessment. Recent advances in Distributed Acoustic Sensing (DAS) offer new opportunities for volcano monitoring by transforming fibre-optic telecommunications cables into dense seismic arrays.

As part of Ex-X, a DAS interrogator has been installed on a subsea fibre-optic cable around northern St Vincent. This provides a unique opportunity to investigate volcanic and tectonic processes in previously unmonitored areas. The enhanced spatial and temporal resolution afforded by DAS can reveal subtle seismic changes indicative of magmatic unrest that are usually missed by conventional networks.

Research Methodology

The candidate will develop automated workflows for processing continuous DAS data from St Vincent. Machine learning and signal-processing approaches will be used to detect, classify and characterise earthquakes. They will integrate DAS observations with the permanent seismic network operated by the University of the West Indies Seismic Research Centre (SRC) and a dense nodal deployment acquired through Ex-X. They will improve earthquake location calculations, apply ambient-noise imaging techniques to investigate subsurface structure, and evaluate how DAS can contribute to volcano monitoring. Particular emphasis will be placed on developing monitoring products that complement existing seismic networks, improve interpretation of unrest and support situational awareness.

Training

The candidate will receive training in seismology, volcanology, DAS, machine learning, scientific programming and geophysical imaging. They will gain experience in developing operational software for geohazard monitoring and working with large datasets. They will undertake fieldwork in St Vincent to maintain the DAS installation. Through a CASE partnership with SRC, they will spend several months embedded within an operational volcano observatory.

Person Specification

We seek an enthusiastic individual with a degree in geophysics or a related discipline. Experience of coding, data analysis or machine learning is desirable. An interest in geohazards and interdisciplinary research is essential.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Manipulating Meiotic Crossover Control in Wheat
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Chris Morgan 

Meiotic recombination generates the genetic diversity on which both evolution and crop breeding depend. In wheat and other cereals, crossovers are strongly biased towards certain regions of the genome, leaving vast stretches almost untouched. This is a major bottleneck for breeders racing to develop climate-resilient varieties, as beneficial alleles within these low-recombination regions cannot easily be separated from linked deleterious variants (""linkage drag"").

This PhD will investigate whether the crossover landscape in wheat can be deliberately manipulated or exploited, combining fundamental meiotic cell biology with applied wheat genetics to generate tools relevant to future-proofing food security. First, you will use TILLING mutant alleles of meiotic genes, together with super-resolution microscopy and genomics, testing whether disrupting specific meiotic mechanisms can redistribute crossovers towards otherwise recombination-poor regions of the wheat genome. Second, you will investigate whether natural allelic variation in meiotic genes achieves the same effect, mining the rich genetic diversity of the JIC Watkins wheat landrace collection. Third, you will develop a high-throughput pollen-typing assay to measure recombination frequency directly in wheat gametes, and use this to run a genome-wide association study across the Watkins panel, hunting for novel loci that could unlock recombination exactly where breeders need it most.

You will be based in the Morgan group, and co-supervised by Dr Simon Griffiths, an expert in wheat quantitative genetics at the John Innes Centre, gaining training across meiotic cytology, molecular genetics, population genomics and quantitative statistical methods. This is a genuinely interdisciplinary project well suited to a student with a background in genetics, plant sciences, or a related bioscience discipline who is excited by fundamental cell biology with a clear route to real-world impact: the alleles and tools this project generates could help breeders develop climate-resilient wheat varieties faster than ever before.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: From climate information to climate action: Evaluating how climate information use shapes local adaptation decision making in English Local Authorities and opportunities for improvement
jobs.description_html:
The Climate Change Committee’s Well Adapted UK report highlights a critical need for practical adaptation solutions to build a resilient UK by 2050. Although information and data to inform adaptation planning is increasingly available through national risk assessments and climate services, there is limited understanding of how such information is interpreted and used by Local Authorities (LAs), which have a central role in managing planning, infrastructure, estates management, public health, and community resilience to climate risks. This includes understanding how organisational roles, professional norms, and internal decision-making processes influence climate information use.

This project will examine how climate information, including hazard, risk and adaptation data, is currently interpreted and incorporated into local public-sector decision-making processes, and how it shapes organisational decision making on climate adaptation. Project findings will shape recommendations that will inform the next generation of climate service tools and enhance the uptake and useability of information by LAs.

Using a qualitative multi-method approach, the research will combine wider documentary analysis of LA adaptation strategies, risk registers, and planning documents with focused semi-structured interviews with staff involved in adaptation decision-making. Existing consultation survey data from leading national climate service providers will provide further contextual insights. The analysis will focus on i) how climate information is accessed and interpreted; ii) where and how this information enters adaptation decision processes; and iii) opportunities to enhance adaptation processes and outcomes. Engagement with the UK Met Office climate services team will support analysis, knowledge exchange and impact.

The student will undertake training in designing and conducting effective interviews, thematic coding, methods to synthesise insights from qualitative data and using software such as NVivo. As a member of the Tyndall Early Career Network they will benefit from an established research group, bespoke training (e.g. science-policy engagement), and opportunities via the Met Office to join user-focused webinars and engage with adaptation and climate experts.

We seek a highly motivated individual with an understanding of climate science and/or adaptation policy in the UK; skills in qualitative and quantitative data collection, analysis and synthesis; interest in engaging with adaptation decision-makers; and excellent written and verbal communication.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Understanding the Evolution of How Plants Perceive Changes in the Environment
jobs.description_html:
Scientific Background 

Plants modify the concentration of calcium ions in their cells in response to different environmental stimuli and stresses. These changes in cellular calcium concentration trigger many downstream responses, including re-programming of gene expression and coordination of growth. Calcium signalling pathways are therefore essential for plants to respond and adapt to environmental stresses. 

Flowering plants, such as the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, have complicated networks of proteins involved in calcium signalling pathways. Genetic redundancy is observed and has hindered further study of these signalling pathways. Our recent genomic analyses have revealed that gene families encoding components of calcium signalling pathways are considerably smaller in other model plant species, including in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha. The study of these pathways in M. polymorpha therefore offer a unique opportunity to understanding calcium signalling pathways in plants and provide an evolutionary assessment of how plants respond and adapt to environmental stresses in the context of global climate change. 

Research methodology 

In this project, we will explore how the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha grows and responds to different stresses in the natural environment. The student will evaluate growth and physiology in plants grown under different environmental conditions, use bioimaging techniques to measure calcium signals, and use qRT-PCR to measure gene expression. They will also build on our recent work identifying stress signalling genes and test how knockout of these genes by CRISPR gene editing can be used to alter stress tolerance in plants. 

Training 

This multi-disciplinary project will offer the student excellent training opportunities in plant biology (including plant physiology and stress biology), cell biology, and the molecular genetics of plant environmental stress signalling. Furthermore, the student will receive training in data analysis (including transcriptomics) and manuscript preparation, whilst also having regular opportunities to present their work at national and international meetings. 

Person specification

jobs.description_html:
Scientific background: 

Carbon dioxide (CO2) is the most important anthropogenic greenhouse gas. The 2015 Paris Agreement aims to avoid dangerous climate change by reducing emissions of CO2 and other greenhouse gases. Independent top-down constraints on emissions require accurate measurements of CO2 concentrations and fluxes, and robust attribution to natural and anthropogenic sources. Recent technological developments now allow analysis of extremely rare isotopic CO2 species, known as polyisotopologues, offering unprecedented insights into carbon sources, sinks and ecosystem productivity across the Earth system.

This studentship builds on the UKRI NERC POLYGRAM (https://polygram.ac.uk/) project and exploits unique datasets and measurement capabilities developed through this programme.

Main aim and hypothesis:

The project aims to determine whether atmospheric CO2 polyisotopologues can provide new quantitative constraints on ecosystem productivity and carbon cycling from local to global scales. It will test the central hypothesis that combined carbon and triple-oxygen isotope signatures contain information about these processes that cannot be obtained from conventional atmospheric CO2 observations alone.

Research methodology: 

You will work with existing and newly collected data from the Weybourne Atmospheric Observatory (WAO), Alice Holt Forest Research Station, Atlantic ship transects and global atmospheric monitoring networks. Specifically, you will:

  •  analyse seasonal and interannual variability in triple-oxygen (16O, 17O, 18O) and stable-carbon (12C, 13C) isotope signatures of atmospheric CO2 at Weybourne

  •  quantify ecosystem-scale isotope variations at Alice Holt to investigate terrestrial carbon cycle processes

  •  evaluate isotope gradients from Atlantic transects and remote monitoring sites as indicators of global primary productivity.

Together, these analyses will test whether CO2 polyisotopologues provide robust indicators of carbon uptake and productivity across scales, while allowing you to develop additional hypotheses arising from the observations.

Training: 

You will join a collaborative research team at UEA (COAS; https://www.uea.ac.uk/groups-and-centres/centre-for-ocean-and-atmospheric-sciences) and Utrecht University (IMAU; https://www.uu.nl/staff/TRockmann). You will develop proficiency in state-of-the-art laser-spectroscopic measurements of CO2 and H2O isotopologues, advanced statistical analysis and modelling of environmental time series, and scientific communication through conferences and peer-reviewed publications. Opportunities will include specialist training, field measurements and a research visit to Utrecht.

Person specification: 

We seek an enthusiastic, self-motivated individual and team player with strong scientific interests and an interest in combining experimental measurements with quantitative data analysis.
