jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Dust, the Atlantic Ocean, and Climate
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background

The Atlantic Ocean has warmed significantly over the last few years partly from increasing greenhouse gases, but other climate forcing agents also play a role. In particular, dust produced and lifted into the atmosphere over Africa and transported thousands of miles over the Atlantic has important and complex effects on climate.

Saharan dust reflects sunlight to space and so cools the ocean, just as its absence warms the ocean. Dust in the atmosphere can alter the atmospheric circulation on vast scales and changes to the Atlantic Ocean sea surface temperature also impact on global atmospheric and oceanic circulation. Understanding changes in dust transport is, therefore, important for making better predictions of changes to temperature, atmospheric and oceanic circulation, and rainfall over the Atlantic ocean region. Observing, modelling and understanding the complexity of the dust cycle and its underlying processes presents a substantial but fascinating scientific challenge.

Research methodology

The project will be in two parts. First, you will analyse global datasets of observations and state-of-the-art climate models to understand the movement of dust, and its effects on temperature, atmospheric circulation, and impacts such as rainfall. Such analysis will involve examining similarities and differences between models to gain a more detailed understanding of the models’ treatments of dust and climate, and evaluating them against observations. Second, you will design, run and analyse experiments using slightly simpler climate models on the UEA high-performance computing system to untangle the mechanisms involved.

Aims and Outcomes

To understand and better predict how dust influences Atlantic Ocean temperatures, and how these changes affect climate, ocean-atmosphere circulation and precipitation patterns.

Training

You will be trained in statistical analysis, including computer coding, and interpretation of observational datasets and output from state-of-the-art climate models. You will also learn to design, run and analyse your own climate model experiments. Training activities also occur within the ARIES DTP.

Person Specification

A degree in a quantitative science. An interest in data analysis and numerical modelling of weather systems and the climate system is essential, while some experience in coding is desirable.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Where do plants make their medicine? Mapping chemical defence one cell at a time
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Dr Tatsuya Nobori

When a pathogen attacks, a plant fights back with chemistry. However, not every cell uses the same defence. Our recent single-cell study revealed an unexpected division of labour in infected leaves: different groups of cells activate genes for different chemical defence pathways. Which cells take on these roles, how are they organised around infection sites, and why does this organisation matter?

This PhD will map that hidden cellular geography and ask whether it can help us discover new pathways. Most genes involved in plant specialised metabolism remain uncharacterised. Bulk tissue analyses average gene expression across whole tissues, potentially hiding pathways used by rare or transient cell states.

You will create fluorescent reporter plants (Arabidopsis thaliana) and use advanced microscopy to follow defence-pathway activation as bacteria and fungi invade. You will then analyse gene-activity and chromatin profiles from around 100,000 infected leaf nuclei, combining them with a curated catalogue of biosynthetic enzymes to identify groups of genes activated together in the same cell state. Finally, you will use multiplex genome editing, pathogen assays, and metabolomics to test what the strongest candidates make and whether they help plants resist infection.

Based at The Sainsbury Laboratory and working with the Osbourn group at the John Innes Centre, you will be trained in plant molecular biology, advanced imaging, single-cell data analysis, genome editing, plant pathology, and natural-product chemistry. The project offers a supported start with established data and methods, followed by real intellectual ownership as you choose and investigate the most promising candidate gene modules.

This PhD would suit someone curious about how plants defend themselves and keen to connect experimental biology with data analysis and chemistry. Experience in all areas is not expected; full training and day-to-day support will be provided.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: How Do the Connections Between a Cell and its Neighbours Control How a Cell Responds?
jobs.description_html:
Plant cells are connected to their neighbours via ‘tubes’ called plasmodesmata, creating an interconnected cytoplasm that joins cells within and between tissues and organs. Many molecules use plasmodesmata to move freely between cells and it is critical for a plant to tightly control how open its plasmodesmata are to enable control over how far molecular information and resources can travel through tissues. Indeed, this control is important to how a plant responds to many different environmental and developmental changes, including immune responses when it is being invaded by a pathogen.

We, and others, have identified that plasmodesmata close when a cell perceives a pathogen, isolating that cell from its neighbours. We recently found that whether plasmodesmata are open or closed is related to immune-associated gene expression changes. This relationship illustrates a significant gap in our knowledge of how plants defend themselves against disease-causing pathogens. Further, we also recently discovered that immune-associated plasmodesmal closure depends on the amount of sugar the leaf is producing – leaves that are consuming rather than producing sugar don’t isolate their cells. We can manipulate whether a leaf is a sugar producer or consumer and so this allows new opportunity for us to investigate the relationship between plasmodesmal connectivity and gene expression.

This project will leverage these advances to investigate how plasmodesmal connectivity influences how cell response to pathogens. The student will take advantage of the extensive tools and resources available in the Faulkner lab to investigate plasmodesmal function and immune responses, and use these to generate new information and hypotheses to be tested. The project will use molecular biology, bioinformatics, genetics and quantitative imaging approaches to pioneer new understanding of how cell-to-cell connectivity via plasmodesmata underpins immune success in different leaves of a plant.

This project is awarded with a 4-year Norwich Research Park Biosciences Doctoral Training Partnership PhD DTP studentship. The studentship includes payment of tuition fees (directly to the University), a stipend to cover living expenses (2026/27 stipend rate: £21,805, and a Research Training Support Grant of £5,000pa for each year of the studentship.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Running on Empty: Metabolic Ageing in Blood Stem Cells
jobs.description_html:
Every blood cell in your body, from oxygen-carrying red cells to virus-fighting white cells, begins life in a rare population of blood stem cells that must stay active for an entire lifetime. As we age, these stem cells lose their edge, contributing to the immune decline and blood disorders associated with growing older. This project tackles a fundamental question in ageing biology: why do blood stem cells run low on metabolic fuel as we age, and can we intervene? You will focus on glutamine, a nutrient we have shown is essential for healthy blood stem cell function, to uncover why its supply falters with age and whether restoring it can reverse stem-cell decline.

Our previous work revealed that an ageing bone marrow environment blunts immune responses in older individuals. Exciting new data now show that blood stem cells themselves also develop intrinsic metabolic defects. This project will be among the first to pin down these cell-intrinsic changes and test directly whether they compromise stem-cell function and blood output, opening a new route to understanding, and potentially reversing, age-related decline in the blood system.

You will receive comprehensive, hands-on training in a broad and highly sought-after skillset: primary cell isolation, in-vivo and in-vitro modelling, metabolomics, stable isotope tracing, flow cytometry (FACS), LC-MS-based metabolite analysis, qPCR, western blotting, ELISA and metabolic flux analysis. This multidisciplinary training will set you up for a competitive career in academic, clinical or industry research.

You will be based in the Rushworth Lab at Norwich Medical School, UEA, a dynamic, well-funded research group with a strong record of high-impact publications and PhD training success, working alongside expert collaborators at the Earlham Institute and across the Norwich Research Park, one of Europe’s leading centres for life-science research.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Functional Genomics of Sexually Antagonistic Selection
jobs.description_html:
Why do harmful genes persist in populations instead of being removed by natural selection? One answer lies in sexual antagonism: when a genetic variant benefits males but harms females, or vice versa. This genetic tug-of-war is one of evolution’s most intriguing puzzles. It can create a burden on populations, influence human health, and even help maintain the variation needed for species to adapt to new environments.

Recent work from the supervisor’s lab has revealed consistent sets of sexually antagonistic genes across independent studies in the fruit fly Drosophila melanogaster. This project will take the next big step: moving from finding sexually antagonistic genes to uncovering what makes them special, how they affect fitness and life history traits, and the molecular mechanisms of the sexual conflict and its resolution.

You will combine cutting-edge bioinformatics, genome engineering, and state-of-the-art sequencing technologies to:

  1. Identify and characterise consistent sexually antagonistic loci across multiple studies.
  2. Validate their effects on sex-specific fitness and traits using CRISPR-Cas9 allele swaps in fruit flies.
  3. Probe underlying mechanisms, from gene regulation to alternative splicing.

This PhD offers the scope to develop independence – pursing promising leads on interesting biology – while addressing one of evolution’s most longstanding challenges. Beyond advancing fundamental evolutionary biology, the project has broad relevance to conservation, pest management, aging, and human health. For example, many sex-specific disease phenotypes are maintained due to their genetic bases having sexually antagonistic fitness benefits in the opposite sex.

You will receive outstanding interdisciplinary training in bioinformatics, molecular genetics, and functional genomics. The supervisory team offers expertise spanning evolutionary genetics, bioinformatics, biological statistics, and CRISPR genome engineering. Additional training and collaborative opportunities are available at neighbouring institutes throughout the broader Norwich Research Park in areas such as long-read sequencing and single-cell transcriptomics.

This project is awarded with a 4-year Norwich Research Park Biosciences Doctoral Training Partnership PhD DTP studentship. The studentship includes payment of tuition fees (directly to the University), a stipend to cover living expenses (2026/27 stipend rate: £21,805, and a Research Training Support Grant of £5,000pa for each year of the studentship.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: How does NRP2 keep blood vessels sealed and calm under stress?
jobs.description_html:
Blood vessels are lined by endothelial cells, which form a living barrier between blood and tissues. These cells must stay tightly connected, sense blood flow, respond to nutrients and communicate with immune cells, while avoiding unnecessary inflammation. How endothelial cells maintain this stable “barrier identity” during stress is still not fully understood.

This PhD project will investigate neuropilin-2, or NRP2, a cell-surface receptor best known for roles in blood vessel development. Our new data suggest that NRP2 also helps endothelial cells stay stable. When NRP2 is lost, endothelial cells lose the junctional protein VE-cadherin, become more inflammatory and show increased adhesion molecules that can recruit immune cells.

The student will test how NRP2 controls endothelial barrier stability in human and mouse endothelial cells. They will study how cells respond to flow, inflammatory stimulation and lipid/nutrient stress, and will ask whether loss of VE-cadherin is the trigger that drives inflammatory activation. The project will also use an endothelial-specific mouse model to test whether NRP2 helps blood vessels adapt to dietary stress in vivo.

The student will receive broad interdisciplinary training in endothelial cell biology, receptor trafficking, live-cell and confocal imaging, flow assays, inflammatory signalling, monocyte adhesion, mouse genetics, vascular physiology, statistics and data interpretation. The project is suited to a student interested in cell biology, vascular biology, inflammation and mechanisms that preserve tissue health.

This is a mechanistic PhD project with strong preliminary data, clear aims and room for the student to shape the direction of the work.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Engineering Fitness in Disease-Resistant Crops
jobs.description_html:
Engineering crop disease resistance to overcome the growth-defence trade-off

Developing crops that are both productive and resillient is one of the major challenges facing agriculture. While disease-resistance genes can protect plants from devastating pathogens, they often come with a hidden cost: reduced growth and lower yields. This PhD will investigate whether engineering biology can overcome this trade-off by precisely controlling when and where resistance genes are expressed.

You will study resistance to potato cyst nematodes, one of the UK's most important pests. A resistance locus from soybean, Rhg1, can protect against these nematodes, but continuous expression also reduces root growth and tuber yield.

We hypothesise that these impacts result from uncontrolled expression in the wrong tissues or at the wrong time, and that programmable expression could maintain resistance while avoiding these growth and yield costs.

Using world-class automation robotics in the Earlham Biofoundry, you will build and test a regulatory-part library, before applying these tools to redesign Rhg1 constructs and evaluate engineered plants for disease resistance, root architecture and tuber yield.

This highly collaborative PhD brings together engineering biology and laboratory automation expertise from the Grandellis Group at Earlham Institute, with the Witek Group at 2Blades - internationally recognised for research into genetic resistance to crop diseases.

Throughout the project, you will gain training in plant molecular biology, synthetic and engineering biology, automated DNA assembly, Biofoundry technologies, and genetic engineering These highly transferable skills are increasingly sought after in both academic research and the biotechnology sector.

The project will be conducted at the Earlham Institute, a world-class BBSRC research centre of excellence in genomics, engineering and computational biology, and AI. You will join a highly collaborative and supportive research community and have access to training and career development opportunities across the Norwich Research Park through the Norwich Research Park Biosciences Doctoral Training Partnership.

This project is awarded with a 4-year Norwich Research Park Biosciences Doctoral Training Partnership PhD DTP studentship. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Drivers and Consequences of Recent Changes in Bird Migration
jobs.description_html:
Background:

Migration enables species to cope with fluctuations in resource availability, but recently dramatic changes have been observed, including reductions in migratory distance, advancement of the migratory timing or abandonment of migratory behaviour. These changes are mediated by interactions between species traits and environmental variables. Recent changes in climate and in resource availability together with information from tracking technologies provide an opportunity to investigate the drivers and consequences of changes in migratory behaviour across species. These can inform conservation strategies to protect migratory species. This project will advance understanding of the determinants of changes in migratory behaviour. 

Objectives and Methods:

Remote sensing and long-term tracking datasets obtained by the supervisors3 and available on Movebank will be used to achieve the following objectives: 

  • Quantify changes in species migratory behaviour, including changes in migration timing, migratory distance and proportion of individuals that have become sedentary in different species and populations 
  • Determine the influence of environmental variables (e.g. resource availability, climate) to changes in migratory behaviour, accounting for species traits and phylogenetic history. 
  • Determine if individuals experiencing lower reductions in resource availability after breeding are less likely to migrate or migrate shorter distances. 
  • Determine the extent to which access to new foraging resources (e.g. predicted anthropogenic food sources) influences migratory behaviour comparing populations and individuals with different degrees of use of these new resources. 

Training:

You will be part of a supportive and dynamic research environment at UEA and work with collaborators at BIOPOLIS/CIBIO, BTO and the University of Lisbon. The project has field work in Portugal with co-supervisors. You will be trained to deploy tracking devices on wild birds and to analyse tracking datasets and spatial data. This project will develop your critical thinking, programming, statistical and oral presentation skills. It will challenge you to think about management of natural resources and conservation strategies for migratory birds, both will enhance your future employability. 

Person Specification:

You should be interested in animal movement and in advancing our understanding of the natural environment. Relevant research experience will be advantageous. This project is available to highly numerate candidates. For further details contact: a.franco@uea.ac.uk

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Plant temperature signalling via modulation of small-RNA signalling
jobs.description_html:
Primary Supervisor - Professor Steven Penfield

Given the accelerating pace of climate change it is important to understand how plants adapt to temperature changes and how to engineer crops to cope with more variable seasonal growth environments. Yet surprisingly, the basic mechanisms by which plants sense and adapt to temperature remain only partly understood. This PhD opportunity will suit candidates interested in studying how plants adapt to changing temperatures, and who wish to learn the latest techniques in single cell analysis, genomics, chromatin biology and molecular biology.

Gene silencing is a fundamental process in all eukaryotes which in plants is necessary for normal development of all organs, and for defence against a range of pathogens. It has been known for some time that the strength of gene silencing is affected by the growth temperature. In this project the successful student will study how this temperature sensitivity adapts the growth and development of plants to seasonal changes in temperature, allowing plants to grow new organs especially adapted to winter, spring, and summer conditions via chromatin modifications.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship project: Rethinking Corporate Governance in Modern Capital Markets: Law, Regulation and Practice
jobs.description_html:
Corporate governance and capital markets are being reshaped by changes in ownership structures, the growth of institutional and passive investment, the expansion of private markets, technological innovation, and increasing demands for corporate accountability. These developments affect how corporations are governed and how power is exercised within modern capital markets. The growing importance of investor stewardship has also expanded expectations of institutional investors as monitors, engaged shareholders and actors responding to portfolio- and system-level risks. At the same time, policymakers and regulators are pursuing reforms intended to promote market competitiveness and economic growth while preserving investor protection, market integrity and public trust. This raises important questions about the purpose of the corporation, the responsibilities of boards and shareholders, the role of institutional investors, and the relationship between corporate governance and capital markets regulation.

The successful applicant will develop an original research project within the broad field of corporate governance, with particular scope for research on investor stewardship and capital markets. Applicants are encouraged to formulate their own research questions and may adopt doctrinal, comparative, transnational, empirical or interdisciplinary approaches. Projects may explore issues relating to institutional investors and investor stewardship, shareholder power and engagement, boards, corporate purpose, sustainability, corporate ownership, the balance between investor protection and market competitiveness, capital markets regulation, public and private markets, financial innovation, digital securities, or other emerging governance and regulatory challenges.

The research gap is both conceptual and practical. Corporate governance scholarship has moved beyond its traditional focus on board–shareholder relations, while capital markets scholarship has examined investor protection, market integrity, market efficiency and regulatory design. Yet the relationship between these areas has received less sustained attention. In particular, further research is needed on how changing patterns of ownership and investor stewardship interact with corporate governance structures and capital markets regulation. Questions about the responsibilities of institutional investors, the exercise of shareholder power, portfolio- and system-level risks, technological innovation, the growth of private markets, and the increasing emphasis on market competitiveness do not fit neatly within a single field of legal scholarship. Existing work is often divided between corporate law, financial regulation and governance studies. The project therefore offers considerable scope for theoretical, doctrinal, comparative or empirical research on the future of corporate governance in modern capital markets.

The project will be supervised by Dr Dionysia Katelouzou and Dr Martin Bengtzen

Applicants should have an interest in corporate law, corporate governance, financial regulation, capital markets, or related areas of legal research. The proposed PhD project will explore the future of corporate governance in modern capital markets, including topics such as investor stewardship, shareholder engagement, institutional investors, corporate purpose, sustainability, capital markets regulation, public and private markets, financial innovation, digital securities, and emerging governance challenges. Applicants are encouraged to develop their own original research questions within this broad field.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Transgenerational Epigenetic Inheritance of Responses to Environmental Stress
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Natural environments are changing rapidly due to anthropogenic climate change. How populations respond to these changes determines whether they adapt to more stressful environments via plasticity and/or evolution, or whether they become extinct. This creates an urgent need to understand the physiological mechanisms that regulate organismal responses to environmental stress. Recent discoveries have suggested that organisms may transfer environmentally induced phenotypic changes to multiple generations of their descendants through non-genetic mechanisms. This phenomenon, called transgenerational epigenetic inheritance, has transformed the way we think about evolutionary processes, and the effect of environments on natural populations. However, much about this process is still unknown. This project asks whether the activation of critical cellular stress responses is transmitted between generations; whether this transmission confers increased survival of populations in stressful environments, and enhanced Darwinian fitness; and how this inheritance is mechanistically achieved. 

Research methodology:

You will determine whether key cellular stress responses can be transmitted via transgenerational non-genetic inheritance following exposure of parental animals to environmental stressors. You will then establish whether this transgenerational inheritance enhances resistance of populations to environmental stress, and whether inherited stress response activation promotes individual fitness. Finally, you will explore the mechanistic basis for this inheritance by using scRNA-seq to establish a transcriptomic signature for stress response inheritance, and by screening candidate regulators for their roles in this process. You will use Caenorhabditis elegans as a model organism to explore these effects - the premier system for the study of transgenerational epigenetic inheritance. Together, these approaches will define a mechanism by which cellular responses to stressful environments can be non-genetically inherited, and determine whether this inheritance serves an adaptive purpose. 

Training:

You will gain a wide range of skills in experimental design, statistical analysis, bioinformatics, scientific writing and presentation. You will also build expertise in evolutionary biology, cell biology, and physiological techniques. In addition, you will participate in external training courses and conferences, local seminars, research discussion groups and journal clubs.

Person specification:

We are looking for an enthusiastic and highly motivated individual with a strong interest in evolution, ecology, genetics, and stress response biology

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Evolutionary Genomics of Mimicry in Neotropical Catfishes
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Mimicry, where unrelated species evolve similar colour patterns through natural selection, is one of the most striking examples of adaptation. In Müllerian mimicry, multiple defended species converge on a shared warning signal, reducing the costs of predator education, whereas in Batesian mimicry harmless species resemble defended models to avoid predation. Although iconic examples occur in Heliconius butterflies and poison arrow frogs, a remarkable and much less well-known mimicry system has evolved in Neotropical Corydoradinae catfishes. 

More than 30 independently evolved mimicry communities ("mimicry rings") have been identified across South America, providing a unique opportunity to investigate whether repeated evolution of similar colour patterns is driven by the same genetic mechanisms. Using comparative and population genomics, this project will address four questions: 

  • Which genomic regions show evidence of divergent selection among different mimicry rings? 
  • Do species within the same mimicry ring show signatures of recent positive selection and selective sweeps associated with shared colour patterns? 
  • Have pigmentation genes evolved more rapidly in mimetic than non-mimetic species? 
  • By comparing multiple independent origins of mimicry, the project will test one of evolutionary biology's central questions: how predictable is adaptive evolution? 

Research methodology:

You will work with a chromosome-level reference genome, additional annotated genome assemblies, RNA-seq datasets and whole-genome resequencing data from mimetic and non-mimetic species. Using state-of-the-art population and comparative genomic approaches, you will identify genomic signatures of divergent selection, selective sweeps and molecular adaptation associated with mimicry. Most samples are already available within the host laboratory, with potential opportunities for collaborative fieldwork in South America. 

Training:

You will receive training in molecular biology, genome resequencing, comparative and population genomics, phylogenomics, bioinformatics, UNIX/Linux, high-performance computing, and programming in R and Python, providing excellent preparation for careers in evolutionary genomics, bioinformatics and academic research. 

Person specification:

Applicants should have (or expect to obtain) a First or Upper Second-Class degree (or equivalent) in Biology, Genetics, Genomics, Evolutionary Biology, Zoology or a related discipline, together with a strong interest in evolutionary biology and genomics. Experience in bioinformatics or programming (e.g. R or Python) would be advantageous but is not essential, as full training will be provided.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Unlocking healthy ageing: harnessing proteostasis pathways to promote extracellular matrix function
jobs.description_html:
Background

Ageing causes increased frailty and higher rates of disease. As societies age, this presents an enormous public health challenge, making understanding the ageing process critically important to develop ways to promote age-related health.

One prominent characteristic of ageing is altered extracellular matrix (ECM) structure and function. Changes in ECM properties have been implicated in age-related conditions including cancer, hypertension and stroke, suggesting that therapies targeting the ECM hold high potential to treat age-associated disease.

Another cause of age-related frailty and disease is a collapse in cellular stress responses, molecular pathways that safeguard cellular health. In fact, recent studies show that driving stress response activation increases longevity and resilience, emphasising their core role in healthy ageing. However, how stress responses may affect ECM ageing remains unexplored.

Our preliminary evidence suggests that driving activation of a key stress response in the model organism Caenorhabditis elegans influences expression of ECM components and promotes healthy ageing. This project will test the effects of stress response activation on composition, structure and function of the ECM during ageing, and determine whether these changes drive prolonged healthspan.

Methodology

You will utilise transcriptomics and proteomics to determine ECM composition, and advanced imaging techniques including confocal microscopy and transmission electron microscopy to examine ECM structure. You will also use genetic approaches coupled with physiological and survival assays to understand how changes to ECM function influence healthspan.

Training

You will gain a wide range of skills in experimental design, bioinformatics, scientific writing and presentation. You will also build expertise in ageing biology, cell biology, ‘omics approaches and genetic techniques. In addition, you will participate in external training courses and conferences, local seminars, research discussion groups and journal clubs.

Person specification

We are looking for an enthusiastic and highly motivated individual with a strong interest in ageing biology and genetics.

Additional Funding Information

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Incentives and Barriers: Patent Law in the Age of the 3Rs
jobs.description_html:
Biological research stands at a juncture: technologies exist and are constantly emerging that could reduce and even replace the use of animal testing. Yet patent law, which is designed to incentivise innovation, may actually be obstructing the technology's adoption.

The 3Rs (replacement, reduction and refinement of animals in research) are central to contemporary science policy. KCL has recently launched a new interdisciplinary centre dedicated to the topic, and the proposed supervisor is a member of its steering group. Governments, regulators and scientists are driving change for animal welfare. The UK government has prioritised alternatives to animal testing, and the US and EU medicines regulators have signalled a shift towards new technologies, including organ-on-chips and AI-based in silico models.

This project will examine the extent to which patent law is aligned and in tension with the objectives of the 3Rs. For instance, it will analyse how patentable subject matter (including the patentability of life forms and computer simulations) and the governance of 3R technologies shape both the development and accessibility of the technology. A primary concern is that patent rights may incentivise the technology but also limit access, leaving some researchers to rely on animal experimentation and raising the possibility that patents indirectly contribute to preventable animal harm.

Although the relationship between patents and the 3Rs has not been directly studied, the project will build on established literature on research tools and licensing mechanisms (e.g., clearinghouses and patent pledges). The project will make an interdisciplinary, policy-relevant contribution at the intersection of intellectual property, technological innovation, and animal welfare.

Value of the award: This is a fully funded studentship that includes 3 years of fees + a maintenance stipend at the UKRI level (2026-2027 rate is 23,805) for three years with small, annual inflationary increases.

The project will be supervised by Dr Johnathon Liddicoat and Professor Tanya Aplin.

Eligibility: Any nationality. Applicants should have an interest in intellectual property law, innovation, technology regulation, animal welfare, or related areas of legal research. The dedicated PhD project will examine the relationship between patent law and the 3Rs (replacement, reduction and refinement of animals in research), with a particular focus on how patent rights affect the development and accessibility of alternatives to animal testing.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Small RNA, Big Impact: The role of SNORD116 in the metabolic development of adipocytes
jobs.description_html:
Investigating the Molecular Basis of Adipocyte Metabolic Development

Understanding how fat cells (adipocytes) develop is fundamental to population-level metabolic health. This project offers the opportunity to investigate an emerging and relatively underexplored area of RNA biology: the role of small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) in regulating adipocyte metabolic development.

Once considered functionally peripheral, snoRNAs are increasingly recognised as important regulators of RNA processing and gene expression. However, their specific contribution to metabolic development remains poorly understood. This project will address that gap, providing genuine scope to generate novel insights in the field.

Using state-of-the-art gene-edited pluripotent stem cells, the successful candidate will examine how snoRNAs influence the mechanisms underlying adipocyte metabolism. The project offers comprehensive training in a range of advanced techniques, including:

  • Stem cell biology and directed differentiation
  • Advanced flow cytometry and single-cell sorting
  • Metabolomics
  • Long-read RNA sequencing

In addition to this specialist training, students will benefit from high-quality instruction in broader scientific and transferable skills, alongside access to a wide range of seminars and professional development opportunities.

The project will be based in the Smith Lab at the Bob Champion Research and Education Building, Norwich Medical School, University of East Anglia, within a collaborative and supportive environment.

This project is well suited to students seeking to develop expertise in cutting-edge molecular and cellular techniques while contributing to a growing area of metabolic research with significant relevance to human health.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Towards Near Real-time Quantification of Fossil Fuel Emissions
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Successful implementation of the Paris agreement relies on countries’ emissions being accurately known and readily available, but our ability to evaluate fossil fuel CO2 (ffCO2) emissions is currently limited.  

‘Bottom-up’ emissions estimates, based on inventory-style accounting and mobile tracking data, can differ significantly from each other at policy-relevant scales, while ‘top-down’ estimates, based on atmospheric measurements and modelling, are hampered by large natural fluxes of CO2 between the terrestrial biosphere and the atmosphere (1). 

Research methodology

The primary objective of this PhD studentship is to develop near real-time capability for top-down ffCO2 quantification, based on synchronous changes in atmospheric CO2 and oxygen (O2) measurements, in combination with complementary tracers such as Radon. Using new data products of fossil fuel O2 and CO2 emission ratios and new measurements from the Weybourne Atmospheric Observatory and the Heathfield Tall Tower in the UK, you will:  

  • Disentangle atmospheric signals into anthropogenic and natural processes (1, 2) to quantify ffCO2, making use of other tracers such as Radon (5);
  • Investigate O2 and CO2 fossil fuel emissions ratios for the UK (3);
  • Work towards near real-time top-down ffCO2 emissions reporting for the UK;
  • Use your new ffCO2 knowledge to re-evaluate land and ocean carbon sink partitioning and investigate carbon budget imbalances (4).

Training:

We will provide extensive 1-to-1 training in:

  • High-precision atmospheric O2 and CO2 measurement;
  • Measurement of related tracers (e.g., Radon);
  • Programming (e.g., R, Python) for advanced atmospheric time-series analyses, including machine learning;
  • Skills for presenting research at scientific conferences and writing peer-reviewed papers. 

This PhD includes 3-6 months spent at the UK National Physical Laboratory (NPL), for research-led training on inferring CO2 emissions using atmospheric datasets and atmospheric modelling.

There is also the opportunity for a 1-3 month research visit in Wellington, New Zealand, working with state-of-the-art CarbonWatch-NZ data (https://niwa.co.nz/atmosphere/carbonwatch-nz). Attendance at summer schools, such as the National Centre for Atmospheric Science summer school (https://ncas.ac.uk/study-with-us/atmospheric-measurement-summer-school/), will provide additional training and networking opportunities. 

Person specification:

We seek an enthusiastic team player with strong interest in the carbon cycle and climate change, self-motivation and numerical skills.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Discovering the Next Generation of Antibiotics
jobs.description_html:
The continued evolution of antibiotic-resistant bacteria presents a significant threat to global health and new compounds with novel mechanisms of action are urgently needed. Most clinical antibiotics are derived from the specialised metabolites of Streptomyces strains, and on average a single Streptomyces strain encodes between 25-50 biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) which encode for their production; many of these molecules will have antibiotic activity. However, more than 90% of these encoded specialised metabolites are not produced under laboratory conditions, meaning many new compounds remain to be discovered. To access the full metabolic potential of Streptomyces species, cryptic pathways encoding new molecules must be switched on under laboratory conditions.

In this crossdisciplinarity project the successful candidate will use genetic methods to systematically target the regulatory networks controlling specialised metabolite production. This will lead to new methods for accessing the silent arsenal of cryptic antibiotics encoded in bacterial genomes. They will develop an understanding of antibiotic function, discovery & development in addition to cutting edge training in molecular microbiology, natural products chemistry, antimicrobial resistance, biochemical analysis, and bioinformatics. These skills are essential to the next generation of bioscientists, and the candidate will be further supported in acquiring transferable skills such as written and spoken communication, problem solving and critical thinking and will help train visitors to the lab so s/he can gain skills in knowledge exchange. This combination of skills and experience will make the successful candidate highly employable in both academia and industry.

This project is awarded with a 4-year Norwich Research Park Biosciences Doctoral Training Partnership PhD DTP studentship. The studentship includes payment of tuition fees (directly to the University), a stipend to cover living expenses (2026/27 stipend rate: £21,805, and a Research Training Support Grant of £5,000pa for each year of the studentship.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Cracking the Chain of Command in Multidrug Efflux Evolution
jobs.description_html:
Are you passionate about understanding antibiotic resistance at the molecular level? Join Professor Mark Webber and Dr Gemma Langridge at the Quadram Institute Bioscience for a cutting-edge PhD project exploring how bacteria evolve multidrug resistance.

Bacteria carry multiple efflux pumps, yet only a few dominate resistance in clinical isolates. Why this is the case is unclear. This project will investigate the hierarchy of multidrug efflux systems in E. coli and beyond, testing whether this hierarchy is condition-dependent and alterable.

Using a massive transposon library of 800,000+ mutants, you'll map fitness impacts across diverse conditions—anaerobic growth, biofilms, serum, and more. You'll explore how pump removal reshapes resistance hierarchies and separate functional from regulatory costs.

You'll gain expert training in microbial evolution, genetics, transposon mutagenesis, and bioinformatics. You will be based within the state-of-the-art Quadram Institute building located on the Norwich Research Park, which host the Centre for Microbial Interactions, a vibrant research community of over 100 microbiology research groups. The project offers a wide range of opportunities for training and personal development in a world class environment.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: A Hostile Niche: How Mutant Blood Stem Cells Damage Their Healthy Neighbours
jobs.description_html:
As people age, some blood stem cells acquire mutations that give them a growth advantage over their normal counterparts. Our recent work suggests the mutant cells don't just outgrow their neighbours, they actively reshape the bone marrow around them. This change causes a functional change in the normal blood stem cells skewing their production of the immune cells. This project aims to understand which cells of the blood system are affected and what is happening to the cells at the gene and metabolic level with the overarching aim of understanding if this causes accelerated ageing of the normal blood cells.

The successful candidate will build a broad and transferable skillset: designing flow cytometry experiments across the full blood hierarchy, tissue culture, in-vivo modelling, gene expression profiles by RNA-sequencing, and metabolic assays. They will be fully integrated into a collaborative, well-supported research group spanning stem cell biology and metabolism, with regular lab meetings, journal clubs and opportunities to present their work across the Norwich Research Park and at national and international meetings.

This is a highly interdisciplinary project, ideal for someone with a background in molecular or cell biology, immunology, genetics or a related bioscience discipline, and an interest in stem cell biology or ageing. You will be based in the Mistry and Rushworth Lab at Norwich Medical School, UEA, working alongside expert collaborators at the Earlham Institute and across the Norwich Research Park.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Balancing Wheat Rust Resilience and Soil Microbial Diversity
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Plant-microbe relationships are shaped by complex, root-exuded metabolites that vary by host genotype and can be augmented to enhance agricultural productivity. In modern agriculture, an emerging, environmentally friendly strategy to enhance resilience to phytopathogens is to disrupt the function of disease susceptibility genes (S-genes), which are targeted by pathogens to promote their growth and infection. However, S-gene disruption often leads to wider changes in the metabolic profile of plants, which can influence colonisation by other pests, pathogens and beneficial microbes.

We previously defined four new S-genes in wheat (TaBCAT1, TaCSP41a, TaICL and TaASIL2) that when disrupted provide protection against wheat rust fungi, the so-called polio of agriculture. In addition, changes in metabolic profiles induced by these S-gene disruptions may provide more expansive beneficial effects against other pathogens and pests. For instance, TaICL disruption leads to hyperaccumulation of glyoxylate cycle intermediates, which when exogenously applied to plants can inhibit various pests and pathogens (e.g., wheat powdery mildew, nematodes, brown plant hopper, aphids etc). Yet, the broader implications of individual S-gene disruptions on shaping plant microbiomes remain to be explored.

Research methodology:

The main aim of this project is to resolve how S-gene disruptions influence root exudation and shape the wheat rhizosphere microbiome, and the implications of this for sustainable agricultural deployment. The individual will: (i) use field and greenhouse experiments, metagenomics and environmental microbiology to characterise the influence of S-gene disruptions in defining root microbial communities, (ii) use GC/MS metabolomics to identify the dominant metabolites influencing microbiome assembly for S-gene disruption mutants, and (iii) use spatial landscape models to establish optimal deployment strategies for S-gene disruption mutants.

Training:

You will join the international, multidisciplinary Saunders and Malone Labs at the John Innes Centre, and develop extensive skills in a breadth of areas, including plant pathology, molecular biology and environmental microbiology. Additionally, you will receive training in landscape modelling by research leaders at Exeter University

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Arctic Wintertime Storms in a Changing Climate
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Polar mesoscale cyclones are smaller scale (<1000 km) rapidly developing Arctic storm systems that occur over sub-polar and polar waters. They are challenging to forecast and a significant natural hazard for people living or visiting polar regions. The strongest class, known as polar lows, occur in winter and have gale force windspeeds with high surface heat and moisture fluxes leading to water mass transformation; so are critical in coupling the atmosphere and ocean within the climate system.

Research methodology 

This PhD project will develop a climatology of polar lows for the future using an ensemble of climate projections, investigate the impacts of polar low changes on the climate system, and examine some polar low cases in a coupled forecast model. The student will 

  • use cyclone detection and tracking tools to quantify the numbers and distribution of polar lows in future projections from a high-resolution climate model; 
  • investigate the impacts of changes in polar low frequencies and distribution on the ocean and on sea ice; 
  • examine one or two polar low case studies, making use of our existing aircraft-based observations, or other in situ observations, and new atmosphere–ice–ocean numerical weather prediction simulations using a Met Office model that has the same science configuration as the climate model.  

Training:

You will receive training in the use and analysis of climate model output as well as scientific training in the dynamics and physics of weather systems and the climate system. You will receive guidance in the use of cyclone tracking software and the visualisation of climate diagnostics, as well as how to interpret meteorological observations from various research platforms. You will also have training in using a state-of-the-art numerical weather prediction model – the Met Office Momentum system – and in the use and analyses of its output. There may be the opportunity to take part in field work.  

Person specification:

A degree in a quantitative science. An interest in data analysis of climate model output and numerical modelling of weather systems is essential, while some experience in coding is desirable.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Winds and Waves in the Alpine Mountains
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Mountains (or "orography") have a substantial effect on the atmospheric circulation. This includes atmospheric disturbances known as orographic gravity waves, generated by the winds flowing over orography. These waves propagate upwards and eventually become unstable and break down, which results in orographic gravity wave drag. This is a frictional force that decelerates upper-level winds and causes clear-air turbulence. However, a lack of understanding of these processes results in a poor representation of orographic gravity wave drag in numerical weather prediction (NWP) models, which subsequently leads to large errors in their representation of atmospheric circulation and thus weather forecasts. Due to the importance of this problem, a major international atmospheric research programme called TEAMx took place over the Alps in 2025 with the aim to improve weather forecasts in complex terrain, which included measurements from weather balloons and aircraft of orographic gravity waves.   

Research methodology

The individual will use the measurements from the TEAMx campaign to improve our process-based knowledge of orographic gravity wave drag and its representation in NWP models. Specifically:

  • Identify case studies periods with substantial orographic gravity wave activity.
  • Use the observations to investigate how orographic gravity waves are generated for the case studies, and how they propagate upwards and eventually break down.
  • Conduct multi-scale simulations of the case studies using Met Office NWP models and assess how realistically they capture orographic gravity waves and their effects.
  • Optimise these models and improve their accuracy

Training:

The individual will receive training in mountain meteorological processes and fluid dynamics, running Met Office NWP models, and data analysis. They will have the opportunity to work alongside other scientists at the British Antarctic Survey and the University of Bath working on another TEAMx project on orographic gravity waves, including opportunities to attend project meetings, as well as international TEAMx meetings. They will also receive cohort residential training, and dedicated funding for conferences and skills development.

Person specification:

The individual should have a degree in Meteorology, Physics, Maths or a similar quantitative science. An interest in meteorology, data analysis and numerical modelling is essential.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Soil Carbon and Soil Health Through Landscape Transition
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Nature-based solutions (NBS) delivered through land-use change can create new habitats, enhance biodiversity, and increase carbon sequestration at landscape scales. Your research will build upon the UKRI OpenLAND project (£4m - 2024-27 - https://tyndall.ac.uk/projects/openland/) to provide new insights into the molecular and ecological mechanisms through which NBS influence soil carbon and microbiome

Research methodology 

In this project, you will assess soil carbon stocks, carbon stability, and soil microbiome responses during landscape transition. Beyond the rolling program of ARIES cohort training, you will receive research specific training in i) dry combustion and thermogravimetric analysis to quantify carbon flows, carbon quality, soil carbon stocks and their entrained energy, and ii) molecular ecology techniques including eDNA extraction, amplification, and sequencing to characterise soil microbial communities as well as habitat classification for Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG). By integrating these approaches, you will investigate how changes in vegetation and land use alter the quantity, quality, and energy value of carbon entering soils, and how these shifts influence microbial community structure and function. Your research seeks to evidence, yet unknown, linkages that connect below ground and above ground BNG.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Antarctic Glacial Meltwater and its Importance for Ocean Circulation and Climate
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

West Antarctica’s fast-melting ice shelves release fresh water into the shelf seas that surround the continent (Sheehan et al., 2023). This alters circumpolar and global ocean currents by affecting temperatures and salt concentrations; it can even alter the ocean’s structure in a way that accelerates melting (Flexas et al., 2022). Our understanding of where the meltwater goes and the processes that determine this is poor – particularly because measurements in key regions have been very hard to obtain. You will uncover where this meltwater is going and why, helping to improve predictions of how it will influence global ocean circulation and ice shelf melting in the coming decades.

Research methodology 

You will analyse new and historical measurements of ocean properties collected by ships, profiling floats, tagged seals and UEA’s fleet of ocean gliders – underwater robots equipped for taking measurements in remote locations – to detect and quantify meltwater flows in the Bellingshausen Sea, Antarctica. You will develop the oceanographic understanding necessary to investigate the processes that control these flows, and you will use output from state-of-the-art ocean models to investigate how and why these processes change over years and decades.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: One Cell at a Time: Uncovering Enhancer Control of Blood and Cardiovascular Fate Using Single-cell Multi-omics
jobs.description_html:
The cardiovascular system - comprising the heart, blood and blood vessels - is the first functional organ system to form during vertebrate development. Cardiac progenitor cells generate the heart, while hematoendothelial progenitors produce blood and vascular endothelium. Although these lineages share an origin in the lateral plate mesoderm, they acquire distinct identities through tightly controlled gene-regulatory programmes. Many transcription factors involved in cardiovascular development are known, but much less is understood about the enhancers that control when and where these genes are activated. Enhancers are non-coding DNA regions that direct cell-type-specific gene expression. Their disruption is increasingly associated with congenital cardiovascular and blood disorders yet identifying functional enhancers and testing their roles in the developing embryo remain major challenges.

In this PhD, you will use single-cell multi-omics, combining gene-expression and chromatin-accessibility data, to investigate how enhancer activity changes as blood, endothelial and cardiac lineages emerge in the chick embryo. You will learn computational approaches to integrate single-cell RNA-sequencing and ATAC-sequencing data, reconstruct gene-regulatory networks and identify candidate enhancers linked to specific cell states and developmental trajectories. Particular emphasis will be placed on how hematoendothelial progenitors generate the first blood and vascular cells, with cardiac development providing an important comparison. Experimentally, you will clone candidate enhancers into fluorescent reporter constructs and visualise their activity in living embryos. CRISPR-based perturbation and motif mutagenesis will then test how selected enhancers control gene expression, cell behaviour and fate decisions in vivo.

You will join a collaborative supervisory team across UEA and the Earlham Institute, led by Dr Gi Fay Mok with Professor Andrea Münsterberg, Dr Iain Macaulay and Dr Wilfried Haerty. The project provides interdisciplinary training in developmental biology, molecular genetics, imaging, single-cell genomics and computational biology.

For further information, contact g.mok@uea.ac.uk.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Future-proofing the Environment: Evaluating the Environmental Impacts of Next-generation Plastics
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Increasing production, low recycling rates (below 10%), and single-use packaging are driving a global crisis in plastic pollution, with millions of tonnes of plastic accumulating in ecosystems each year. In response, governments and industry are investing heavily in biodegradable alternatives to conventional fossil fuel-derived plastics. However, the perception that these materials are ‘safer’ for the environment means far less attention has been paid to their consequences for organisms and some of the more recent and promising alternative materials have not been tested at all. Emerging evidence suggests that because biodegradable plastics break down more rapidly than traditional plastics, they may be more immediately harmful. Wider assessment of the effects of these alternative materials on environmental health are urgently needed to determine whether they provide genuine ecological benefits over conventional plastics.

Research methodology:

A series of laboratory and in situ field experiments will compare the impacts of biodegradable plastics, conventional plastics and paper-based alternatives on aquatic ecosystems. Experimental manipulations will be conducted at environmentally relevant concentrations in the River Yare (Norfolk) and Breydon Water estuary (Great Yarmouth), representing freshwater and transitional marine environments where plastic litter commonly accumulates. Biodiversity associated with each treatment will be characterised at the beginning and end of the experiment. Ecosystem functioning will be assessed through measurements of sediment oxygen demand and carbon cycling using benthic chambers, and nutrient exchange from core incubations. Findings will provide much-needed evidence on whether recently developed biodegradable plastics offer ecological benefits over conventional plastics and will support policies aimed at reducing the environmental impacts of plastic pollution, including delivery of the UK Marine Strategy and UN Sustainable Development Goal 14.

Training:

The candidate will join the Centre for Ecology, Evolution, and Conservation group. The supervisory team will provide comprehensive training in experimental design, laboratory and field skills, ecotoxicology, biogeochemical cycling, taxonomy, bioinformatics, statistical analysis, and science communication. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The Cycling of Climate-active Sulfur Compounds by Major Crops
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Dimethylsulfoniopropionate (DMSP) is known as a marine anti-stress compound made by algae and bacteria. It has key roles in global nutrient and sulfur cycling, signalling, and microbial DMSP catabolism releases climate-active gases (CAG), notably dimethylsulfide (DMS). However, DMSP is also produced by many terrestrial plants, including maize that is farmed to 1.22 billion metric tons annually, and is found at appreciable levels in maize rhizosphere samples. Little is known about microbial DMSP catabolism in terrestrial plant settings and key questions remain unanswered, e.g., what microbes degrade plant-made DMSP, which pathways do they use and what is their impact on CAG production? 

Research methodology:

This multidisciplinary PhD will address these unknowns by working on maize cropped in East Anglia. The student will conduct a seasonal field study of DMSP production and cycling on maize plantations. DMSP production, accumulation, microbial catabolism and CAG flux will be investigated at the process (using e.g., gas and liquid chromatography with mass spectroscopy) and molecular (using e.g., RT-qPCR) levels in/from plant tissue and soils –to explore their environmental significance. To complement this process-led work, the PhD will conduct culture-dependent (isolation and characterisation of model organisms) and -independent microbiology (e.g., DNA-stable isotope probing) to identify microbes importing and catabolising DMSP as a nutrient in maize samples, their biodiversity, the pathways used, the CAG liberated and how environmental changes impact these. Finally, they will be encouraged to develop the project to their interests, e.g., to investigate plant growth promoting effects of microbial isolates or novel DMSP cycling genes

Training:

You will join the productive and well-resourced teams of Todd, Miller and Oram at UEA and QIB, and receive exceptional interdisciplinary training spanning DMSP biology, molecular ecology and microbiology, plant physiology, bioinformatics, analytical chemistry, fieldwork and in scientific writing and presentation. You will present your findings at weekly team meetings, (inter)national conferences, and in peer-reviewed scientific publications and your PhD thesis.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Ecosystem Responses to Changes in Ocean Circulation
jobs.description_html:
Marine ecosystems are highly sensitive to the rapid physical reorganisation of the ocean under climate change. Large-scale circulation changes, including a weakening Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) and strengthening in Southern Ocean upwelling, combined with increasing surface ocean stratification, are altering light and nutrient availability and modulating phytoplankton growth (Guest et al. 2026). With turnover times of around one week, marine ecosystems respond almost instantaneously to these physical changes. This PhD will investigate how ecosystem functional groups and trophic structure reorganise as ocean circulation changes (Xue et al. 2024), and determine the implications for the ocean carbon storage (Jarníková et al. 2025). It will thus contribute to understanding the interactions between marine biodiversity and climate change (Le Quéré and Mayot, 2022).  

This PhD will combine observational analysis with modelling studies. Observational analysis will examine satellite data, in situ observations and paleo reconstructions, to assess recent shifts in large-scale marine ecosystems. The modelling work will use NEMO-PlankTOM global ocean biogeochemistry model (Le Quéré et al. 2016). The PhD candidate will design, set up and run model simulations to explore ecosystem responses to circulation changes over multiple centuries (e.g. from 1800 to 2300), their coherence with observational signals, and implications for ocean carbon storage. 

The PhD candidate will be part of UEA’s Greenocean research group and benefit from international collaborations. The candidate will receive specific training in ocean ecosystem modelling, AI-based code development and data analysis, and access to UEA-led courses including on python, Linux, High-Performance Computing, and data/code sharing with GitHub. They will have opportunities to attend relevant summer schools. They will acquire valuable transferable skills including Data Analysis and Management, Computer Programming and Modelling, Systems Thinking, Critical Thinking and Problem Solving, Scientific Communication, Collaboration and Networking, opening opportunities in academic and non-academic careers.  

This project is particularly suited for candidates with first degrees in any sciences and an interest in marine ecosystems and climate change. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Deciphering the Formation, Emplacement, and Ore-Forming Processes of the Rogaland Anorthosite Complex, Norway
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background:

Anorthosites represent one of the most unique and widely debated rock formations in Earth's crust. They are characterised by their almost monomineralic plagioclase composition, making them unusual among intrusive bodies. These rocks have been central to advancing our understanding of the formation of the Earth's Moon and potentially other planetary bodies. However, the origin of their monomineralic nature remains contentious, with no clear consensus regarding their source (mantle versus crust), tectonic setting, or emplacement mechanisms. Beyond their scientific significance, they have economic significance as they are associated with economically important Fe-Ti oxide deposits. The study area for this project is the Rogaland Anorthosite Complex in southern Norway, the largest massif-type anorthosite complex in Europe. The project will focus on the Egersund-Ogna massif and its associated ore bodies. 

Research methodology:

The project will address three key questions: 

  • What are the main dynamic flow regimes within large anorthosite plutons (e.g. magma mixing and convection within anorthosite magma chambers)? 
  • What was the emplacement mechanism of the Egersund-Ogna massif? 
  • How are the lenticular ore bodies related to the broader architecture of the Egersund-Ogna massif? 

The project will rely on 1) fieldwork and petrography; 2) electron backscatter diffraction analyses EBSD; 3) Magnetic fabric analysis and electron microprobe and 4) mineral chemistry. Fieldwork will be carried out in year 1 (two weeks) on Egersund – Ogna pluton, south-west Norway.  

Training:

The student will receive bespoke training in (1) digital (i.e. tablet-based) and traditional (i.e. pen and paper) mapping techniques; (2) petrology and advanced microstructural analysis; (3) rock magnetic techniques. Training will be largely one-to-one, working closely with supervisors at their modern laboratory facilities. Student will also have access to ARIES training program, providing further opportunities for professional and research skills development.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Postreproductive Maternal Care and the Evolution of Sex Differences in Lifespan
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background 

Why do some animals continue to live long after they have stopped reproducing? Classical evolutionary theory predicts that they should not. The force of natural selection on survival declines with age and falls to zero once reproduction ceases, so organisms are expected to die soon after their final reproductive event. Yet substantial postreproductive female lifespan occurs in humans, elephants and several toothed whales, and remains a striking unresolved problem in evolutionary ecology. 

The leading explanation is intergenerational transfer theory, which posits that a female who no longer reproduces can still increase her fitness by provisioning her descendants. If care extends the period over which selection acts on survival, then species where mothers care after reproduction should evolve longer-lived females. This idea is compelling but almost untested, because it has only been studied in protected long-lived mammals which precludes experimental approach. 

We have discovered a system where we can text this theory experimentally. In the nematode Caenorhabditis kamaaina, females that have finished reproducing secrete a nutritive fluid that their larvae eat, and provisioned larvae grow substantially faster. Remarkably, this is also one of the very few Caenorhabditis species in which females outlive males. 

Research methodology 

You will test whether postreproductive maternal care explains sex differences in lifespan. Using an available living collection of wild nematode species, you will measure sex-specific survival, reproduction and postreproductive maternal provisioning across phylogenetically diverse species, and test the prediction that the caring sex is the longer-lived sex. You will then use custom genetic tools developed in our lab to understand the fundamental biology linking postreproductive care and long life. 

Training 

You will gain skills in experimental design, phylogenetic analysis, statistics and coding in R, evolutionary theory, molecular ecology and genetics, scientific writing and presentation. You will receive multi-disciplinary training in evolutionary ecology/biology and in bio-gerontology, thereby increasing opportunities for employability after the PhD. You will participate in career-enhancing external training courses and in-house research discussion groups and journal clubs.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: From Spectra to Marine Litter: Multispectral Imaging and AI for Aerial Detection and Monitoring
jobs.description_html:
Scientific Background

Marine litter threatens ocean health and the coastal livelihoods that depend on it. Scalable automated methods to detect, classify and quantify litter are needed to improve understanding of its sources, pathways and impacts, yet reliable monitoring at scale remains challenging. This PhD will help address that gap, supporting marine litter assessment in the United Kingdom, Europe and beyond, contributing evidence relevant to international action on plastic pollution.

The Centre for Environment, Fisheries and Aquaculture Science (CEFAS) is developing a visible-light deep learning classifier trained on a dataset covering 89 categories of litter, alongside laboratory facilities for characterising material reflectance. This project will extend that work using multispectral and hyperspectral imaging to improve discrimination between material types. A key challenge is to develop robust methods that account for sensor sensitivity, changing daylight illumination and diverse material reflectance properties.

Research methodology

You will combine existing labelled visible-light images with spectral measurements collected using laboratory imaging systems spanning approximately 380 to 1650 nanometres. You will characterise representative litter materials, curate imaging datasets, and develop machine-learning models for material detection and classification.

You will investigate model performance under changing illumination and across different imaging sensors. Approaches will include device-independent representations, transfer learning and domain adaptation. You will evaluate model robustness and explore translation into practical multispectral systems for large-scale drone-based monitoring.

Training

You will be based in the Colour & Imaging Laboratory within the School of Computing Sciences and work closely with scientists and engineers at CEFAS. Training will include imaging principles, laboratory measurement, computer vision, deep learning, geospatial analysis and experimental design, with potential opportunities for fieldwork including drone-flying. You will develop expertise in spectral imaging, artificial intelligence, environmental monitoring, data analysis and interdisciplinary research.

Person specification

We seek an enthusiastic and curious individual with a scientific, quantitative or computational background and a genuine interest in environmental challenges. Applicants from computer science, mathematics, physics, engineering, environmental science or biological science are warmly encouraged. Prior expertise across all these areas is not expected. Curiosity, analytical thinking and willingness to learn are essential.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Investigating the ‘cry-for-help’ Effect in Wheat
jobs.description_html:
Soil microbial associations with roots are highly complex and incredibly important for healthy plant growth. Consequently, plants secrete diverse metabolites to attract/repel key microorganisms from the surrounding soil. Plant-recruited microbes contribute to plant health in multiple ways, including nutrient solubilisation, growth promotion and pathogen antagonism. Recent evidence suggests that plant roots actively recruit beneficial microbes in response to pathogen attack, the so-called ‘cry-for-help’ effect. While we understand the broad principles of the cry-for-help effect, many details of this phenomenon are poorly understood.

In this project, the student will analyse wheat split-root microcosms inoculated with microbial communities of varying complexity to explore the relationship between pathogen challenge, root metabolite secretion and soil microbiome recruitment. Using a combination of molecular and environmental microbiology, bioinformatic analysis, metabolomics and plant-microbe interaction assays, they will dissect the wheat cry-for-help effect in unprecedented detail. The project will ultimately lead to a comprehensive understanding of wheat metabolite secretion and its role in recruiting microbial communities and maintaining healthy soils. This knowledge will be crucial to the development of the next generation of sustainable, high-yielding wheat varieties.

The studentship will be based at the John Innes Centre and the neighbouring Earlham Institute. Both partners provide cutting-edge research facilities and a stimulating research and training environment, working alongside world-leading experts in soil microbiology and plant-microbe interactions. They will be part of a friendly, collaborative research team and will gain excellent training in a range of skills and techniques. The combination of transferrable, technical skills associated with the project will make the successful candidate highly employable, in industry or academia.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Investigate How Bacterial Hosts Control Domesticated Viral Machines to Drive Horizontal Gene Transfer in Marine Environments?
jobs.description_html:
Scientific background

Horizontal gene transfer (HGT) is a major driver of bacterial evolution, shaping adaptation at both species and community levels. While HGT by plasmids, transposons and bacteriophages are well understood, HGT by gene transfer agents (GTAs) is under-explored and under-appreciated. GTAs are phage-derived particles that package random fragments of the host chromosome and transfer them to neighboring cells. Unlike bacteriophages, they are non-infectious/non-replicative and instead represent remarkable examples of viral machinery domesticated by bacteria i.e. a selfless virus. 

Despite their widespread distribution in marine Alphaproteobacteria, fundamental questions remain: why have bacteria retained these inherently dangerous systems, how are they regulated, how abundant are they in marine environments, and what ecological benefits do they provide?

Ruegeria pomeroyi DSS-3, a producer of functional gene transfer agents (RpGTA), is an excellent model to answer these questions. R. pomeroyi plays a pivotal role in marine carbon, sulfur and nitrogen cycling by recycling phytoplankton-derived organic matter in the phycosphere. We hypothesize that these transient nutrient-rich hotspots support dense microbial communities/biofilms where GTA-mediated gene exchange accelerate adaptation and influence the ocean ecosystem. 

Research methodology

By integrating molecular genetics, cell imaging, and marine metagenomics and metatranscriptomics, the student will investigate how the host controls viral systems to drive gene exchange.

Aim 1. Define the regulatory network controlling RpGTA production

Aim 2. Identify the ecological signals that trigger GTA production

Aim 3. Determine the abundance, expression and diversity of GTAs in marine Roseobacter communities by deep metagenomic and metatranscriptomic sequencing

Training

Based primarily in the Le lab at the JIC, the student will receive interdisciplinary training in bacterial genetics, molecular biology, biochemistry, genomics (ChIP-seq, RNA-seq, Tn-seq) and live-cell imaging. The Todd lab, a world leader in R. pomeroyi biology and marine sulphur cycling, will provide complementary expertise in marine microbial ecology, metagenomic sampling and bioinformatics. Additional mentoring and training in specialised methodologies, experimental design and data analysis will be provided by long-term postdoc and scientific platform scientists at the JIC, Quadram Institute and UEA.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Designing Plant Gene Expression with Explainable AI
jobs.description_html:
Plants survive drought, heat and disease by rapidly changing which genes are switched on, where, and when. But we still cannot reliably design the regulatory DNA that controls these expression patterns. This PhD asks an ambitious question: can explainable AI discover plant DNA “design rules” that are strong enough to survive experimental testing?

You will join Earlham Institute’s AI for Biology group led by Professor Ke Li. As one of the most active AI groups in the UK, you will work in a highly supportive and collaborative group, equipped with unique technical platforms for building in-house large-scale foundation models. You will receive scientific training in foundational AI methods and push the boundary of AI for biology. Meanwhile, you will also develop skills in experimental design, reproducible software and FAIR data management.

You will also obtain complementary experience in plant genomics and engineering biology, supported by Prof. Anthony Hall’s plant genomics expertise and Dr Carolina Grandellis’s Earlham Biofoundry team. You will collaborate with experimentalists on the design of compact libraries of cis-regulatory modules, assemble them into a standard reporter system and test them in potato protoplast assays. Successful and failed designs will both be valuable: they will reveal which AI-derived rules are biologically meaningful, where models fail, and how future design cycles should be improved.

The project will be conducted at the Earlham Institute, a world-class BBSRC research centre of excellence in genomics, engineering and computational biology, and AI. You will join a highly collaborative and supportive research community, interact with AI researchers, plant scientists, bioinformaticians, automation specialists, and have access to training and career development opportunities across the Norwich Research Park through the Norwich Research Park Biosciences Doctoral Training Partnership.
