jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Deciphering Critical Regulators in Wheat Rust Immunity
jobs.description_html:
Successful plant pathogens hijack plant metabolism and biosynthetic pathways to enrich nutrient availability. However, exploiting host physiology creates changes in metabolites that plants can sense and interpret as indicators of pathogen infection. This includes branched chain amino acids (BCAAs), which represent important energy sources for pathogens, yet BCAA accumulation in plants also increases levels of the defence compound salicylic acid (SA), which plays a central role in directing immune signaling against biotrophic pathogens. We previously showed in bread wheat (Triticum aestivum), that infection by the biotrophic yellow rust pathogen (Puccinia striiformis f. sp. tritici; Pst) upregulates the gene for BCAA AMINOTRANSFERASE 1 (TaBCAT1), which modulates catabolism of BCAAs to prevent BCAA accumulation and promote Pst colonisation. In contrast, disrupting TaBCAT1 function leads to hyperaccumulation of BCAAs and SA, resulting in reduced susceptibility to Pst. Furthermore, we found that BCAA-mediated SA accumulation is dependent on a MYB/SANT transcription factor (TF), termed TaASIL1, which represses expression of TaSIZ1, a SUMO E3 ligase that is a key negative regulator of SA homeostasis. However, how BCAA accumulation enhances TaASIL1 activity remains to be resolved.

The aim of this proposal is to elucidate how BCAA availability activates SA-mediated defence and/or modulates metabolic signalling in plants, by: (i) resolving the unknown link between BCAA accumulation and activation of TaASIL1 function, and (ii) characterising additional BCAA-dependant gene targets of TaASIL1. This research will ultimately determine how MYB TFs mediate environmental signals, such as BCAAs, to modulate metabolic signalling in plants and provide critical new insight into basal plant defence responses in wheat.

The student will be embedded in the Saunders Lab at the John Innes Centre, which is a multidisciplinary research lab, providing the opportunity to develop extensive skills in a breadth of areas, including plant pathology, wheat genetics, molecular biology, and bioinformatics.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Understanding the Evolution of Calcium Signal Decoding Mechanisms in Plants
jobs.description_html:
Plants need to respond to the environment in order to adapt and grow. Plants often modify the concentration of calcium ions in their cells in response to different environmental stimuli and stresses [1]. These changes in cellular calcium concentration trigger many downstream responses, including re-programming of gene expression. Calcium signalling pathways are therefore essential for plants to respond and adapt to environmental stimuli and stresses.

Flowering plants, such as the model plant Arabidopsis thaliana, have extensive networks of proteins associated with calcium signalling pathways, and traditional genetic studies have identified mutants in components of these pathways. However, genetic redundancy is often observed and this has hindered further study of these signalling pathways. Recent genomic analyses have revealed that the gene families encoding components of calcium signalling pathways are considerably smaller in other model plant species, including in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha [3]. The study of these pathways in M. polymorpha will therefore offer unique insights and understandings into calcium signalling pathways in plants and may identify new potential targets that could be manipulated to improve stress tolerance in crop species.

This PhD project will undertake a multi-disciplinary approach combining molecular genetics, cell biology and biochemistry to dissect calcium signalling and decoding mechanisms in the liverwort Marchantia polymorpha.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Sweet and Sticky: The Role of Protein Glycosylation in Bacteria Colonisation and Adaptation to the Gut
jobs.description_html:
The accessory secretion (aSec) system is a protein export pathway that is uniquely present in Gram-positive bacteria and is dedicated to the secretion of large, glycosylated cell wall-anchored adhesins called serine-rich repeat proteins (SRRPs). We previously identified aSec pathways and strain-specific glycosylation of SRRPs in Limosilactobacillus reuteri, a health-promoting gut commensal bacteria showing high host specialisation. This PhD studentship provides an exciting opportunity for the successful candidate to address fundamental questions on the role of protein glycosylation in bacteria adaptation in the gut.

In this PhD project, the student will use in vitro and in vivo approaches including organ-on-chip technology and mouse models to investigate the role of SRRP glycosylation in biofilm formation and colonisation.

The PhD student will join a large and dynamic multidisciplinary team at the Quadram Institute Bioscience and receive mentoring and training in relevant experimental models and state-of-the art analytical tools. Through this PhD studentship, the student will acquire expertise in molecular microbiology, glycobiology, biochemistry, imaging, bioinformatics, advanced microbe-host models (gut organoids) and in vivo skills.

The student will benefit from the established network of international collaborations of the host Labs in this research area. Training will embrace research practice and theory, research integrity, management, communication (to scientific and lay audiences) and technical writing, intellectual property, teamwork. The student will present his/her work at internal seminars and to relevant Microbiology and Glycobiology international meetings, and be encouraged to participate into outreach activities and innovative competitions.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: One Health (meta)genomics of E. coli-associated Urinary Tract Infections in Pregnancy
jobs.description_html:
Urinary tract infections (UTIs) affect up to 35% of pregnant women and are associated with maternal sepsis, pre‑term birth and markedly higher health‑care costs. Uropathogenic Escherichia coli (UPEC) accounts for 82–85% of these infections, and there are various bacterial factors that predispose to higher infection morbidity including certain phylogenetic groups, sequence types and virulence factors. 

In this project, the student will investigate the hypothesis that the increased risk of UTIs observed in pregnancy may be in part due to differences in the types of E. coli causing the infections, including variations in phylogenetic group, virulence genes and antimicrobial resistance (AMR) determinants. Working with clinicians at the Norfolk and Norwich University Hospital, the student will collect urine and faecal samples from pregnant women, and use long-read genome and metagenome sequencing to characterise urine microbial compositions in these groups and 18S qPCR to examine human DNA load and cytokine quantification to evaluate disease severity. Whole genome sequence data will be used to obtain an understanding of where the infections might be coming from: the genotypes of UTI-causing E. coli will be compared with 1) those in the patients’ own guts, 2) publicly available genomes obtained from non-pregnant individuals, 3) E. coli genomes from food and other environmental sources, as it’s been suggested some infections might come through the food chain.

The outcomes from this One Health and microbiome project will help combat infectious disease and antimicrobial resistance, and will provide the student with a valuable skillset in interdisciplinary research, encompassing bioinformatics, (meta)genomics and statistics with public health relevance.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Can Blood Reveal the Body? Trustworthy AI for Tissue Gene Expression
jobs.description_html:
A blood sample can be collected repeatedly, but a biopsy from the brain, liver or intestine cannot be. Could the molecular signals in the blood reveal what is happening in other tissues, and tell us when the inference is trustworthy?

This PhD will develop Blood2Tissue, a tissue-conditioned AI modelling framework that predicts tissue-specific gene expression programmes from blood. Existing studies demonstrate feasibility for some genes and tissues, but predictions are often population average, accuracy varies substantially, and current approaches rarely identify which individual predictions can be trusted.

You will build on CHROMATIN, our team’s cross-modal attention framework for imputing missing modalities in multi-omics datasets, and MOCHA, our uncertainty framework with a preprint expected shortly. The aim is not simply to create another blood-to-tissue predictor.

You will benchmark existing methods using GTEx dataset, develop and calibrate Blood2Tissue, and use IBDverse and reference cell atlases to investigate fundamental questions such as why some molecular programmes are blood-visible while others remain tissue-autonomous. Confirmed visits to Ellen McDonagh's Open Targets team at European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) will provide experience connecting reliable molecular signals to genetic and disease evidence. The project will deliver reusable computational methodology and new biological understanding of cross-tissue regulation, with longer-term relevance to Digital Twins of living systems.

Training will span transcriptomics, machine learning, uncertainty quantification, genetics, single-cell genomics, HPC, reproducible software and responsible AI, including supervised use of emerging AI-assisted and agentic tools for coding, benchmarking and workflow automation. The project will be conducted at the Earlham Institute, a world-class BBSRC research centre of excellence in genomics, engineering and computational biology, and AI.

You will join Dr Rahuman Sheriff’s AI integrated Digital Twins Group within Earlham Institute’s data-intensive bioscience environment, with Prof Irene Papatheodorou contributing expertise in cellular genomics and FAIR data. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: From Defence to Antibiotic production: Uncovering New Roles for NLR Signalling in Multicellular Bacteria
jobs.description_html:
Nucleotide-binding and oligomerisation domain-like receptors (NLRs) are famous for driving immune responses in plants and animals. However, their extensive presence in multicellular, antibiotic-producing Streptomyces hints at a much richer, untapped functional diversity. This PhD project aims to challenge the paradigm that bacterial NLRs solely function in phage defence, uncovering their broader roles in multicellular development, complex signalling networks, and the regulation of natural products.

By combining computational mining with hands-on experimental biology, you will explore the full spectrum of the Streptomyces ""NLRome"". You will deploy synthetic activation tools to trigger candidate NLRs, investigating how they control bacterial viability, phage immunity, morphological development, and antibiotic biosynthesis. Beyond fundamental biology, this project holds high-impact applied potential: synthetic activation of specific NLRs offers a novel route to switch on silent gene clusters and trigger the production of new bioactive molecules.

As a PhD researcher on this project, you will gain comprehensive, interdisciplinary training across: 

  • Computational Biology & Bioinformatics: Large-scale genome mining, structural modelling (AlphaFold, Foldseek), and pipeline development.
  • Molecular Microbiology & Genetics: Phenotyping, heterologous expression, phage assays, and genetic engineering of multicellular bacteria.
  • Protein Biochemistry & Omics: Protein-protein interaction studies, catalytic assays, transcriptomics, and metabolomics.

Based at the John Innes Centre, you will join a supportive, highly collaborative research environment supported by world-class platform facilities and leading experts in plant and bacterial NLR biology.

You will also develop key professional skills through conference presentations, manuscript preparation, and public science outreach.

This project is ideal for a motivated student eager to blend computational analysis with experimental biology to redefine our understanding of ancient signalling proteins.

Informal enquiries to Prof Susan Schlimpert (susan.schlimpert@jic.ac.uk) are welcome.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Data-driven Control Engineering for Large-scale Uncertain Systems
jobs.description_html:
Research Studentship in Control Theory, Optimization and Learning

3.5-year D.Phil. studentship 

Project: Data-driven control engineering for large-scale uncertain systems.

Supervisors: Prof Antonis Papachristodoulou and Prof Kostas Margellos

This project will focus on solving fundamental challenges at the modernization of Control Engineering using tools from data-driven algorithms, advancements on optimization and statistical learning. Cross-fertilizing ideas across these domains can be of mutual benefit for all areas. This project will focus on how the use of learning tools can be used to improve control engineering tools. This could look at the problem of algorithm scalability and efficiency, or at how concepts such as “world models” can be used to extend our thinking about traditional modelling frameworks in control. At the same time, this project will investigate how control theory can offer robustness guarantees when employed in conjunction with such modelling concepts.

The approaches taken will depend on the candidate’s skills and interests, but may include developing control theoretic and AI methods that advance our ability to design reliable and robust control systems. Potential project applications will involve applying these skills to large scale uncertain systems and integrate them with “world models”. The project will enable candidates to build a broad skillset in theory and algorithm design, engineering, and the application of control to new AI technologies, providing an ideal foundation for future careers in academia, the bioscience industry, or entrepreneurship/start-ups.

The studentship will integrate with research activities carried out within the new MSc on AI for Engineering Biology, hosted within the Department of Engineering Science, University of Oxford. As such the candidate will be exposed to research by a multidisciplinary team of academic and industrial experts with experience in related areas of biotechnology and have opportunities to collaborate with industrial and academic partners nationally and internationally.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Research Studentship in Control Engineering- Sustainable and Circular AI Systems
jobs.description_html:
Research Studentship on Sustainable and Circular AI Systems

3.5-year D.Phil. studentship 

Project: Sustainable and Circular AI Systems

Supervisors: Prof Lucia Corsini

The DPhil student will investigate how the rapid growth of Artificial Intelligence (AI) can be supported by more sustainable and circular hardware and infrastructure. While existing research on the environmental impacts of AI has largely focused on energy use and carbon emissions, much less is understood about the growing demand for hardware, critical raw materials, and the opportunities to reduce these impacts through circular economy strategies.

The student will develop new approaches to connect AI computational performance with the physical hardware and materials required to deliver it. They will examine how alternative pathways for UK AI and data centre development could affect demand for critical and secondary raw materials, while considering how strategies such as lifetime extension, reuse, repair, upgrading and remanufacture could reduce environmental impacts and dependence on critical raw materials.

The research will develop scenarios for how future growth in UK AI computing could translate into demand for physical infrastructure, including processors, accelerators, memory, storage and networking equipment. The student will map these hardware requirements to their underlying materials, identifying critical material dependencies and potential supply-chain hotspots. They will then investigate how different hardware lifetimes and circular economy strategies could change future material requirements while maintaining computational performance.

The DPhil student will join the Circular Economy and Sustainability Lab and contribute to the Circular Electricals and Electronics Project, which seeks to enable a low-carbon, Circular Economy for Electrical and Electronic Equipment.

Eligibility

This studentship is funded through the Department of Engineering Science and is open to Home and overseas students (full award – fees plus stipend).

Award Value

jobs.title: PhD project: Railway Asset Degradation and Management Modelling for Climate Change
jobs.description_html:
Supervised by Rasa Remenyte-Prescott (Faculty of Engineering)

Aim: To include climate change effects into railway asset degradation and asset management modelling

Bridges are vital to the UK’s economic and societal infrastructure, and railway bridges are critical infrastructure for Network Rail, forming a vital part of the 30,000 bridges, tunnels and viaducts which they manage across Britain. Increased traffic demand, limited maintenance, and ageing structural systems have pushed many bridges beyond their original design capacities. In addition, climate change is altering environmental exposure conditions, particularly temperature and relative humidity, which further accelerate the deterioration of bridges. Physics-based formulations with probabilistic models are necessary to capture uncertainty and environmental variability in bridge component degradation modelling. The processes of atmospheric and pitting corrosion, chloride-induced corrosion, thermal cycling and fatigue, protective painting and coating degradation, to name a few, are most affected by increased rainfall and humidity, extreme heat conditions and air pollution, especially due to increasing effects of climate change.

It is envisaged that the approach will incorporate climate-dependent parameters and their influence on the deterioration of a bridge, and it will allow a clear integration of regional/national climate projections. Climate projections will be taken from the UK Climate Projections (UKCP18) based on multiple Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) and used along the probabilistic models of deterioration to capture uncertainty and environmental variability. The proposed approach will consider interdependencies, providing a realistic system-level variability in condition-state evolution, ranging from baseline ageing to pessimistic climate change effects, which would indicate acceleration of deterioration.

jobs.title: PhD Project: Modelling Resilience of Water Distribution Networks
jobs.description_html:
Supervised by Rasa Remenyte-Prescott (Faculty of Engineering)

Aim: To develop a modelling approach for assessing water network resilience

One of the essential networks for society is water distribution networks. The delivery of water to the customers is affected through different threats to the system. These include failure of components in the system, which are accelerated through the aging of the infrastructure; climate change, due to changing weather conditions and environmental factors impacting on the system; and deliberate planned acts, such as targeted terrorist activities.

This exciting project will focus on developing a mathematical model (and a supporting research software) to predict the key performance indicators of a water network, when links in the network are fully or partially failed. It will investigate the impact of the different threat types and identify the critical links in the network, which most affect the network performance. Resilience evaluation will consist of proposing a method for the best use of resource allocation, which will make water networks robust and resilient to these threats.

jobs.title: PhD Project: Microgrid Resilience
jobs.description_html:
Supervised by Rasa Remenyte-Prescott and Marco Rivera (Faculty of Engineering)

Aim: To develop a modelling approach for assessing microgrid resilience

The deployment of renewable energy resources is a viable option to mitigate the emissions of greenhouse gases which have become one of the major concerns on a global scale, and the UK is committed to reaching net zero by 2050. To ensure a reliable electricity supply using renewables, deployment of distributed energy resources and their efficient operation require an interconnected energy system, known as a microgrid, which can operate autonomously when the upstream grid fails. In this way, microgrids can improve the resilience of the electricity system by reducing the amount of energy not supplied, and excess microgrid generation can be sold to the main grid to provide customers with financial benefits, such as reductions in electricity bills.

This exciting project will focus on modelling a small-scale converter-dominated microgrid, integrating renewable generation, hybrid electrical storage and hydrogen technologies. On the energy generation side, photovoltaic generation, batteries and supercapacitors will be used, and on the conversion and utilisation side, a hydrogen electrolyser and a fuel cell will allow hydrogen production, storage and reconversion to be actively controlled as part of the microgrid operation. Microgrid resilience metrics and their modelling and analysis approach will be proposed. A variety of disturbances (low/high frequency and high/low impact) and their effects on microgrid’s ability to resist incidents efficiently and provide quick recovery and restoration will be analysed under uncertainty.

jobs.title: PhD project: Resilient Processes of Nuclear Fusion Plant Maintenance and Decommissioning using Robotic Technologies
jobs.description_html:
Supervised by Rasa Remenyte-Prescott (Faculty of Engineering)

Aim: To develop a modelling approach for nuclear fusion plant maintenance and decommissioning processes

More than 80% of the world’s energy still comes from fossil fuels. Climate change and diminishing fuel reserves mean that it is becoming essential to find alternative, sustainable technologies to supply a growing global population. With no greenhouse gas emissions, inherent safety features and virtually limitless fuels, nuclear fusion has a key role to play in the energy market of the future. Major projects, like ITER in France and STEP in the UK, are providing potential avenues for solutions of this clean, abundant, and safe energy. Robotics and remotely operated tools are a fundamental part of operating fusion power plants, therefore, a fusion power plant must be designed to be inspected, maintained, and upgraded remotely using robots.

This exciting project will focus on different qualitative and quantitative risk assessment techniques, considering their suitability for risk analysis of the robotics-based maintenance and/or decommissioning of a nuclear fusion plant. System failure modes and contributing elements in success of a mission will be identified and analysed, followed by modelling a variety of threats and their effects on the mission, as well process recovery and restoration under uncertainty.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship with the Leverhulme Trust - Experimental Investigation of Phase Change Mechanisms in Aircraft Contrail Formation
jobs.description_html:
Contrail formation remains one of the least understood yet most climate-relevant impacts of aviation. Persistent contrails can evolve into cirrus-like clouds that significantly affect Earth's radiative balance, but the physical mechanisms governing their formation particularly in the near-field region immediately downstream of aircraft engines remain poorly characterised.

This fully funded PhD studentship is part of a Leverhulme Trust Research Project entitled "Bridging the scale gap: From non-equilibrium thermodynamics to contrails". The project combines laboratory-scale experiments with high-fidelity numerical modelling to investigate vapour-liquid-solid phase transitions in aircraft exhaust plumes under controlled conditions, with particular relevance to emerging low-soot propulsion technologies such as sustainable aviation fuels and hydrogen.

The PhD project focuses on the experimental investigation of early contrail formation, using a dedicated facility that generates contrail-relevant exhaust flows by injecting a high-speed moist jet into a controlled, cold environment. The student will contribute to the development and application of advanced optical and laser-based diagnostics to characterise condensation, freezing, and particle populations in the evolving plume.

The project includes close interaction with numerical simulations, enabling quantitative comparison between experiment and CFD and supporting physical interpretation of the measured processes. While the primary focus of the PhD is experimental, the student will gain experience working at the interface of experiment and high-fidelity modelling in a collaborative research environment.

The 3-year studentship is fully funded for home students and includes tuition fees and a tax-free stipend at the UKRI rate. The expected start date is 1 October 2027. Applications should include a CV, academic transcripts, and a brief statement outlining the applicant's motivation and relevant background. Informal enquiries are welcome.

Applicants should have (or expect to obtain by the start date) at least a good 2.1 degree in Engineering or a closely related subject. A strong interest in experimental fluid mechanics and thermodynamics is essential. The project involves multiphase and particle-laden flows relevant to contrail formation; prior experience in these areas is welcome but not required. Experience with laboratory instrumentation, data acquisition, or optical diagnostics is desirable but not essential. Familiarity with coding or data analysis (e.g. MATLAB, Python, LabVIEW) would be an advantage. Good written and spoken English communication skills are expected.

Applications should be submitted via the University of Cambridge Applicant Portal (via the ‘Apply’ button above), with Dr Katharina Tegethoff identified as the potential supervisor. Applications may close early if the position is filled before the advertised date. Please note there is a £20 application fee attached to using the Cambridge Applicant Portal.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship (EPSRC FIBE3 CDT) with National Highways - Extreme Weather Implications for Concrete Behaviour
jobs.description_html:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at https://www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk/

The project is funded in collaboration with National Highways.  National Highways is the UK government company which plans, designs, builds, operates and maintains England's motorways and major A-roads, known as the strategic road network.

Due to geological abundance of its constituents, and its strength and resilience, concrete is used widely across National Highway's strategic road network in both ancillary and primary structures. However, conventional ordinary Portland cement concrete is carbon intensive so any new construction must have embodied carbon reduction at the fore and, wherever possible, the lifetime of existing infrastructure must be extended. In parallel, external weather demands on concrete during placement, and in service, are escalating due to climate change. This project therefore has elements of both concrete climate change mitigation, and adaptation.  One particular area of uncertainty is whether lower carbon concretes may exhibit greater sensitivity to harsher early age curing conditions leading to detrimental longer-term chemical or microstructural effects, and thus an undesirable reduction in quality.  Acceleration of concrete exposure conditions in practice will also be investigated to consider the effects on concrete of more extreme temperatures and repeated wetting and extended drying not previously seen in modern history.

The project objectives include: to exploit advanced digital measurement techniques in tandem with concrete characterisation experiments under controlled and/or accelerated exposure conditions e.g. temperature, humidity, carbonation; to investigate macro-scale and micro-scale models for prediction (AI tools will be used as appropriate) to infer correlation and for physics-informed modelling; to conduct evidence-based analyses of trade-offs between quality and embodied carbon.

The new knowledge derived through the project will frame guidance on acceptable weather conditions during placement and enable pre-emptive prediction of any detrimental effects due to more severe in-service exposure conditions to thereby future-proof both new and existing infrastructure.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship (EPSRC FIBE3 CDT) with National Highways - Rapid, Low Risk, Adoption of Lower Carbon Concrete
jobs.description_html:
This is a four-year (1+3 MRes/PhD) studentship funded through the Cambridge EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Future Infrastructure and Built Environment: Unlocking Net Zero (FIBE3 CDT). Further details can be found at https://www.net-zero-fibe-cdt.eng.cam.ac.uk/

The project is funded in collaboration with National Highways. National Highways is the UK government company which plans, designs, builds, operates and maintains England's motorways and major A-roads.

Concrete has traditionally used Portland cement as the primary binder material but the high embodied carbon penalty associated with high proportions of Portland cement is no longer tenable in a climate emergency. The construction industry is responding by actively replacing cement with other constituents with lower carbon footprints. The challenge is to rapidly adopt promising binder alternatives while ensuring that mix compositions with a relatively short performance track record will successfully meet the demands of infrastructure over 50-100 years.  

This project seeks to derisk the adoption of newer lower carbon concretes. Binders with higher levels of cement replacement through supplementary cementitious materials (SCMs) and/or filler materials will be scrutinised in the context of concrete material properties e.g. microstructure, and performance measures e.g. durability. A combination of digitally enhanced experimental work and multi-physics modelling will help establish performance comparisons for compositions with SCM replacement to thereby identify and validate appropriate limits on proportion and composition thresholds. The project objectives include: to quantify the alignment of lower carbon concrete combinations against current design standards; to identify promising multi-component binder concretes that sit within, or outside, design standards e.g. through combinations of limestone, calcined clay, fly ash and GGBS replacement, but for which testing compliance is needed to address knowledge gaps to provide confidence in future performance; to undertake comprehensive experimentation and theoretical investigations to support service-life modelling. 

The project outcomes will give greater confidence in the fundamental behaviour of lower carbon concrete mixes to accelerate uptake in UK infrastructure to help meet net zero aspirations.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Development of Intra-Red Thin Film Optoelectronic Devices
jobs.description_html:
Optoelectronic devices, like thermal imaging cameras and night-vision sensors, require clear optical “windows” that allow infrared light to pass through while strictly blocking environmental oxygen and moisture, which degrade the sensitive internal components. Currently, the most effective moisture barriers use polymer materials, but these block infrared light. This project aims to solve this by creating a new type of multilayer filter, combining polymer layers with thin films of metals and ceramics, that will successfully block gases without sacrificing infrared transmission, directly benefiting the next generation of devices. 

This project will appeal to a materials scientist/engineer who is excited by materials discovery, but also enthusiastic to see how their research can be translated into real-world devices. The work will take place in the Surface Engineering Laboratory in the Dalton Building at Manchester Met and at the premises of our industrial partner, Brinell Vision Ltd in Irlam, Manchester, giving the successful candidate experience of working in both academic and industrial facilities. 

You will be supported by an experienced multidisciplinary supervisory team with access to state-of-the-art laboratories equipped with production, characterisation and testing facilities.

Objectives

There is a critical gap in the production of ultra-barrier encapsulation that maintains high optical transmission in the 1.5– 15 µm regime, a range vital for thermal imaging and night-vision technologies.  Consequently, the objective of this project is to address this requirement for broad-spectrum, highly transmissive interference coatings that double as hermetic gas barriers (O2 and H2O) for active optoelectronic elements operating in this range. 

The specific aims are to develop Ge/GeOxNy multilayer structures, produced by magnetron sputtering, with the required optical properties and, by incorporating novel polymer layers, demonstrate that they exhibit the required durability for demanding applications and, furthermore, demonstrate that these structures can form the basis for new generations of optoelectronic devices.

Funding

Home students can apply only. Home tuition fees will be covered for the duration of the 3-year award, which is £5,238 for the year 2026/27.  

The student will receive a standard stipend payment for the duration of the award. These payments are set at a level determined by UKRI, currently £21,805 for the year 2026/27.

Candidate requirements

Essential:

  • Undergraduate degree (first or upper second-class honours ) in engineering, materials science, or closely related subject
  • Must be willing to learn new skills.
  • Ability to undertake experiments accurately and safely and make verbal or written reports. 

Desirable:

  • Relevant postgraduate (MEng, MSc, MSci, MRes, etc.) degree.
  • Prior research project experience, especially in thin films production and testing or optical modelling. 

How to apply

If you have any questions, please contact the proposed Principal Supervisor, Dr Justyna Kulczyk-Malecka (J.Kulczyk-Malecka@mmu.ac.uk).  

To apply you will need to complete the online application form for a full time PhD in Engineering.

Please complete the Doctoral Project Applicant Form, and include your CV and a covering letter to demonstrate how your skills and experience map to the aims and objectives of the project, the area of research and why you see this area as being of importance and interest.  

Please upload these documents in the supporting documents section of the University’s Admissions Portal or email the requested documents to pgradmissions@mmu.ac.uk.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Development and Application of Next-Generation Instrumentation to Quantify the Chemical Drivers of Particle Oxidative Potential
jobs.description_html:
Application deadline: All year round

This 4-year PhD project is fully funded; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27) and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year. The start date is January 2027.

We recommend that you apply early as the advert may be removed before the deadline.

Air pollution exposure is a major global health issue, responsible for millions of premature deaths each year and is a leading cause of respiratory and cardiovascular disease worldwide. Despite compelling evidence associating exposure to particulate matter (PM) with adverse health effects, the most harmful PM chemical components remain unclear. Current air quality regulation targets total PM mass regardless of composition, an approach increasingly recognised as inefficient, since it treats all particles as equally hazardous, irrespective of their chemical composition or biological activity.

Oxidative potential (OP), the capacity of PM to deplete antioxidants and generate reactive oxygen species, has emerged as a leading metric for capturing the biologically relevant hazard of PM, reflected in its inclusion in the recently updated European Union Air Quality Directive. Unlike mass-based measurements of PM, OP reflects particle chemical reactivity and their capacity to promote oxidative stress, offering a route to identifying which components and emission sources are most harmful to health.

We have recently pioneered the development a novel instrument that provides continuous, high time-resolution quantification of OP which has been deployed in proof of concept laboratory and field studies. Building on this state-of-the-art platform, this studentship will advance the next generation of the instrument, apply it in controlled laboratory studies at the Manchester Aerosol Chamber (MAC), and deploy it in real-world field campaigns to generate comprehensive high time-resolution OP datasets to determine the PM components and emission sources which drive OP.

The student will first lead the design, optimisation and characterisation of an improved instrument iteration, gaining hands-on experience in analytical instrument development, including microfluidics, chemical reagent optimisation, and laboratory performance testing, establishing it as the leading platform for real-time OP quantification.

Second, the student will deploy the instrument at the MAC, a leading atmospheric simulation facility, to investigate the chemical mechanisms driving PM oxidative activity. Experiments will explore how particle composition of different PM emission sources and atmospheric processing, including photochemical ageing, humidity, and interactions between redox-active metals and secondary organic aerosol, influence OP.

Third, the student will deploy the instrument at an established urban air quality monitoring site, generating high time-resolution OP datasets alongside complementary PM composition measurements, gaining critical insights into the temporal variability and PM components which drive OP.

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, at least a 2.1 honours degree or a master’s (or international equivalent) in chemistry, biochemistry, atmospheric or environmental science, chemical engineering, or a related discipline, and a genuine enthusiasm for hands-on laboratory and field measurements.

We strongly recommend that you contact the supervisor(s) for this project before you apply. Dr Steven Campbell (steven.campbell@manchester.ac.uk) would be pleased to discuss this project further with interested candidates prior to application. Please include details of your current level of study, academic background and any relevant experience and include a paragraph about your motivation to study this PhD project.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Modelling Actinide Speciation in Solution with Multiconfigurational Quantum Chemistry Techniques
jobs.description_html:
Application deadline: 21/12/2026

This 3.5-year PhD project is fully funded; students who are eligible to pay tuition fees at the Home rate are eligible to apply. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27) and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year. The start date is October 2027.

We recommend that you apply early as the advert may be removed before the deadline.

Nuclear power is a central part of the UK’s plans for energy security and net zero, but the legacy of the nuclear fuel cycle remains a major challenge, with waste management alone estimated to cost over £120bn. Decommissioning, waste treatment and disposal all rely on understanding the chemical form of actinides in solution and in the environment. Oxidation state and coordination environment determine how these elements behave in the environment, and the ability to characterise actinide species with high accuracy has become increasingly important.

X-ray absorption and emission spectroscopies are highly sensitive to oxidation state, local structure and bonding. Actinide spectra are notoriously difficult to interpret due to strong multiplet and spin-orbit effects, leading to a rich spectrum. In solution the picture is further complicated by solvent, counter-ions and coordinating ligands. Multiconfigurational relativistic methods can treat these effects explicitly, and they are now the state of the art for simulating X-ray spectra of heavy elements.

In this project, the student will develop and apply multiconfigurational approaches to study actinide speciation in solution. A key part of the work will be accounting for the effects of the solution environment, combining a range of computational techniques with high-level electronic structure methods. The resulting simulations will be compared with experimental data to help interpret the spectra of different actinide species. The aim is a transferable computational framework for understanding actinide speciation under conditions relevant to the nuclear fuel cycle.

Applicants should have, or expect to achieve, at least a 2.1 honours degree or a master’s (or international equivalent) in Chemistry, Physics, or related discipline.

To apply, please contact the main supervisor, Dr Meagan Oakley - meagan.oakley@manchester.ac.uk. Please include details of your current level of study, academic background and any relevant experience and include a paragraph about your motivation to study this PhD project.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Multiscale Physics of Deformation and Failure in Polymer Networks
jobs.description_html:
3.5-year D.Phil. studentship

Supervisor: Professor Laurence Brassart

Many soft materials, such as elastomers and hydrogels, consist of networks of interconnected polymer chains. Their properties can be tuned through molecular composition, polymer chain length, network architecture, and interactions with solvents, resulting in a broad range of mechanical behaviours and functionalities. This versatility underpins applications ranging from soft structures and adhesives to medicine, energy, and sustainability technologies. A major challenge for the design of these materials is to understand and predict their deformation and failure behaviours and their relationships to the underlying network topology.

The aim of this DPhil is to develop a mesoscale modelling framework to predict the time-dependent deformation and failure of polymer networks based on a description of the underlying chain-level physics. Building on previous works in the Brassart Group, we will use a coarse-grained discrete-network model to explicitly represent the network architecture. A major focus will be the development of physically grounded descriptions of viscoelasticity and time-dependent chain scission, drawing on statistical mechanics and stochastic thermodynamics. The framework will be used to investigate time-dependent deformation and failure, with predictions tested against existing experimental data and, where appropriate, molecular simulations.

This project would particularly suit a student who enjoys physical and mathematical modelling, and who is excited by challenging theoretical problems in soft matter physics and mechanics. Candidates are not expected to have prior experience in this specific area, but intellectual curiosity, a desire to understand problems from first principles, and strong analytical and computational skills are essential. A background in mechanics, physics, applied mathematics, materials science, or chemistry could provide a suitable starting point.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Exploring How Mycobacterium Tuberculosis Uses Nutrients
jobs.description_html:
Research theme: Microbiology, Chemical Biology

This 3.5-year PhD project is fully funded, and home students are eligible to apply. The successful candidate will receive an annual tax-free stipend set at the UKRI rate (£21,805 for 2026/27) and tuition fees will be paid. We expect the stipend to increase each year. The start date is January or April 2027.

We recommend that you apply early as the advert may be removed before the deadline.

This PhD project will investigate how Mycobacterium tuberculosis utilises nutrients and how changes in nutrient transport influence pathogen biology by combining microbiology, biochemical and analytical approaches.

Tuberculosis (TB), caused by the bacterial pathogen Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb), remains the leading cause of death worldwide from a single bacterial pathogen. The latest World Health Organisation report estimates that ~1.3 million people died from TB in 2024 and more than 10 million were diagnosed with the disease. Therefore, there is an urgent need to develop new therapeutic and diagnostic strategies to control this major global health challenge.

Mycobacterium tuberculosis is a remarkably successful and unusual pathogen that can survive in the human body for decades. However, we still do not fully understand which nutrients this pathogen can access and use during infection. This project will use a combination of microbiology, genetic, biochemical and analytical techniques to determine the nutrients that M. tuberculosis uses to survive and reveal how pathogen biology is altered when the nutrient transport is disrupted. This builds on our previous work (for example PMID: 40818611, 39144457, 34296047) and will provide new insights into how M. tuberculosis adapts and survives in the human host. By understanding how nutrient utilisation shapes pathogen biology, we have an opportunity to exploit this knowledge to develop new strategies to combat this deadly pathogen.

This exciting interdisciplinary PhD project will be based at the University of Manchester, within the Manchester Institute of Biotechnology and the Michael Smith building. The successful candidate will receive multidisciplinary training across microbiology, biochemical and analytical methods while working within a collaborative research environment with access to world-class facilities and expertise. This provides a unique opportunity to address a global health challenge while developing new approaches to manipulate the biology of an important human pathogen.

Applicants should have, or be about to obtain, at least a 2.1 UK honours degree and ideally hold a master’s level qualification at merit or distinction (or international equivalent) in a relevant subject. Applicants with a strong interest in pathogen biochemistry are encouraged to apply. Research experience in microbiology and analytical methods is desirable.

jobs.description_html:
Mining Mineral Life: Extracting the Energy Transition in Southeast Asia 

Now Recruiting: Fully Funded 4 year PhD Opportunity at NTU Singapore, including fieldwork and conference funding. 

Open to applicants worldwide, this opportunity welcomes candidates from all academic backgrounds, with those holding at least one degree in the humanities especially encouraged to apply. 

The Project

Mining Mineral Life: Extracting the Energy Transition in Southeast Asia examines how mining for energy transition critical minerals is transforming landscapes and livelihoods in Southeast Asia. The project aims to break new empirical and conceptual ground in the understanding of extraction by integrating geoscience, artisanal knowledges, mineral cosmologies, and histories of critical minerals. At the centre of the project is an interrogation of the category of minerality, the distinction between the bio/geo, and new visions of ‘mineral life.’ 

The School of Humanities and NTU Asian School of the Environment at Nanyang Technological University Singapore, invite applications for a fully funded four-year PhD position under Mining Mineral Life: Extracting the Energy Transition in Southeast Asia, led by Principal Investigator Assistant Professor Dr Adam Bobbette. 

Develop your own research project while contributing to a multidisciplinary research programme spanning research, artistic collaborations and public engagement. 

We ask that candidates propose a research project related to critical mineral extraction in Southeast Asia. Proposals might also engage the following: 

  • Political geology: Histories and politics of critical mineral extraction, geological surveys, political geology, and economic geology in Southeast Asia. What is the modern history of critical mineral extraction in Southeast Asia? How have geological surveys shaped the region, including conceptions of state spaces, subterranean realms, and national deep time histories? Is there anything new about energy transition critical mineral extraction or is it an extension of much older imperial dynamics? What is the history of the category of critical minerals in Southeast Asia? 
  • Geo-solidarities: Conceptualising and mapping critical mineral commodity chains, displaced volumes, and landscape change. What forms of geo-solidarity might emerge in critical mineral mining sites? What experimental cartographies can bring together social forces, landscape morphology, and mineral trajectories across deep temporal ranges and contemporary renewable energy technologies. 
  • Mineral cosmologies: Histories of artisanal mining knowledges, techniques, mineral cosmologies, and craft. What is the history and politics of the distinction between the organic and inorganic in Southeast Asia? What is a decolonial minerality? Are minerals alive? Should the rights of nature be extended to geological materials? 

Application deadline: 15 November 2026 

For application details please click Apply button above.

Contact Assistant Professor Adam Bobbette for enquiries: adam.bobbette@ntu.edu.sg

jobs.title: Efficient Physical AI for Real-World Robotics – Funded PhD Studentship
jobs.description_html:
Fully funded PhD supported by Intel

[Covers Home tuition fees and a tax-free stipend. Open only to Home fee-status applicants. Co-supervised by Durham academics and an Intel co-supervisor. State your UK Home eligibility in all communications and applications.]

Physical AI moves beyond analysis to systems that perceive, reason, learn and act in the world, combining foundation models, computer vision, machine learning and robotics. Deployment is limited by dependence on very large models, extensive data, costly compute, cloud inference and large-scale robot data collection, while robots must run continuously under constraints on compute, memory, latency, power and training data.

This PhD will develop capable, efficient, deployable Physical AI for real robots, shaped to the student’s strengths. Topics may include: robot foundation and vision-language-action models; efficient reasoning and planning for long-horizon, real-time tasks; data-efficient learning with fewer demonstrations and less physical interaction; reinforcement and continual learning for adaptation and recovery; world models and predictive learning; multimodal perception; learning from simulation, synthetic data, human video, demonstrations and unstructured experience; compact models (compression, distillation, efficient inference); edge AI on embedded hardware; hybrid intelligence linking reactive control with higher-level reasoning; and the gap between simulation, benchmarks and physical platforms.

Research may cover new algorithms, foundation-model evaluation, learning pipelines, benchmarks, robot integration, or computational and practical limits. Focus may be machine learning, computer vision, reinforcement learning, robotics, embodied AI, efficient inference, or a mix. The aim is capable, efficient, adaptive, reliable, practical systems.

Durham hosts Bede (UK regional supercomputer), a departmental GPU cluster, and labs with LiDAR, RADAR, EEG, drones, cameras, embedded devices and robots, such as the Unitree G1 humanoid, Unitree Go2 quadruped, unmanned ground vehicles and aerial platforms. Intel collaboration targets edge AI, compact models, efficient deployment, intelligent sensing and Physical AI.

Supervisors: Dr Amir Atapour-Abarghouei and Prof Toby Breckon (Durham); Dr Samet Akcay, Principal Engineer, Edge Computing, Intel Client Computing and Physical AI. Expertise spans computer vision, machine learning, robotics, deep reinforcement learning, autonomous systems and efficient AI, with papers in CVPR, ICCV, ECCV, ICML and related venues.

Training covers regular supervision, help building an independent profile, training in writing, publication and presentation, access to GPUs, robots and sensors, and contact with Intel. Style: independent, problem-driven research in a supportive setting.

Durham is a Russell Group university in historic North East England, with a collegiate system, strong community and affordable living costs. Intel’s Edge Computing team brings efficient AI and robotics intelligence to devices outside the cloud.

Applicants need a relevant undergraduate or master’s degree (computer science, AI, engineering, mathematics, physics or related); strong programming; interest in machine learning, computer vision, robotics, embodied AI, foundation models or autonomous systems; motivation to research and publish; ability to link theory, implementation and evaluation; and Durham’s English language requirements. Robotics, reinforcement learning, foundation or vision-language models, efficient inference or embedded AI experience is useful, not essential.

Email CV, transcripts and supporting documents to Dr Amir Atapour-Abarghouei (amir.atapour-abarghouei@durham.ac.uk). Applications are considered on a rolling basis until the post is filled.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Probabilistic Combinatorics
jobs.description_html:
The probabilistic method is a powerful tool which has been especially influential in the fields of combinatorics and computer science. In the context of combinatorics, this method was pioneered by Erdős, who demonstrated that random constructions could often be effective in settings where explicit constructions are infeasible. These ideas, establishing a correspondence between counting and probability, allow for the application of tools from probability theory to combinatorial problems and motivate the study of the typical properties of various combinatorial models, such as the Erdős–Rényi random graph, and discrete random processes. The aim of this project is for the student to develop an understanding of these tools and to apply these techniques to open research problems in the field.

The project will be supervised Dr by Joshua Erde (j.erde@bham.ac.uk).

Entry requirements:

We are looking for an enthusiastic and highly-motivated graduate with

  • A first class degree in Mathematics at the Master’s level (or equivalent);
  • A strong background in combinatorics and discrete probability, or related fields;
  • Good communication skills (oral and written).

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Theory of Topological Quantum Many-Body Systems
jobs.description_html:
This PhD project will explore theoretical questions at the interface of topological physics, quantum many-body systems and quantum simulation with ultracold atoms.

Modern quantum platforms such as ultracold atoms provide unprecedented opportunities to engineer and study new forms of quantum matter in new ways. A central goal of this PhD project will be to understand how topology and quantum geometry interact with interactions, dynamics, nonlinearity and dissipation. The results of this PhD would feed into future optical lattice experiments using ultracold atoms. This project would involve working closely with the EPSRC-funded Programme Grant on "Quantum Advantage in Quantitative Quantum Simulation", which brings together experimental and theoretical researchers across the UK.

The project would suit a student interested in condensed-matter theory, AMO physics or quantum information, who enjoys combining physical intuition, analytical calculations and computational techniques to uncover new quantum phenomena.

Funding notes:

Funding for this position is available on a competitive basis. Please contact Prof. Hannah Price at: H.Price.2@bham.ac.uk for more information.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship in Advanced Numerical Modelling and Predictive Maintenance of Buried Infrastructure
jobs.description_html:
Buried infrastructure underpins essential urban services, yet its deterioration often remains hidden until significant damage or service disruption occurs. Ageing pipelines face increasing pressures from climate change, groundwater fluctuations and nearby construction. Their integrity is closely linked to the surrounding ground. Pipe defects can initiate water leakage and internal soil erosion, leading to loss of support, subsidence and potentially sinkhole formation. Conversely, ground movement can impose additional stresses on pipelines, accelerating damage and leakage. Understanding and predicting this dynamic, coupled deterioration process is essential for timely and effective maintenance.

This PhD project will develop a hybrid physics-based and data-driven framework for assessing the condition and predicting the performance of buried infrastructure, with a focus on water pipelines and associated ground instability. The central research question is how advanced computational models and monitoring data can be combined to identify infrastructure deterioration and predict its progression towards failure.

The project will innovate computational modelling techniques to simulate interactions between structure damage, water leakage, soil erosion and ground deformation. Building on these physical models, the research will investigate AI-assisted surrogate modelling and data assimilation to connect numerical predictions with monitoring observations, potentially including distributed fibre-optic strain measurements, hydraulic data and ground displacement. The anticipated outcome is a validated computational framework linking deterioration mechanisms, monitoring-informed prediction and maintenance decision-making. The project will support earlier intervention, reduced water losses and service disruption, and greater resilience of buried infrastructure to urban ground hazards.

The successful candidate will be based in the School of Engineering at the University of Birmingham, which hosts the National Buried Infrastructure Facility (NBIF, www.birmingham.ac.uk/nbif). They will have access to advice and support from a multidisciplinary team of experts in numerical modelling, AI-solutions, physical sensing for buried infrastructure, alongside documented experimental datasets obtained using a wide range of instrumentation and measurement techniques, including fibre-optic sensing, laser scanning, and force and strain measurements.

This project is expected to start before/in September 2027.

Requirements: The successful candidate will be motivated and enthusiastic about working across disciplines to address challenges in buried infrastructure resilience. Applicants should have:

  • A First- or Upper Second-class Honours degree, or an equivalent qualification, in civil engineering, geotechnical engineering, mechanical engineering, applied mathematics, computer science or a closely related discipline. A relevant master’s degree and/or research or industry experience would be an advantage.
  • Strong analytical and mathematical skills, with an interest in computational mechanics and numerical modelling.
  • Experience in programming or scientific computing using languages such as Python, and C++.
  • Good written and verbal communication skills.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Physics-informed AI for the Thermodynamic Co-design of Emerging Cooling Technologies
jobs.description_html:
Cooling demand is rapidly increasing due to economic development and climate change-induced temperature increase. Vapour compression cycle has been the main technology to satisfy the global cooling demand, from household refrigerators and room air conditioners to industrial size chillers. Their environmental impacts from energy input and refrigerants leakage have pushed the development of alternative cooling technologies, such as sorption-based and solid-state caloric cooling. However, the deployment of these technologies has been hindered by limited cooling capacity, thermodynamic irreversibilities, inefficient heat transfer, and impractical driving forces.

This PhD project will focus on developing a physics-informed artificial intelligence framework for systematic design and optimisation of alternative cooling mechanisms and their corresponding refrigeration cycles. The project will integrate thermodynamic modelling, machine learning, and multi-objective optimisation to identify high potential combinations of cooling mechanisms, refrigeration cycles, and operating conditions. Experimental investigations will validate selected combinations and refined the models. The successful candidate will have the opportunity to allocate and balance the experimental and computational work depending on their background and interests.

At Birmingham, the candidate will join the School of Chemical Engineering which hosts several world-leading cooling-related research centres, including the Centre for Sustainable Cooling and Birmingham Centre for Energy Storage. The candidate will develop a wide range of skills in thermal energy experiments, simulation, optimisation, data analysis, and project management which are applicable to a wide range of future career options.

Applications must be made through the university’s on-line application system via the above 'Apply' button.

Applications will be accepted until 31 January 2027 but the position will be filled as soon as an appropriate candidate is found. For informal enquiries about the project, please contact Dr. Renaldi Renaldi at r.renaldi@bham.ac.uk.

Entry requirements

A good bachelor’s degree (first or upper second-class honours degree) or an MSc degree in Mechanical Engineering, Chemical Engineering, Material Science, Physics, Energy or other relevant disciplines. A strong interest in thermal energy engineering and prior experience in combining computational and experimental work would be beneficial. Candidates should be able to work both independently and collaboratively as part of a research team.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Tandem Catalysts for Selective Acidic CO₂ Electrolysis - PhD (Faculty Funded)
jobs.description_html:
Electrochemical CO₂ conversion offers a promising route to produce fuels and chemicals using renewable electricity. Acidic CO₂ electrolysis has the potential to improve carbon utilisation compared with conventional alkaline systems, but achieving high selectivity and stability remains a major challenge.

This PhD will develop advanced Cu-based and tandem catalysts for selective acidic CO₂ electrolysis, with particular emphasis on multicarbon products such as ethylene.

The research will investigate how catalyst composition, nanostructure, support properties and spatial organisation influence electrolysis performance. Possible approaches include nanostructured Cu catalysts, catalyst confinement within porous supports and tandem architectures that combine complementary catalytic functions.

The student will undertake catalyst synthesis, materials characterisation and electrochemical testing using gas-diffusion electrode and flow-cell systems. The work will evaluate catalyst performance in terms of product selectivity, reaction rate, carbon utilisation and long-term stability.

A central aim will be to identify catalyst designs that maintain strong electrochemical performance under practically relevant operating conditions, linking materials development directly with electrolysis performance.

The project is closely aligned with the Royal Academy of Engineering Research Fellowship led by Dr Mengnan Wang, which is developing scalable acidic CO₂ electrolysers for sustainable chemical manufacturing. Within this wider programme, this PhD will focus specifically on catalyst development and electrochemical performance.

The student will join an interdisciplinary research environment spanning electrocatalysis, electrochemical engineering and advanced materials, with opportunities to engage with academic and industrial collaborators.

Applicants should have, or expect to obtain, a First or Upper Second Class UK Honours degree or equivalent in Chemical Engineering, Chemistry, Materials Science or a related discipline. Previous experience in electrochemistry, catalysis or materials synthesis would be beneficial but is not essential.

This is a fully funded 3-year PhD studentship at the University of Exeter. Both UK and international applicants are eligible. The award will cover tuition fees and provide an annual tax-free stipend of at least £21,805 per year.

jobs.title: PhD Studentship: Developing Treatment Guidance to Support Military Personnel Affected by Deployment-related Psychological Distress
jobs.department: Department of Psychological Medicine, School of Academic Psychiatry, Institute of Psychiatry, Psychology & Neuroscience
jobs.description_html:
We are looking to recruit a PhD candidate who is interested to develop understanding of how mental health causalities can be assessed and triaged during potential future large-scale combat operations (LSCO).

This studentship is funded by a grant from the Ministry of Defence, focussing on large-scale combat operations. The project is delivered against three core research questions, all of which focus on how best to support the Defence Medical Command with preparing for the mental health consequences of deployment to a LSCO:

  1. How can we accurately predict psychiatric casualty rates in a contemporary LSCO?
  2. What preparation or intervention can feasibly be provided at scale within war zones?
  3. How do we identify those likely to recover via early intervention versus those likely to require a longer treatment pathway?

The studentship will focus primarily on the third research question: ‘how do we identify those who are likely to recover via early intervention versus those likely to require a longer treatment pathway?’ Although there is extensive historical literature, there is comparatively little contemporary evidence to guide how clinical decisions about the assessment and triage of mental health casualties should be made in the context of LSCO.

The specific direction of the studentship is flexible, but is proposed to involve using a knowledge mobilisation framework to conduct:

  1. A scoping review of best practices to reduce psychological distress of serving personnel pre-, during, and post-deployment with an emphasis on combat operations.
  2. Qualitative interviews with clinicians, from a range of specialities and with varying lengths of experience, about clinical decision-making when assessing mental health casualties in a combat zone.
  3. A Delphi consensus study (informed by the above and by findings from other work packages within the wider LSCO project) to develop treatment guidance for clinicians to use when assessing mental health casualties in a combat zone.

This studentship will include comprehensive training in relevant research methods and skills, and the possibility of teaching as a Graduate Teaching Assistant.

Essential criteria

  • 2:1 honours (or Overseas equivalent) bachelor’s degree in a relevant subject area (epidemiology, psychology, or a related health field). A 2:2 degree may be considered only alongside a master’s with a Merit or above.
  • Ability to work independently and as part of a team
  • Strong time and personal management skills and ability to work to deadlines

Malaria remains a major global health challenge, with drug resistance threatening the effectiveness of existing treatments. This project will explore a fundamentally different way to kill malaria parasites: harnessing their own protein-degradation machinery to selectively destroy proteins they need to survive. jobs.title: PhD Studentship: The role of icebergs in heat, freshwater and nutrient exchanges in Greenland’s fjords
jobs.description_html:
We have an exciting opportunity to support a 3.5 PhD project as part of the UKRI-funded “Fjords Exchange Heat, Freshwater and Nutrients between the Greenland Ice Sheet and the North Atlantic Ocean (FEISO)” project. The successful candidate will join a growing team investigating Greenland ice-ocean interactions.

Background

Mass loss from the Greenland Ice Sheet has accelerated rapidly, especially at marine-terminating glaciers, which flow into fjords. These fjords are a natural bottleneck between the ice sheet and the ocean, through which warm ocean water and fresh meltwater must transit. The fjords and nearby coastal waters also host productive fisheries that form the backbone of Greenland’s economy. Therefore, fjords are key to understanding Greenland ice-ocean interactions.

This PhD project will investigate how icebergs, which are abundant in Greenland’s fjords, affect the transfer of ocean heat to the ice sheet, the export of freshwater to the ocean and the productivity of Greenland’s fisheries. Icebergs act as mobile heat sinks and localised freshwater sources, which alter fjord circulation and have poorly-constrained impacts on marine-terminating glaciers. Furthermore, iceberg melting releases nutrients and drives localised upwelling, which draws nutrient-rich deep water into sunlit surface waters. This stimulates phytoplankton blooms, sustaining the rich marine ecosystems and local fisheries upon which Greenlandic communities rely. Modelling of icebergs in fjords is in its infancy, with some processes poorly represented or underexplored; therefore, coastal primary production, freshwater export, and up-fjord heat transport may be misrepresented in these models or poorly characterised in our conceptual understanding of these systems.

Objectives

This PhD project will use an ocean circulation model and remote sensing to quantify the impacts of iceberg deterioration on Ilulissat Kangerlua, an iceberg-congested fjord in west Greenland that hosts one of the world’s fastest glaciers and connects to highly productive fisheries. Potential objectives are:
1. Quantify iceberg-induced changes to glacier melt rates: simulate the feedbacks between iceberg melt and fjord circulation to quantify how icebergs have influenced oceanic heat delivery to marine-terminating glaciers over the past three decades.
2. Determine the fate of freshwater from iceberg melt: use tracer experiments to characterise the timing, distribution and modification of iceberg meltwater as it transits and eventually exits fjords.
3. Quantify nutrient upwelling dynamics: examine how changes in iceberg concentration, depth and distribution over the past three decades has affected the primary productivity of Ilulissat Kangerlua and nearby coastal waters.

The successful candidate will have the freedom and support to focus on one or multiple of these objectives, and adapt the research to their interests as the project progresses, within the scope of FEISO.

Novelty and timeliness

Over the past three decades, research into Greenland’s tidewater glaciers has focused on the glacier-ocean interface and the impact of glacial meltwater on fjords. It is only in recent years that icebergs have been recognised as an important component of the glacier-fjord system. Thus, their impacts remain insufficiently understood and may be misrepresented in projections of ice sheet, climate and sea level changes. Recent developments in numerical modelling and remote sensing capability, and increasing availability of in-situ observations, now allow for accurate measurements and simulations of iceberg production, drift, deterioration, and impacts on fjord dynamics. By bridging physical glaciology, oceanography, and marine biogeochemistry, this project will provide vital insights into the behaviour of the Greenland Ice Sheet and its coastal waters.
